name: AsciiImage
description: A picture set in characters, where each cell takes the glyph whose shape fits the edge running through it rather than the one whose brightness matches

notes: Every ASCII renderer ever written does the brightness version: order characters by how much ink they carry, measure the average tone of a cell, look up the glyph at that position. The fault is always the same. A cell sitting on a hard edge averages to a midtone, a midtone glyph is a texture rather than a line, and every contour in the picture turns to mush

So each cell is measured twice. A Sobel pass gives the direction and strength of the edge through it, and where that edge is strong the cell takes a glyph lying along it, quantised to four angles. Only the cells with nothing much going on fall back to the ramp

The glyph lies along the edge, which is the gradient turned a quarter: a gradient points across an edge, not along it. Getting that backwards gives a picture whose every contour is drawn at right angles to itself, and it looks like a weave

The Sobel is taken over neighbouring cells rather than neighbouring pixels, because the question is about the picture at the scale of a cell. Measured at pixel scale a strand of hair fills the kernel and every cell comes back as an edge

`glyphs` is the tone ramp only. The four directional characters are not an option because they are not a palette: each is there because it lies along one of four angles, and a different character in the same slot is a character pointing the wrong way

The glyphs are drawn once into a texture atlas in the element's own monospace face, so the picture is set in the type the page is set in. They are rendered at 64px and minified, because a glyph rasterised straight into a 9px cell is four pixels of aliasing
The 2D canvas that sets the type is used once and never drawn to again. It is not a second live rendering context
Rec. 709 luma rather than a mean of the channels. A straight mean makes red and blue too light, which on a face is the difference between skin and a mask
The picture arrives cell by cell in reading order with a little jitter, so the front is a ragged edge rather than a diagonal line. A teleprinter delivers a character at a time
Recast for paper. The original is green on black, which is a terminal; this is ink on a sheet, which is what a teleprinter actually produced
The stays in the document, hidden. Its alt text is the accessible version of the picture and a page whose script never runs still shows the photograph
Nine samples of the source per pixel, for the Sobel, plus one of the atlas. The nine are the cost of knowing which way the edge runs, and they are the whole item
The atlas is built once per glyph set and per face. Nothing is allocated per frame

The reveal is a comparison against a cell index, so a finished picture costs exactly what an arriving one does. There is nothing to be gained by stopping the loop, and the runtime stops it anyway once the element is off screen

cell.description: Size of one character cell. This is the resolution of the whole thing: at 6 it is a halftone made of letters and the subject is readable, at 20 it is a pattern and the subject is a rumour. Below about 5 the glyphs stop being distinguishable and the shape-aware half stops earning its keep.

glyphs.description: The tone ramp, lightest first, used only where no edge was found. Order it by how much ink each character carries rather than by anything else: this is the one place in the effect where brightness is the right question. The four directional characters are not here on purpose.

paper.description: The sheet. Set this and the ink the other way round and you have the terminal version, which is what everybody else ships and what this was recast away from.

ink.description: The ink. A soft black rather than a true one: a teleprinter ribbon is never quite black and a page of hard black characters on warm paper reads as a screenshot.

contrast.description: How hard the tone is pushed away from the midtone before the ramp is read. A photograph with a narrow range gives a picture made of three characters, and this is what opens it out. It does not affect the edge detection at all.

threshold.description: Edge strength above which a cell takes a directional glyph instead of a tone one, on the scale a Sobel over luminance produces, which tops out near 5.6 for a black-to-white step. The single most important number here, and it was set by looking: at 0.17 almost every cell claims an edge and the picture is a weave of dashes with no tone in it, and by 1.2 only the hardest boundary in the frame still gets one, so the contours go back to mush and you have an ordinary ASCII renderer. 0.7 keeps the horizon, the cliff line and the edge of the fog while leaving the grass and the sea as tone.

shapes.description: Turn the shape-aware half off, leaving an ordinary brightness ramp. It is here to be turned off once, so the difference is a thing you have seen rather than a claim in a file.

reveal.description: Milliseconds for the picture to come in, cell by cell in reading order. A teleprinter is not fast, and the arrival is most of the pleasure: at 300 it is a fade, at 2600 it is something being printed.

hold.description: Milliseconds of blank paper before it starts.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. For a one-shot arrival this should be a time after it has finished, so the whole picture is simply there. The picture is the point; the typing is how it gets in.

instruction: press replay to print it again

credit.what: Choosing the glyph by the shape of the edge in a cell rather than by its average brightness, from a Codrops article on a shape-aware ASCII renderer
credit.author: Codrops

intro:
AsciiImage sets a photograph in characters, where each cell takes the glyph
whose **shape** fits what is in it rather than the one whose brightness matches.

Every ASCII renderer ever written does the brightness version: order a set of
characters by how much ink they carry, measure the average tone of a cell, look
up the glyph at that position. It works, and it always has the same fault. Edges
come out as mush, because the average tone of a cell sitting on a hard edge is a
midtone, and a midtone glyph is a texture rather than a line. Set a face that
way and the jaw disappears.

So each cell here is measured twice. A Sobel pass gives the direction and
strength of whatever edge runs through it, and where that edge is strong enough
the cell takes a glyph that lies along it: a bar for a vertical edge, a slash
for a diagonal, an underscore for a horizontal. Only the cells with nothing much
going on fall back to the tone ramp.

The picture keeps its contours, which is the whole point.

Two details that are easy to get backwards:

**The glyph lies along the edge, not across it.** A gradient points across an
edge. Using the gradient angle directly gives a picture in which every contour
is drawn at right angles to itself, and it reads as a woven texture rather than
as a drawing.

**The Sobel is taken over neighbouring cells, not neighbouring pixels.** The
question is which way the edge in this cell runs, which is a question about the
picture at the scale of a cell. Measured at pixel scale, a strand of grass fills
the kernel and every cell in the frame comes back as an edge.

name: AuroraCurtain
description: The northern lights on a night sky, folded into curtains and lit from the bottom up

notes: Built for a dark ground and declared as one. On warm paper it is a worse aurora for no reason, and the house style is a house style rather than a rule about what may exist

The shape follows the physics rather than a reference photograph. Emission runs along near-vertical magnetic field lines, which is the striation; the electrons stop at an abrupt floor around 100km and thin out upwards over hundreds of kilometres, which is why the bottom edge is sharp and the top has no edge at all

The colour is altitude. Oxygen's green line at 557.7nm low down, its red line at 630nm higher up where collisions are rare enough to let the slower transition happen. Green at the foot running to red at the top, never a hue cycle

Every moving term is a sum of sines whose time coefficients are whole numbers of turns over the period, so the loop closes exactly. A noise field advanced by time never returns to its first frame and the recorder needs it to
Three curtains at different depths, each lower, dimmer and folded on a different scale. Sharing a scale makes them read as one curtain drawn three times
The stars do not twinkle. Scintillation is strongest near the horizon and nearly absent overhead, and faking it evenly costs a per-frame change in every pixel for something nobody looks at
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes
No texture reads and no noise lookups. The whole frame is around twenty sines and two hashes per pixel, which is cheap enough that the cost is the pixel count rather than the shader
The curtain loop is bounded at three and breaks early, so one curtain costs a third of three

sky.description: The night sky behind it. Dark, and not black: a real sky has a colour, and the shoulder that keeps the bright parts from clipping lifts pure black into a flat grey anyway.

low.description: The colour at the foot, which is oxygen's green line at 557.7nm and the brightest thing in the display. Shifting it far from green stops reading as an aurora, because this is the one colour everybody has seen.

high.description: The colour at the top, which is the slower red transition high up where the air is thin enough to let it happen. Magenta rather than pure red is what a camera records and what most people picture.

curtains.description: How many curtains. Each is further away: lower in the frame, dimmer, and folded on a different scale. One is a quiet backdrop, three is a display.

height.description: How far up the frame the light reaches, as a share of its height. It is a falloff rather than a limit, so a curtain has no top edge: it runs out.

fold.description: How hard the curtains fold along their length. At 0 you have flat bands, which is a real thing a quiet aurora does and is also the safest setting behind text.

rays.description: Contrast of the vertical rays. This is the most recognisable thing about an aurora and the first thing to raise if it looks like a gradient.

pitch.description: How fine the rays are, as turns across the frame rather than a count: x spans the aspect ratio, so 40 is roughly a dozen ribs on a wide canvas. Past about 90 they stop resolving on a small panel and read as noise.

brightness.description: Overall strength of the light. A soft shoulder keeps it from clipping, so a high value compresses rather than flaring into a white patch.

stars.description: Stars. They sit under the aurora rather than over it, and they are brighter overhead than near the horizon, because low stars are seen through more air.

horizon.description: Light on the horizon. Nowhere on Earth is the bottom of the sky as dark as the top, and the gradient is most of what stops a flat sky colour looking like a swatch.

grain.description: The sensor noise of a long exposure. Static rather than crawling: film grain that moves is a different effect and a far noisier one.

period.description: Seconds for one full cycle, and the pace control. Long on purpose: a backdrop has to survive being ignored, and an aurora that hurries is a screensaver.

instruction: it drifts on its own
intro:
The northern lights, on a night sky.

This is the first item in the library built for a dark ground rather than for
warm paper, and it declares that in its meta so the site shows it on one. Paper
is the house style here, not a rule about what may exist, and an aurora on paper
would be a worse aurora for no reason.

It is not a rainbow gradient with noise on it, and that is most of why those
read as wallpaper. An aurora is emission, and every part of its shape follows
from that.

**It hangs in vertical rays.** Electrons spiral down the magnetic field lines,
which are near vertical at those latitudes, and light up the gas along the way.
The striation is the single most recognisable thing about an aurora, and an
effect without it is a coloured cloud.

**The bottom edge is sharp and the top is not.** The electrons stop where the
air finally gets thick enough, an abrupt floor at around 100km, and thin out
upwards over hundreds of kilometres. So the foot is a hard line and the top has
no edge at all: it runs out.

**The colour is altitude.** Atomic oxygen gives the green line at 557.7nm low
down, and the red line at 630nm higher up, where collisions are rare enough to
let the slower transition finish. Green at the foot running to red at the top,
never the other way round and never a hue cycle.

**It folds along its length.** You are looking at a sheet edge on, so a fold
reads as a bright rib rather than as a wave passing through.

name: BlockDissolve
description: Content uncovered a block at a time, where the order is chosen so the blocks spread rather than clump

notes: Every wipe is the same effect. Cut the element into cells, give each cell a number saying when its turn comes, uncover the cells whose number has come up. A left-to-right wipe, a clock sweep, rings growing outward and a film dissolve are one mechanism fed four different orders

A shuffle is not an order. At half way through a shuffled wipe there is a patch of cells that arrived together in one corner and a hole the same size in the other, and the eye reads both as a fault in the rendering rather than as a dissolve. It is the same objection as white noise being the wrong noise for a halftone
So each cell is the best of `spread` random candidates, best meaning furthest from every cell already taken. At `spread: 1` that is exactly a shuffle, which is there to be set once

Going further does not help. An exhaustive version, taking the true furthest cell every time, was written first and produces a chequerboard: every tie in a regular grid breaks the same way, the sequence locks onto the lattice, and half coverage is a perfect chequer. That reads as a deliberate pattern, which is the same failure as the clump seen from the other side

Distance is measured on a torus. Without the wrap the cells along the edges have fewer neighbours, so they measure as further from the taken set than they are and the wipe opens with a frame round the outside
Candidates are drawn without replacement. Drawing with replacement means a high `spread` still misses a third of the pool, which quietly caps how spread it can get

`clip-path: path()` on the element itself, one subpath per uncovered block. Nothing is added to the DOM and the content is untouched: it selects, scrolls, translates and reads the whole time, it is simply not all visible yet

`path()` takes user units and rejects percentages. Unlike `polygon()` the geometry cannot follow a resize for free, so it is rebuilt in CSS pixels when the box changes. The first version of the probe for this used percentages, which made the property invalid, silently ignored, and the element came back unclipped looking like a pass

Rows follow from columns and the aspect so the cells come out square. A fixed row count gives tall thin cells on a hero and wide flat ones on a sidebar, and a dissolve made of letterbox slots does not read as a dissolve
Blocks grow from their centres rather than switching on, so the front is blocks blooming rather than blocks appearing. `grow: 0` is the version that looks like a slide transition
No colour in it at all, which is why it declares `either` without hedging. There is nothing to tune against a background because it clips whatever you put it on
Measured at 0.058ms to rebuild a hundred and forty-four subpaths and set the property, including a forced layout. A clip is composited, so the content under it is not repainted

The order is built once per grid, per order and per seed, not per frame. It costs roughly columns squared times rows times spread, which at the default 16 columns is about 120 thousand comparisons and invisible; at 40 columns on a wide element it is nearer 5 million and worth knowing about. It is paid at mount and on resize
The path string is only assigned when it differs from the last one, so a finished wipe sets nothing

order.description: Which order the blocks arrive in, and the only difference between a dissolve, a wipe, a clock sweep and rings growing outward. `scatter` is the dissolve and the one the item is about; the other five are a sort on one number per cell and are each a single line.

columns.description: Blocks across. Rows follow from it and the aspect so the cells come out square. This is the resolution of the whole thing: at 6 it is a slide transition made of panels, at 40 it is close enough to a film dissolve that the blocks stop being the subject. Note that the order costs roughly this squared, so 40 on a wide element is a few million comparisons at mount.

spread.description: Candidates considered per pick, for `scatter`. A dial between two failures rather than a quality setting. At 1 every pick is random, which is a plain shuffle, and it clumps: patches arrive together and holes the same size linger. Taking the true furthest cell every time goes the other way and settles onto the lattice, so half coverage is a chequerboard. Set it to 1 once so the difference is a thing you have seen.

grow.description: How much of its size each block grows through, from its centre. At 0 the blocks arrive at full size, which is the switch and the thing that makes this look like a slide transition. At 1 they come up from nothing, which is softer but loses the blocks. This is how much, not how long: the timing is `overlap`.

overlap.description: How long one block takes, as a share of the whole wipe. It is what gives the front a width: at the default about forty blocks are mid-arrival at any moment, so the edge is made of blocks in flight rather than being a hard boundary. At 0.02 the blocks arrive one at a time and it reads as a counter.

duration.description: Milliseconds from the first block to the last.

hold.description: Milliseconds of stillness before it starts.

seed.description: Seed for the order. The same seed gives the same dissolve, which is what makes the take reproducible. It does nothing to the five geometric orders.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. For a one-shot uncovering this has to be a time after it has finished, so the content is simply there. The content is the point; the dissolve is how it arrives.

instruction: press replay to run it again. set spread to 1 to see what a shuffle does

credit.what: That every wipe is one effect fed a different coverage, a number per cell saying when it goes, from the Shader Effects library's reveals. Their shuffle is a plain shuffle; the spread order here is the answer to what that does
credit.author: Shader Effects Inc.

intro:
BlockDissolve uncovers whatever you mount it on, a block at a time.

The idea underneath it is that **every wipe is the same effect**. Cut the
element into cells, give each cell a number saying when its turn comes, and
uncover the cells whose number has come up. A left-to-right wipe, a clock
sweep, rings growing outward and a film dissolve are one mechanism fed four
different orders. Nothing else about them differs.

That is why `order` is the first option here and the only one that changes what
the thing is. Five of the six orders are a sort on one number per cell and are
a single line each. The sixth, `scatter`, is the dissolve, and it is the one
the item exists for.

name: CardStack
description: A pile of prints being leafed through, where the card changes its stacking order only while it is clear of the pile

notes: The card changes its stacking order only while it is clear of the pile, and that is the difference between this and every version that fades the card out. A card going from front to back has to pass the others, and there is no interpolating between being in front of something and behind it: at some instant the order flips. Done while the card is still over the pile it is visible, as a flicker that reads as a dropped frame; done at the far point of the travel, where nothing overlaps, it cannot be seen at all
The card goes out to the side and back rather than straight through, which is what makes the far point exist. A card that crosses the pile face on has nowhere clear to change order

Nobody squares a pile. The scatter is fixed to the card rather than to the position, so the third card is always the one sitting a degree crooked wherever it happens to be, and the pile keeps its own character as the cards move through it. A pile with an even offset per position is a diagram of a pile
The cards are the author's own markup and are never replaced. They are positioned absolutely over one another, because a pile is a pile and the element keeps the height of one card
destroy() puts every property it set back, including the element's own position
Pure in t: which card is moving and how far through its travel it is are both arithmetic on the clock, and the scatter is a hash of the card's index

A pile seen straight on is one card and a few edges, however much the cards are offset, because they are the same object at the same angle. That is honest and it is also why the scatter and the tilt are worth having: the corners are what tell you there is more than one
One transform per card per frame, composited, plus a z-index and a shadow written only when they change. Four cards is four transforms
The box shadow is the one painted property here. It is written per card and only on change, so a pile at rest writes nothing at all

interval.description: Milliseconds each card spends at the front before it is moved. This sets the length of the whole loop, which is the interval times the number of cards, so four cards at 1800ms is a 7.2 second cycle and that is what the recording has to span.

travel.description: Milliseconds the move itself takes, clamped to the interval so a card cannot still be moving when the next one starts. Half the interval is a good rule: it leaves the pile still for as long as it is moving, which is what makes the movement read as a deliberate act rather than as a carousel.

aside.description: How far aside the card goes, as a share of the pile's width. It has to clear the pile, because the far point of the travel is where the stacking order changes: below about 0.4 the card is still overlapping when it flips, and you can see it happen.

spread.description: How far each card sits from the one beneath. This is what makes it a pile rather than a single card: at 0 the cards are exactly aligned and the whole thing reads as one object until something moves.

shrink.description: How much smaller each card down the pile is drawn. A little perspective, and it should be very little: a pile seen from above has almost none, and anything more reads as a fan of cards rather than a stack.

tilt.description: Degrees of scatter. Nobody squares a pile, and at 0 this looks like a specimen diagram. Fixed per card rather than per position, so a card keeps its own angle as it moves through the pile.

lift.description: How far the moving card lifts as it goes. A hand picks a card up before moving it sideways, and the lift is most of what makes the move read as a hand rather than as a slide.

seed.description: Seed for the scatter. The same seed gives the same pile, so a recording and a live page match card for card.

instruction: the pile deals itself
intro:
CardStack is a pile of prints being leafed through. The top one is lifted, taken
aside, and put at the back, and the pile shuffles up a place.

Two things carry it, and the second is the one every version gets wrong.

**Nobody squares a pile.** Each card sits at a slight angle and a slight offset,
and the scatter is fixed **to the card** rather than to the position. So the
third card is always the one sitting a degree crooked, wherever in the pile it
happens to be, and the pile keeps its own character as the cards move through
it. An even offset per position is a diagram of a pile.

**The card changes its stacking order only while it is clear of the pile.** A
card going from front to back has to pass the others, and there is no
interpolating between being in front of something and behind it: at some instant
the order flips. Do it while the card is still over the pile and you see it, as
a flicker that reads as a dropped frame. Do it at the far point of the travel,
where nothing overlaps, and it cannot be seen at all.

That is why the card goes out to the side and back rather than straight through:
the arc is what makes the far point exist. It is also why every other version of
this fades the card out: fading hides a switch you could simply have made
somewhere invisible.

name: CastShadowScene
description: Matte forms on paper, and one sun making a full circuit of them

notes: three.js must already be a dependency of the project. It is not bundled
A 2048² shadow map is allocated; on a very old integrated GPU drop it to 1024
Falls back to a still frame under prefers-reduced-motion, handled in the runtime
Seven meshes and one ground plane, drawn twice: once for the shadow map, once for the frame
The shadow map is the cost, not the geometry

paper.description: The paper the forms stand on. Match it to your page background or the panel reads as a pasted-in rectangle. `auto` takes it from the page, so the effect adopts whatever it is dropped onto.

stone.description: The forms. Slightly lighter than the paper is what makes them read as objects standing on it rather than holes cut in it. A light-dark() pair picks by the ground it lands on.

accent.description: One form carries colour. This is the obvious place to put your own brand colour. A light-dark() pair picks by the ground it lands on.

elevation.description: How high the sun sits. Low is long dramatic shadows; above about 60 the shadows disappear under the objects and the whole thing goes flat.

softness.description: Shadow edge softness. Zero is a hard midday edge, one is heavy overcast.

shadow.description: How dark the shadows fall on the paper. The paper is never lit. It stays exactly the colour you set, so the shadow is the only thing drawn on it.

zoom.description: How much of the frame the group fills.

tilt.description: Camera height. Zero is eye level with the paper, one looks straight down. Around 0.35 is a table seen from a chair.

period.description: Seconds for one full circuit of the sun. Slow on purpose: this is meant to sit behind a heading, and the thing that pulls a reader off a headline is movement in the corner of their eye, so the shadows should creep rather than sweep. Below about 15 it reads as a time-lapse.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. Pick a sun angle that composes. For those users the still is the whole effect.

instruction: watch the shadows come round
intro:
Sundial is a still life. Seven matte forms stand on paper, lit by one sun that
makes a complete circuit over the loop. The forms never move. The shadows are the
subject: they lengthen, swing round, cross each other, and arrive back exactly
where they started.

It is a real three.js scene. A perspective camera, seven meshes, standard
materials, a directional light with a shadow map, and a dim bounce light standing
in for light coming back off the paper. Not a full-bleed shader pretending to be
three-dimensional.

The paper is never lit. It is the scene background, and the ground plane is a
`ShadowMaterial` that draws nothing but the shadow. A lit plane picks up the sun
at a grazing angle and lands around 85% of its own colour, which on warm paper is
a warm grey. This way the paper comes out the colour you asked for.

The forms sit in the middle and the sun keeps the edges clear, so there is room
for a headline over the top. That is what it is for.

name: ChromeForm
description: A turned metal form rotating in a studio built for it to reflect, with no image files to ship

notes: Most of this item is the room rather than the object. A mirror has no colour and no shading of its own, so chrome in an empty scene looks like grey plastic: there is nothing for it to be a reflection of

The environment is painted into a canvas at runtime and used as an equirectangular map, so nothing is shipped: no HDR, no cube faces, no image files at all. A dark surround, a brighter floor and a few soft strip lights, which is what a photographer would put round something shiny

The strips are what say metal. A gradient alone gives a smooth tonal wash that still reads as plastic; what reads as polished is a hard edge between light and dark sliding across a curve. The horizon step in the surround does the same job round the waist

Lamps are spaced on an irrational step. Evenly spaced lamps put evenly spaced highlights round the object, and evenly spaced highlights read as a pattern printed on it rather than as a room it is standing in

Prefiltered through PMREM rather than used raw, because otherwise roughness does nothing but darken: a raw map is sampled at one level however rough the surface claims to be, and the blurred levels are what a rough surface needs

A lathe, not a torus knot. A knot is what every WebGL demo reaches for and says nothing about anything; a revolved profile is how a metal object of this kind is actually made, it gives the long uninterrupted curves that show a reflection off best, and the profile is three numbers rather than a model file

ACES tone mapping, which is unusual here and is the one case that needs it. A mirror genuinely produces values above one, and clipping a strip light gives a flat white shape with a hard edge where the roll-off should be
Geometry and environment are rebuilt only when their inputs change, because update() can be called on every frame by a framework re-render and PMREM has no business running at 60Hz

Built for a dark ground and declared as one. The room is dark so that the strips read as light; on paper the background would have to be pale, and a pale fill behind a dark-roomed mirror looks like a hole cut in the page
One lathe mesh of 128 segments and one prefiltered environment, both rebuilt only when their inputs change. The per-frame work is a single draw of about twelve thousand triangles
Measured with `pnpm budget` at 1280 by 720: 1.2ms for a draw and a forced flush, against TerrainRelief at 1.80 on the same run

0.035 mean absolute change per frame on a 0 to 255 scale, worst 0.042, against TerrainRelief at 0.450 and DustMotes at 0.016. One of the quietest items here: a single object turning slowly against a flat fill changes very few pixels, which is what a backdrop wants
PMREM runs once per change of `studio` or `lamps`, not per frame. Animating either of those at 60Hz would be the one way to make this item expensive

background.description: The page behind the object. Nothing reflects it, so it is only a fill, but it wants to be close to the dark end of the room or the object reads as cut out and pasted on.

tint.description: The metal. Near white is chrome; warm it towards #e8c89a for brass and cool it for steel. On a fully metallic surface this multiplies the reflection rather than adding a colour of its own, which is why a saturated one looks like coloured glass instead of metal.

studio.description: The strip lights, and therefore the bright part of every reflection. Slightly warm by default, because a neutral white room makes the metal read as grey.

roughness.description: How polished. At 0 it is a mirror with the room sharp in it; by about 0.4 the strips have softened into a sheen and it reads as brushed. Past about 0.6 there is nothing left to reflect and it goes to grey.

lamps.description: Strip lights round the room. Two is a photographer's key and fill. More than four and the object has highlights everywhere, which flattens it: the dark between the strips is what gives the form its shape.

height.description: Height of the form in scene units, where the camera frames about four.

waist.description: How far the middle pulls in, as a share of girth. At 0 it is a plain capped barrel. The waist is what gives the reflection somewhere to bend sharply, which is the most metal-looking thing on the object.

tilt.description: Degrees the axis leans. A little off vertical is the difference between an object and a diagram of one.

period.description: Seconds for one full turn. Exactly one turn, so the loop closes with no join.

instruction: it turns on its own
intro:
ChromeForm is a turned metal form, rotating, with a studio built for it to
reflect.

Most of this item is not the object. It is the room.

A mirror has no colour and no shading of its own: everything you see on a
chrome object is somewhere else in the room. That is why chrome rendered in an
empty scene looks like grey plastic, and it is the one thing that goes wrong
with this kind of effect. So the environment is painted into a canvas at
runtime and used as an equirectangular map. Nothing is shipped: no HDR file, no
cube faces, no images at all.

name: CircularText
description: Type set round a ring that closes exactly, because the string is fitted to the circumference rather than placed letter by letter

notes: An SVG textPath, which is the thing in the platform built for this, rather than a rotation and a translation per character. Placing letters by hand loses kerning, because the browser is handed ten one-character strings and kerning happens between characters in a string, and it never closes the ring, because the spacing comes from a guess at the arc each letter subtends

The fit is the whole trick: the string is given a textLength equal to the circumference and lengthAdjust of spacing, so the browser opens or closes the spaces until it fits exactly. The ring closes at any radius, in any face, with any string, and there is no number to tune
spacing rather than spacingAndGlyphs. A fit that stretches the letterforms has changed the typeface, which is the one thing a typesetter may not do. The option to do it anyway is there and it is off
The circle is drawn as two arcs. A single arc of 360 degrees is degenerate, its start and end points coincide, and the renderer has no way to know which way round to go, so it draws nothing
Letters hang inside the ring by reversing the path rather than by flipping the text: the baseline side follows the direction of travel, so the letters turn over without being touched
The turn is one transform on one group. Animating startOffset instead re-lays out the text sixty times a second to produce a picture that is a rotation of the one before it
The path gets an id unique to the instance. Two rings on a page sharing a path id is the one failure here that nothing in the markup hints at: the second textPath silently uses the first one's circle
The face, weight and tracking are inherited from the element. A text effect that picks its own typeface is a graphic
destroy() puts the original text back, leaving the element as it was found
One attribute write per frame, and it is a rotation. The text is laid out once, when an option that affects the shape changes, and never per frame
The cheapest item in the library. A ring of forty characters turning for a minute does the same work as one that is standing still

radius.description: Radius of the ring, as a share of the box. 0.5 puts the baseline on the very edge, which leaves the ascenders outside it: the overflow is visible rather than clipped, on purpose, but 0.38 is the largest that keeps everything inside a square box.

repeat.description: How many times the text goes round. Because the string is fitted to the circumference, this is really a density control: one copy of a short phrase is set very wide, four copies of it are set tight. Pick the one that gives the tracking you want.

separator.description: What sits between one copy and the next. A middle dot is the one every seal and every bottle label uses, for the good reason that it reads at any size and has no direction to it. It is also what tells a reader the ring repeats rather than running on.

size.description: Letter height, as a share of the radius, so the ring scales as one object. It does not affect the fit at all: the string fills the circumference whatever size the letters are, and this only decides how heavy the ring looks.

spin.description: Degrees the ring turns over one period. Negative turns it the other way. A whole number of degrees over the period, so the loop closes exactly; 360 is one unhurried revolution.

inside.description: Hang the letters inside the ring rather than standing them on it. This is the half of a seal that reads along the bottom, and it is done by reversing the path rather than by flipping the text, so the letters keep their own shapes.

distort.description: Let the fit stretch the letterforms as well as the spaces. Off, and it should stay off: it is here so that the choice is visible rather than hidden. Turn it on once to see what a stretched face looks like, then turn it off.

period.description: Seconds for one revolution. Long: a ring is a mark, not an animation, and a seal turning fast enough to notice is a loading spinner. Twenty-four seconds is fifteen degrees a second, which is about the slowest a turn can be and still read as turning.

instruction: it turns on its own
intro:
CircularText sets type round a ring and turns it slowly. A roundel, a seal, the
stamp on a bottle of something.

Nearly every version of this on the web places each character by hand, with a
rotation and a translation per letter, and it is wrong in two ways that are hard
to unsee once you know about them.

The letters are positioned but never **fitted**, so the spacing comes from a
guess at the arc each one subtends and the ring never quite closes. There is
always a gap, or an overlap, at the join.

And each letter is rotated as a rigid block, so nothing **kerns**. The browser
has been handed ten separate one-character strings, and kerning happens between
characters in a string.

This uses an SVG `textPath`, which is the thing in the platform built for
exactly this, and gets both back for free. The text is laid out as text, so it
kerns and it ligates. And it is given a `textLength` equal to the circumference
with `lengthAdjust="spacing"`, so the browser fits the string to the ring by
opening or closing the spaces and never by distorting the letterforms.

The ring closes exactly, at any radius, in any face, with any string. There is
no number to tune.

name: ClickSpark
description: A burst of sparks where you click, drawn as streaks that shorten as they slow

notes: Each spark is drawn as a streak whose length is its current speed, which is what a short exposure of something hot and moving looks like. The streaks shorten on their own as the sparks slow, with nothing extra to animate, and it is the single difference between this and a particle demo

The sparks slow down. A spark meets air, so the distance is the integral of a decaying speed rather than speed times time. Linear motion outwards is the giveaway of every version of this: the burst expands like a diagram of an explosion instead of like one
A little gravity, so the burst is not symmetrical. Not enough to read as falling, just enough that it is not a snowflake

A fixed pool of elements, built once and reused. Bursts create and destroy nothing: a click takes the oldest slot, so forty clicks in a row cost exactly what four do. That matters because clicking it repeatedly is the first thing anybody does

The element keeps its own content. The streaks go in a layer over the top with pointer-events none, and the press is listened for on the element itself, so a button inside stays clickable and the feedback belongs to the thing that was pressed

Scripted presses and real ones are the same kind of event and go in the same list. The scripted ones are rebuilt from the options each frame rather than remembered, which is what keeps a scripted take pure in t: seeking backwards un-fires them
destroy() removes the layer and the listener and puts the element's position back
count times bursts elements, written every frame while anything is in the air and left alone when nothing is. At the defaults that is 44 elements, each one a composited transform and an opacity
No canvas, no WebGL context and no allocation during a burst. The arithmetic is two exponentials per spark

count.description: Streaks in one burst. An odd number is better than an even one: an even fan has a streak opposite every other streak, which the eye reads as a cross.

bursts.description: How many bursts can be in the air at once. The newest win, so clicking faster than this does not cost more, it just drops the oldest burst early. Raising it raises the element count by the same factor.

colour.description: The spark. One colour, not a gradient and not a palette: a palette of sparks is confetti. If it has to work on both grounds, pick something that is neither nearly white nor nearly black.

speed.description: How fast a spark leaves, as a share of the shorter side of the element per second. Relative rather than in pixels, so the same burst looks right on a small button and on a full-page panel.

drag.description: Seconds for a spark to lose most of its speed to the air. Short, and it is what makes the burst read as thrown rather than as expanding: the sparks go a long way in the first fifth of a second and then barely move.

gravity.description: How far the burst droops, as a share of the shorter side per second. At 0 the burst is perfectly symmetrical, which reads as a snowflake. It should be small enough that nobody would name it as falling.

life.description: Seconds a spark lasts. This is feedback for a click, so it has to be over before the next thing happens: much past a second it stops being an acknowledgement and starts being an animation somebody has to wait out.

streak.description: How long a streak is, given as the seconds of travel it represents, so it is literally a shutter speed. At 0 the sparks are dots and the effect is confetti; long, and they are comet trails.

thickness.description: Thickness of a streak, in pixels rather than relative, because a hairline is a hairline at any size and a thick spark at small sizes is a blob.

scatter.description: How uneven the burst is. At 0 it is a perfect star, evenly spaced and all one length, which no two things striking each other have ever produced.

seed.description: Seed for the scatter. Every burst already differs from the last, because the burst's own number goes into the hash; this moves the whole series, so two of these on one page are not twins.

instruction: click the sheet
intro:
ClickSpark throws a burst of sparks where you click. It is the cheapest piece of
feedback there is and it is genuinely useful, which is why everybody ships one
and why most of them look like confetti.

Three things make a spark read as a spark rather than as a dot moving.

**It is a streak, not a point, and the streak is as long as the spark is fast.**
That is what a short exposure of something hot and moving looks like, and it is
the single difference between this and a particle demo. The streaks shorten on
their own as the sparks slow down, with nothing extra to animate: the length is
the speed.

**It slows down.** A spark meets air, so the distance travelled is the integral
of a decaying speed rather than speed times time. Linear motion outwards is the
giveaway of every other version: the burst expands like a diagram of an
explosion instead of like one.

**It falls, a little.** Not enough to read as gravity. Just enough that the
burst is not symmetrical, because a symmetrical burst is a snowflake.

name: CountUpNumber
description: A number counting up to the one already written in the element

notes: No canvas and no WebGL. It reads the number already in the element and counts up to it
Formatting goes through Intl.NumberFormat, so grouping and the decimal mark follow the locale rather than a hand-rolled separator
The finished figure stays in the accessibility tree as one string, because a screen reader on a live-updating number reads every value it passes
There is no target option. The number lives in the element, which is what makes the figure correct before any script runs and correct forever if none does
One Intl.NumberFormat and one textContent write per frame
Text changes cause layout. Give the element a tabular-nums font or a fixed width or the line will jitter as digits change

from.description: Where the count starts. Counting down works: set it above the target.

duration.description: Milliseconds from start to finish. Under a second reads as a flicker rather than a count. Over three and people have stopped watching.

decimals.description: Decimal places. Left at 0 it follows the element's own text, so 12.50 keeps its two places.

locale.description: BCP 47 locale for grouping and the decimal mark, for example en-GB or de-DE. Empty follows the browser, which is usually right.

prefix.description: Text before the number. Keep currency symbols here rather than in the element's text, so the parser sees a clean figure.

suffix.description: Text after the number, for a percent sign or a unit.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. For a count this should be a time after it has finished, so the final figure simply appears.

instruction: press replay to count it again
intro:
Tally counts a number up to the one already written in the element. No canvas, no
WebGL, no npm dependency.

It reads the target from the text content, and there is no option to override
that. The real figure is therefore in the HTML before any JavaScript runs, stays
there if none ever does, and is what a search engine indexes. A counter that
renders `0` until hydration is a counter that is wrong most of the time.

Formatting goes through `Intl.NumberFormat`. That is the part most counters get
wrong: 1,284 in Britain is 1.284 in Germany, and a hand-rolled thousands
separator is wrong in about half the world. Tally also parses both conventions on
the way in, so `1.284,50` and `1,284.50` both mean the same thing to it.

`destroy()` puts the original text back.

name: CrosshairCursor
description: A viewfinder that follows the pointer and squares up around anything you can press

notes: The part worth having is the lock: when the reticle passes over something you can press, the brackets leave the cursor and square up around that element. Without it this is two divs tracking a mouse. Nothing locks on to empty space

What counts as a target is a CSS selector rather than a guess at what is clickable. Sniffing gets it wrong in both directions: it misses the div somebody wired a handler to, and it locks on to every link in a paragraph of running text

The lock comes from a hit test at the pointer rather than from a listener for entering an element. A scripted path moves no real pointer and fires no events, so an effect that locked on only for a live cursor would record as a reticle that never finds anything
The hit test is skipped while the pointer is still. It flushes layout, and the answer cannot have changed if nothing moved
The brackets take a target faster than the crosshair follows the hand. A reticle that drifts lazily into place has not locked on to anything: the snap is the feedback
Four corner brackets rather than a box, because a box round a button is a selection and a bracket at each corner is a sight. Each is the same two borders turned a quarter further round
Like every pointer effect here it eases against its own last frame, so it is deliberately not pure in t, and the recorder drives it from the scripted path in this file

The element keeps its own content: the reticle is drawn in a layer over the top that the pointer cannot touch. Set `cursor: none` on the element yourself if you want the real one hidden, which is a decision about the page rather than about the effect
Six elements, all composited transforms. Nothing is created or destroyed after mount
One hit test and two rects per frame in which the pointer moved, and none at all in a frame where it did not

colour.description: The lines and the brackets. One colour: a reticle is an instrument, and an instrument is drawn in one ink.

thickness.description: Thickness of a hairline. 1 is right, and anything above about 2 stops being a sight and starts being a frame. In pixels rather than relative, because a hairline is a hairline at any size.

size.description: Half-width of the reticle when it is not locked on to anything. Small, so that locking on is a visible change: a free reticle the size of a button has nowhere to go when it finds one.

corner.description: Length of a bracket's arms. Fixed rather than a share of the box it is framing, which is what keeps a bracket round a wide button from turning into a box round it.

padding.description: Space left around a locked target. At 0 the brackets sit exactly on the element's edge, which reads as a border rather than as a sight trained on it.

ease.description: How fast the crosshair follows the hand, per frame. At 1 it is welded to the pointer, which is the same as not having an effect. Low enough to have weight, high enough that it is never somewhere the hand has left.

snap.description: How fast the brackets take a target, per frame. Higher than the ease on purpose. This is the one number that decides whether the effect reads as locking on or as catching up.

target.description: What the brackets will lock on to, as a CSS selector. The data attribute is there so you can nominate anything else without changing the selector: put it on the card, the image, the row.

lines.description: Draw the long hairlines as well as the brackets. Off leaves the brackets alone, which is quieter and better over text: the lines cross everything on the page, and over a paragraph that is a strikethrough following the cursor.

instruction: move the pointer over the buttons
intro:
CrosshairCursor draws a pair of hairlines across a panel and four corner
brackets where they meet, following the pointer. A viewfinder rather than a
cursor.

The part that makes it worth building, rather than two divs tracking a mouse, is
what happens when it passes over something you can press: the brackets leave the
cursor and square up around that element instead. It stops being a decoration on
the pointer and becomes a statement about the page, which is the whole idea of a
reticle. Nothing locks on to empty space.

Three decisions worth knowing about.

**What counts as a target is a CSS selector, not a guess.** Anything that sniffs
for clickability gets it wrong in both directions: it misses the div somebody
wired a handler to, and it locks on to every link in a paragraph of running
text.

**The lock comes from a hit test at the pointer, not from a listener.** A
scripted path moves no real pointer and fires no events, so an effect that
locked on only for a live cursor would record as a reticle that never finds
anything. The test is skipped while the pointer is still, because it flushes
layout and the answer cannot have changed.

**The brackets take a target faster than the crosshair follows the hand.** A
reticle that drifts lazily into place has not locked on to anything. The snap is
the feedback.

name: CrtScreen
description: A picture shown on a tube rather than on a panel: the glass bows, the phosphors sit in columns and the beam overshoots

notes: Scanlines drawn over a flat image read as an image with stripes on it. The thing that makes a picture read as a cathode ray tube is a short list that has to be there together, and most of it is not the scanlines

The glass is curved. The picture bows outward, straight lines near the edge bend and the corners pull in. Without this nothing else helps: a rectangle with stripes is a rectangle. The bezel is whatever falls outside the bent picture, which is why it is in the shader rather than in CSS

The phosphors are in columns. A tube has an aperture grille, red green and blue side by side, which is why a white area in a photograph of a CRT is never white up close. The scanlines are the rows and the grille is the columns, and it is the columns that stop the rows reading as a venetian blind
The grille is measured in device pixels rather than CSS ones. It is a physical thing on the glass, so it should get finer on a denser display rather than staying the same size in points

The grille is lifted towards white rather than multiplied straight, and by a long way. Multiplied in at full strength it sends two thirds of every cell to black, and at three device pixels a cell is below the size at which a stripe can be drawn cleanly, so on a page scaling the canvas what reaches the eye is coloured noise rather than a grille. `mask` is that lift, and at 1 you get the macro view

The beam overshoots, so a bright area bleeds into its neighbours. Three taps across the grille, not a blur: the grille is about to throw away most of the horizontal detail anyway, so a wider and more expensive kernel buys nothing visible

The channels do not land on each other. Red and blue are pulled either side of green along the radius, by an amount that grows towards the corners, because that is where the deflection coils are working hardest
The scanlines are counted down the glass rather than measured in the picture, so they stay put when the image changes. Fixed to the screen, which is what they are
Only the rolling bar moves. Animating the scanlines or the grille turns the whole thing into a pattern sliding over a photograph, which is the usual mistake
The stays in the document, hidden. Its alt text is the accessible version of the picture and a page whose script never runs still shows the photograph
Five samples of the source per pixel: three for the convergence split and two for the overshoot. Everything else is arithmetic on the result
Nothing is allocated per frame and the texture is uploaded once
The bar is the only thing that moves, so the item is drawing a near-identical frame most of the time. The runtime stops the loop once the element is off screen, which is where the saving is

curve.description: How much the glass bows the picture. The one that does the most work: at 0 you have a flat image with stripes on it and nothing below will rescue it, and by 0.35 it is a fish-eye rather than a tube. 0.12 is about a late consumer set, where the curve is obvious at the corners and unremarkable in the middle.

grille.description: Width of one phosphor cell in device pixels, so three subpixels fit across it. 0 turns the grille off, which is worth doing once to see how much of the effect is the columns rather than the rows. This is the pitch; `mask` is how strongly it shows. Above about 6 the stripes stop being a texture and become the subject.

mask.description: How strongly the grille shows, from a tint over the picture to the macro view. At 1 the stripes are drawn at full strength, which sends two thirds of every cell to black; at three device pixels a cell is below the size at which a stripe can be drawn cleanly, so on a page that is scaling the canvas what reaches the eye is not a grille but coloured noise. 0.55 is what a tube looks like from the sofa. Set it to 1 once and look at it an inch from the screen.

scanline.description: How dark the gaps between rows go. The number everybody reaches for first and the one that matters least: past about 0.6 the picture is half black and you are looking at a blind.

scanCount.description: How many lines down the glass. This is a count of lines on a screen, not a frequency in the picture, so it stays put when the image changes. Broadcast was 576 visible lines in Europe and 480 in America; 200 is well under either on purpose, because at a real line count on a dense display the rows fall below a pixel and alias into a moire.

bloom.description: How far a bright area bleeds into its neighbours. Only the parts of the picture above a threshold spill, which is why this reads as a beam overshooting rather than as the whole image going soft.

converge.description: How far red and blue miss each other at the corners, in roughly thousandths of the frame. Small numbers only. Convergence error is something you notice on white type at the edge of the screen and nowhere else, and a set this badly out would have gone back to the shop.

vignette.description: How dim the edges of the tube go. It is doing two jobs: a tube really is dimmer at the edges, and it also hides the corners where the curvature is working hardest and the picture is most stretched.

roll.description: How strongly the bar rolling down the glass shows. 0 removes it and makes the whole item a still, which is the right setting behind text. Keep it low: this is a set very slightly out of step with the mains, not a set that is broken.

brightness.description: Applied before the grille and the scanlines take their share, which is why it sits above 1. The rows and the columns together remove roughly a quarter of the light at the default mask, so a picture passed through at 1.0 comes out a little darker than it went in. Raise it with `mask`, not on its own.

contrast.description: Pushed away from the midtone before the grille, for the same reason as brightness. A tube crushes its shadows, and a little of this is what separates the lit parts of the picture from the glow the grille leaves in the black.

tint.description: The cast of the tube, multiplied over the picture. Warm on purpose: a phosphor is not neutral, and a tube that renders white as white reads as a flat panel doing an impression. Cool it towards #ddeeff for a monitor rather than a television.

bezel.description: Whatever falls outside the curved glass. Near-black rather than black, so it sits against the page instead of punching a hole in it. If it reads as a visible frame, the curve is too high rather than this being too light.

period.description: Seconds for one pass of the bar down the glass. The loop closes exactly on it, so the last frame is the first frame. Longer is calmer and almost always better: at 2 it is a strobe.

maxDpr.description: Device pixel ratio ceiling. The grille is measured in device pixels, so this changes how fine the stripes are as well as what it costs to draw them.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. Anything works: the bar is the only thing that moves, and the tube is the point.

instruction: the bar is the only thing moving. turn curve to 0 to see how much of this is the glass

credit.what: The parameter set for a CRT filter, from the Shader Effects library. Curvature is not in theirs and is added here because it is the one that matters most
credit.author: Shader Effects Inc.

intro:
CrtScreen puts a picture on a tube instead of on a panel.

Almost every version of this is scanlines: a dark stripe every other row, drawn
over the image, done. It never works, and the reason is easy to state. A flat
rectangle with horizontal stripes on it is a flat rectangle with horizontal
stripes on it. Nothing about stripes says cathode ray tube.

What says cathode ray tube is a short list of things that have to be there
together, and most of them are not the scanlines.

**The glass is curved.** The picture bows outward, straight lines near the edges
bend, and the corners pull in. This is the one that does the work. Set `curve`
to 0 and every other setting here stops helping; set it to 0.12 and the item is
most of the way there before the grille has drawn a single stripe.

**The phosphors are in columns.** A tube has an aperture grille: red, green and
blue stripes side by side, which is why a white area in a photograph of a CRT is
never white when you get close to it. The scanlines are the rows. The grille is
the columns. It is the columns that stop the rows reading as a venetian blind,
and you can check that by setting `grille: 0` and watching the thing collapse
back into an image with stripes on it.

**The beam overshoots.** A bright area bleeds into what is next to it, because
the electron beam does not stop where the signal does.

**The channels do not land on each other.** Convergence is never perfect, so red
and blue sit a fraction either side of green, and the error grows towards the
corners because that is where the deflection coils are working hardest.

**The tube is dim at the edges, and a bar rolls down it**, from the signal and
the mains being very slightly out of step.

The bezel is drawn in the shader rather than in CSS, because the bezel is
defined as whatever falls outside the bent picture. A CSS frame cannot know
where that is.

name: DecodeText
description: Text resolving out of a run of cipher glyphs, one character at a time, without the line moving while it does

notes: No canvas and no WebGL. It splits the text already in the element and swaps the characters that have not landed yet

Pure in t. The usual way to write this is Math.random on a timer, which cannot be seeked, cannot be recorded, and shows something different every time anybody looks at it. The glyph at each position is a hash of the position, the seed and the frame number, so the same t always gives the same frame

The glyphs change on their own cadence rather than once per frame. A per-frame swap is a grey blur at 120Hz and a legible stream at 30, which means the effect would look like a different effect depending on the monitor

Each character is held in a box the width of the letter it will become, so a line decoding in the middle of a page does not push the page about. Turn `steady` off for monospace, where every box is the same width anyway

Whitespace and punctuation are left alone. They carry the shape of the sentence, and scrambling the spaces turns text being decoded into a block of noise. It is also what keeps the word wrapping intact
The original string stays in the accessibility tree as one label, so a screen reader reads the sentence rather than a live stream of junk
destroy() puts the original text back, leaving the element as it was found

One text swap per unlanded character per cadence tick, and nothing at all once a character has landed. The comparison before each write matters: setting textContent every frame on a paragraph is a layout invalidation per character per frame for a string that is usually the one already there
Widths are measured once, again when the webfont arrives, and again on resize. Never per frame

glyphs.description: The characters it cycles through before each letter lands. Keep them the same case and roughly the same weight as the text, or the line flickers between dark and light as it runs. Katakana is the one everybody reaches for and the one that dates the effect hardest.

order.description: The order the characters land in. Forward reads as something being typed or decoded. Random reads as something settling, and is the better one for a paragraph, where a left to right sweep takes long enough to watch.

stagger.description: Milliseconds between one character landing and the next. This is the control that sets the length of the whole run, because the last character lands at hold plus stagger times the number of characters. Short text can afford to be slow; a paragraph at 45ms is a run most of a minute long.

hold.description: Milliseconds of cipher before the first character lands. A short hold is what makes it read as text arriving from somewhere rather than as text already there and merely untidy.

rate.description: Glyph changes per second, and a cadence rather than a frame rate: everything still running changes on the same tick, which is what makes the line read as one mechanism rather than a row of independent ones. Past about 30 the characters stop being readable and the whole thing greys out.

dim.description: How much paler an unlanded glyph is than the settled text. The reason to have it at all is that it separates the two states by more than the letters themselves do, so the text reads as arriving rather than as correcting itself.

steady.description: Hold each character in a box the width of the letter it will become. On for anything set in a proportional face, where an I becoming a W is enough to shift the rest of the line. Off for monospace, where the boxes are all the same width and measuring them is work for nothing.

seed.description: Seed for the glyphs and for the random order. The same seed always gives the same run, so a recorded video and a live page match character for character.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. For a one-shot reveal this should be a time after the run has finished, so the text simply appears.

instruction: press replay to set it again
intro:
DecodeText resolves text out of a run of substitute glyphs, one character at a time.
It is the effect on the hover of every studio nav bar, and on a good number of
the headlines that win awards for being difficult to read.

It takes an element that already contains text, splits it into characters, and
swaps the ones that have not landed yet. There is no canvas, no WebGL and no npm
dependency.

Three things it does that the version written in an afternoon does not.

It is pure in `t`. The obvious implementation calls `Math.random()` on a timer
and mutates as it goes, which cannot be seeked, cannot be recorded, and shows
something different every time anybody looks at it. Here the glyph at each
position is a hash of the position, the seed and the frame number, so the same
`t` always gives the same frame.

The glyphs change on their own cadence rather than once per display frame. At
120Hz a per-frame swap is a grey blur with no characters in it; at 30 it reads as
text being typed by something in a hurry. Fixing the cadence means the effect
looks the same on a 60Hz laptop, on a 144Hz monitor, and in a recording of
either.

Nothing moves. Each character is held in a box the width of the letter it will
become, and the substitutes are chosen from the glyphs that fit that box, so a
line decoding in the middle of a page neither pushes the page about nor collides
with itself while it runs.

`destroy()` puts the original text back. The element is left as it was found.

name: DepthPointCloud
description: A photograph taken apart into points and pushed into depth by its own brightness

notes: There is no depth map, and the item does not pretend otherwise. It reads luminance and treats it as height, which is wrong about the world and right about photographs: a photographer lights the subject and lets the ground fall away, so in most pictures the bright parts really are nearer. A bright sky or a dark subject breaks it, and `relief` is how much you are willing to claim

Rec. 709 luminance rather than the average of the channels. The eye is far more sensitive to green than to blue, and an average puts a blue sky and a green field at the same height when nobody sees them that way

Every point keeps the colour of the pixel it came from, which is what keeps the picture readable as it comes apart. A point cloud in one colour is an abstract, and an abstract is a much weaker thing than a photograph you can still recognise

The picture is read by drawing it into a small canvas at grid resolution and reading that back, so every cell is a proper average. Picking every nth pixel of the full-size image aliases badly, and a photograph is nothing but detail
The wander is in the vertex shader. Twenty thousand points moved on the CPU is twenty thousand vectors uploaded every frame; moved on the GPU it is one uniform, and the positions never change
Each point carries a phase, so the cloud does not travel as a sheet, and the displacement is a sine of whole turns per period, so every point is exactly where it started when the loop comes round
Point size falls off with distance. Without that the far points are as large as the near ones and the whole thing flattens into a texture, which is the usual way this kind of effect fails
Points are round, cut from the square the hardware gives you. Square points read as a screen door laid over the picture: the grid becomes the subject
The cloud turns a little either side of square-on rather than rotating. A point cloud seen edge-on is a line and a photograph seen from behind is nothing, so the useful range is small
Built for a dark ground and declared as one. The points are the picture's own colours against the fill, and on paper the pale half of the photograph disappears into the page

The may not have decoded when the effect mounts, so the cloud is built on the first frame where the picture is readable rather than once at setup. A cross-origin image taints the canvas and cannot be read back at all, in which case nothing is drawn

The phase hash is a sine hash of the two grid coordinates, not the index times a constant. Walking the index through a modulus steps through phases in a regular cycle, and since the index runs along each row that cycle lines up with the grid: the first version drew visible vertical stripes across the whole cloud, which is the grid announcing itself

The default density is as much about the codec as about the picture. A field of tiny high-contrast dots is the worst case a video encoder can be given: at 240 across, the take came out at 57MB against a 3500kB budget, which is sixteen times over and not a thing crf can rescue. Fewer and slightly larger points compress enormously better and, as the recipe already said, read better at card size, so the coarsening was owed anyway
About twenty-two thousand points at the default density, drawn in one call, with the movement done in the vertex shader so nothing is uploaded per frame

Measured with `pnpm budget` at 1280 by 720: 0.8ms for a draw and a forced flush, which is the cheapest of the four items added with it. Points are cheap; it is the per-pixel shaders elsewhere that cost

0.399 mean absolute change per frame on a 0 to 255 scale, worst 0.496, against MetaballField at 0.360 and WaterCaustics at 0.222. A field of small bright dots is the hardest case for that measurement, because any movement at all switches whole pixels between a dot and the background rather than shading them. `drift` and `spin` are the two dials and both were brought down twice before this: at drift 0.035 it measured 1.485, which is past the point where a backdrop is something happening
Cost is the square of `density`. The default is already past the point where more points stop making the picture more legible

background.description: Behind the cloud. Dark, because the points carry the photograph's own colours and a pale fill swallows the pale half of it.

relief.description: How far the brightest points stand off the darkest, in scene units where the picture is two wide. This is the claim the item is making about the photograph, and it is a claim: at 0 it is a flat plane of points, and past about 2.5 the bright areas tear away from everything else.

density.description: Points across the picture. The square of this, near enough, is the point count, so it is the whole cost. Below about 100 the picture stops being recognisable, which is the thing worth keeping.

size.description: Point size in scene units, converted to pixels against the viewport height so it looks the same on a phone and a monitor. Large enough to close the gaps and the cloud becomes a solid sheet; small enough to see between them is the point.

drift.description: How far points wander from where the picture puts them. Very small: this is a photograph breathing, not a particle system. It is also the main thing that decides how busy the item is, and at 0.035 the whole frame changes faster than a backdrop should. Past about 0.1 the image stops being legible and you have confetti.

spin.description: Degrees the cloud turns either side of square-on. Enough to show the picture has thickness, not enough to lose the picture.

period.description: Seconds for one cycle of the turn and the wander. Both complete whole turns in it, so the loop has no join.

wash.description: How far the points are pulled towards `ink`. At 0 you get the photograph's own colours, which is the most legible. At 1 the picture is one colour and reads as data rather than as a photograph, which is occasionally what you want.

ink.description: The colour points are pulled towards. Only does anything when `wash` is above 0.

instruction: the cloud turns and breathes on its own
intro:
DepthPointCloud takes a photograph apart into points and pushes it into the
third dimension using its own brightness.

There is no depth map, and the item does not pretend there is. A photograph
does not carry one. This reads luminance and treats it as height, which is
wrong about the world and right about pictures: a photographer lights the
subject and lets the ground fall away, so in most photographs the bright parts
really are the near ones. Where that is false, which is a bright sky or a dark
subject, it fails interestingly rather than wrongly.

`relief` is how much you are willing to claim.

Every point keeps the colour of the pixel it came from, and that is the whole
trick. A point cloud in a single colour is an abstract; a photograph you can
still recognise while it comes apart is a much stronger thing.

name: DitherImage
description: A photograph reduced to two tones by error diffusion, which is the kind of dither a shader cannot do

notes: Every dithering effect on the web is an ordered dither: a fixed matrix of thresholds compared against the picture one pixel at a time. It is the only kind a fragment shader can do, because a fragment shader has to answer for one pixel without knowing anything about its neighbours

Error diffusion is the other kind and the one that looks like something. Quantise a pixel, work out how much tone you threw away, hand that error to the pixels you have not reached yet. It is why a dithered Macintosh picture has grain that follows the subject instead of a crosshatch laid over it, and it is strictly sequential, so there is no way to put it on a GPU

It runs on the CPU, and it does not run at the frame rate. Time is quantised to `rate` steps a second and the pass only runs when the step changes, so every other frame is one scaled drawImage. That is what lets the dots be fine: the pass costs four times as much each time the dot halves, so at sixty frames a second anything under about five pixels was unaffordable and the picture came out as big soft squares. It is still pure in t, because the step is a function of t alone

Do not dither in linear light. A trap, and the first version here fell into it. The argument for linear is good as far as it goes: a half-and-half field of black and white dots averages in the eye to half the light, and light adds linearly. But a mid grey is 128, which is 0.50 encoded and 0.22 linear, so dithering in linear lays down 22 per cent white dots where the photograph says 50 per cent grey, and most of the frame goes solid. The flaw is that a photograph is not a scene: it has already been tone-mapped for a display, and undoing its encoding undoes the tone mapping with it. The quantity to preserve is the one the picture is stored in, which is why every implementation since 1976 works on the bytes as they come

Atkinson throws a quarter of the error away. Floyd and Steinberg pass all of it over four neighbours; Atkinson passes six eighths over six, and the missing two eighths is not an oversight. Losing error pulls flat areas towards whichever tone they were nearest, so highlights go clean white and shadows go clean black, which is the whole reason the Macintosh look reads as contrasty rather than as a field of grey speckle

Scan alternate rows backwards. Always going left to right drags the error one way, and in a smooth gradient that comes out as diagonal streaks running down and to the right. A serpentine scan cancels the drag, and the kernel is mirrored with it so a backwards row pushes its error the way it is travelling

The source is sampled through a canvas the size of the grid, so the browser's own downscaler does the averaging. Taking one source pixel per dot aliases badly and a picture of foliage comes back as noise rather than as tone
Scaled up with image smoothing off. With it on the browser interpolates the two tones back into the greys the dither existed to avoid, and the result is a slightly noisy photograph

Animated error diffusion boils. The error propagates, so lifting the exposure by a hair flips one pixel, which changes what every pixel after it inherits, and whole runs of grain reorganise at once. At sixty frames a second that is television static; at eight it reads as grain, which is the other reason the rate is low
A 2D canvas, so this is the one image item that costs nothing against the sixteen-million-pixel WebGL budget and can sit on a page beside a shader without competing with it
The stays in the document, hidden. Its alt text is the accessible version of the picture and a page whose script never runs still shows the photograph

Two numbers, not one, because the dither does not run at the frame rate. The pass costs 4.8ms at 1280 by 720 with a three-pixel dot; every frame in between redraws the plate it already has, which is one scaled drawImage at 0.003ms. At the default rate of eight a second that is about 38ms of work per second of animation

That split is what lets the dots be fine. The pass costs four times as much each time the dot halves, so at the frame rate anything under about five pixels was unaffordable and the picture came out as big soft squares, which is exactly how the first version of this item shipped and exactly what was wrong with it. 12.6ms at dot 2, 4.8 at 3, 2.7 at 4, 1.2 at 6
It is also what a one-bit display did. A Macintosh did not re-dither its screen sixty times a second; the bitmap sat there until something changed it

The pass itself went from 3.5ms to 2.0ms at the old six-pixel dot before any of that. The kernel was an array of triples destructured six times per cell, and the output was written four bytes at a time when for one bit there are only two possible words
The source is resampled only when the grid changes. The plate context asks for willReadFrequently, which keeps it where putImageData is cheap
Holds no WebGL context at all, so it costs nothing against the sixteen-million-pixel budget and can sit on a page beside a shader

dot.description: Size of one dot, in CSS pixels. The resolution of the whole thing, and the first version of this item had it at 6, which is wrong: at 6 the picture is big soft squares and the subject is mush. At 3 it is a legible one-bit photograph, which is the point. The pass costs four times as much each time this halves, which is why it only runs `rate` times a second rather than every frame: 4.8ms at 3, and 12.6ms at 2, which is a dropped frame every time it runs.

mode.description: Which dither. `atkinson` throws away a quarter of the error, which cleans the highlights and the shadows and is the Macintosh look. `floyd` keeps all of it, which holds more midtone and reads greyer and flatter. `ordered` is the Bayer matrix, the only kind a shader can do, and it is here to be switched to once: notice that it sits over the picture rather than in it.

levels.description: How many tones. 2 is one bit and it is the whole point. Past about 4 there is enough tone that the dither stops doing any work and you have a posterised photograph, which is a different and much less interesting thing.
