ink.description: The dark tone. A soft near-black rather than a true one: a screen printed in true black against true white reads as a screenshot of a bitmap rather than as something on a page.

paper.description: The light tone. Set this and the ink the other way round for the terminal version, which is green on black and which everybody else ships.

exposure.description: Multiplies the tone before quantising. The main tone control. It works on the picture as stored rather than on reconstructed light, which is deliberate and is explained in the notes, and it means this behaves like an ordinary brightness rather than like a stop of exposure.

contrast.description: Pushes tone away from the midpoint before quantising. A photograph with a narrow range gives a picture that is all one grain size, and this is what opens it out. Past about 2.5 the midtones are gone and you have a stencil.

swell.description: How far the exposure swells over the period. Small. Animated error diffusion boils, because the error propagates and one flipped pixel changes everything downstream of it, so whole runs of grain reorganise at once. At 0.3 it is static. At 0 it holds still and the item draws one frame and stops.

period.description: Seconds for one swell. The loop closes exactly on it. Long, for the same reason the swell is small: slow, the boil reads as film grain on a plate that is breathing, which is the one kind of motion this technique is any good at.

serpentine.description: Scan alternate rows backwards. Always going left to right drags the error one way and a smooth gradient comes out with diagonal streaks running down and to the right. Turn it off once on a sky: the streaks are not subtle, and they are the reason this option exists rather than being hard-coded.

rate.description: How many times a second the dither is recomputed. Every other frame redraws the plate it already has, which is one scaled drawImage and costs nothing. This is the option that lets the dots be fine, because the pass is expensive and running it eight times a second instead of sixty is near enough an eighth of the work. It is also what a one-bit display did: a Macintosh did not re-dither its screen sixty times a second, the bitmap sat there until something changed it. And it is what stops the boil reading as television static.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. Any time works here: the swell is the only thing that moves and the picture is the point, so this is just a choice of exposure.

maxDpr.description: Device pixel ratio ceiling. It changes how crisply a dot's edges land on the display, not how many dots there are: the grid is measured in CSS pixels so the picture is the same picture on any screen.

instruction: switch mode to ordered to see what a shader can manage

credit.what: Error diffusion and its kernels are from the printing and computer-graphics literature: Floyd and Steinberg's 1976 paper, and Bill Atkinson's variant written for the Macintosh. The observation that it cannot be a fragment shader, and what to do about that, are this item's own
credit.author: Robert Floyd and Louis Steinberg

intro:
DitherImage reduces a photograph to two tones by **error diffusion**, which is
the kind of dither a shader cannot do.

Every dithering effect on the web is an *ordered* dither: a fixed matrix of
thresholds, usually Bayer's, compared against the picture one pixel at a time.
That is not a stylistic choice, it is the only kind a fragment shader can do. A
fragment shader has to answer for one pixel without knowing anything about its
neighbours, and ordered dithering is the only dither with that property.

Error diffusion is the other kind, and it is the one that looks like something.
Quantise a pixel, work out how much tone you threw away, and hand that error to
the pixels you have not reached yet. The grain then **follows the subject**
rather than lying across it as a crosshatch. It is also strictly sequential:
every pixel depends on the ones before it, so there is no way to write it
per-pixel and no way to put it on a GPU.

Switch `mode` to `ordered` once. The difference is not subtle and it is the
whole argument for this item existing.

name: DustMotes
description: Dust hanging in a lit room, built as a field rather than a particle system, with most of it out of focus

notes: A field, not a particle system. The frame is a lattice, each cell holds one mote whose position is a function of the cell, a seed and the clock, and a pixel looks only at the nine cells around it. Nothing is stored and nothing is advanced

That is not an optimisation, it is what makes the item possible here. An array of particles advanced each frame cannot be seeked, so it cannot be recorded; it drifts on a dropped frame, because each position depends on the last; and its cost grows with the count. This way the count is a division rather than a loop, so ten thousand motes cost exactly what a hundred do

Most motes are out of focus, and that is the clearest difference between dust and snow. A real mote is a few micrometres across, so at any focal distance nearly all of them are blurred smudges and only a handful are sharp

A blurred mote is drawn both wider and fainter, because a lens spreads the same light over more area. Those two together are what make a wide smudge and a tight point read as the same object at different distances rather than as two different things
The motes catch the light rather than emitting it, so where one sits in the frame decides how bright it is. Without that the field has no direction and reads as static
They rise as often as they fall. Dust in a lit room is moved by convection rather than by gravity: it hangs. Falling dust is snow
Each mote is a gaussian rather than a disc, because a mote has no edge whether it is in focus or not
Built for a dark ground and declared as one. This is light caught on something, and on a pale ground there is nothing for it to be brighter than
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes

Measured at 0.018 mean absolute change per frame on a 0 to 255 scale and 0.37ms at 640 by 360, with a loop seam of exactly zero. The first version drifted 0.7 turns on the vertical and the seam measured 2.59: a time coefficient has to be a whole number of turns over the period or the loop never comes home

Nine cells per pixel, each one four hashes and an exponential. That is the whole cost and it does not change with the mote count: `pitch` sets the density, and a finer pitch costs nothing extra per pixel because the neighbourhood is still nine cells
No textures, no buffers and no feedback. There is nothing to allocate and nothing to respawn

ground.description: The air, and what shows where there is no dust. Dark, because everything drawn here is light caught on something: on a pale ground the motes have nothing to be brighter than and the whole thing disappears.

mote.description: The motes. Warm rather than white, because the light catching them came from somewhere and nothing in a room is lit by a pure white source.

pitch.description: Cell size, and so the density: one mote per cell. A fine pitch costs nothing extra per pixel, because a pixel always looks at the same nine cells, so this is the one density control in the library that is free to turn up. Below about 15 the motes start to overlap into a fog.

size.description: Radius of a mote in perfect focus, in pixels. Small: a sharp mote is a speck, and it is the blurred ones that take up room. Raising this makes the sharp ones into dots, which is the look of snow.

haze.description: How much of the field is out of focus. High, because at the scale of a mote the depth of field is almost nothing and nearly everything you see is a smudge. At 0 every mote is sharp, which is the single clearest way to make dust look like a screensaver.

light.description: Where the light comes from. It decides which side of the frame the dust is visible on, which is what gives the air a direction. Pair it with LightShafts set to the same angle and the motes are in the beam.

falloff.description: How hard the light falls off across the frame. At 0 the dust is evenly lit everywhere, which reads as a texture rather than as a room with a window in it.

drift.description: How far a mote wanders, as a share of the cell. It travels a closed path, so it comes back: dust hangs rather than going anywhere. At 0 it is a still field, which is a legitimate way to use this and very quiet.

sparkle.description: Share of motes bright enough to read as sharp specks. A few, and they are most of what makes the air look occupied: it is the thing you notice in a sunbeam. Past about a third it stops being dust and becomes glitter.

seed.description: Seed for the field. The same seed gives the same air, so a recording and a live page match mote for mote.

period.description: Seconds for one cycle of the drift. Long, because dust moves slowly and a backdrop has to survive being ignored.

instruction: the dust hangs on its own
intro:
DustMotes is dust hanging in a lit room. It is a **field**, not a particle
system, and that is the most important thing about it.

Every version of this keeps an array of particles, advances each one every
frame, and respawns the ones that drift out. That costs three things and buys
nothing. It cannot be seeked, so it cannot be recorded. It drifts on a dropped
frame, because each position depends on the last. And its cost grows with the
count, so a thousand motes is a thousand objects to walk.

This is a shader over a lattice. The frame is divided into cells, each cell
holds one mote at a position that is a function of the cell, a seed and the
clock, and a pixel only ever looks at the nine cells around it. Nothing is
stored and nothing is advanced, so **the count is a division rather than a
loop**: ten thousand motes cost exactly what a hundred do.

name: EmberRise
description: Embers lifting off the bottom edge of an element, cooling and slowing as they go, on a transparent canvas

notes: A fixed cast with staggered lives, not an array that grows and shrinks. Ember k is always ember k: its lane, its size, its sway and its place in the queue are hashes of k, and its age is fract(t / life + phase). Nothing is created or destroyed, and the frame at t is the same frame whenever you ask for it

That is what makes it recordable. The page this came from pushes particles onto a list, advances each one against the last frame and splices out the dead, so there is no value of t you can ask it for and two machines disagree after a minute
It also makes `count` exact. An emitter with a spawn rate gives you a number of embers that depends on the frame rate

2D rather than WebGL, deliberately. The budget is one live WebGL context per page and this is an effect you might want on three buttons at once. A couple of hundred small arcs cost almost nothing, and what makes embers look like embers is additive compositing rather than per-pixel work
The canvas is cleared to transparent and never filled, so it composites over whatever is behind it. An ember effect that paints its own background is one you cannot put on top of a button
`life` is snapped so a whole number of lives fits the period. Without it the cast is part way through a life when the loop comes round and the video jumps once a cycle
Small embers go further and live longer in the air. That is the only depth cue in here, and without it the field reads as one object at one distance
Built for a dark ground and declared as one. The compositing is additive, which on paper makes a hot ember brighter than white and a cool one invisible
Two arcs per ember, a wide dim halo and a tight core. A radial gradient per ember per frame would be the one thing that made this expensive, and two flat discs read the same at this size

Measured with `pnpm budget` at 1280 by 720: 1.9ms for a draw and a forced flush at the default count of 120, against DustMotes at 0.7 on the same machine. Cost is linear in `count`, and that is the knob

0.163 mean absolute change per frame on a 0 to 255 scale, worst 0.354, sampled at six phases. At the top of the quiet band and deliberately so: this is a decoration on a control rather than a backdrop, and it is measured over a full 720-pixel canvas. On the strip of a button, where the rise is a couple of hundred pixels rather than seven, the same settings move far less
`life` was 3.2s and `count` 150 until that was measured at 0.358, which is past where a thing you are not looking at should be. 4s and 120 is the same fire, slower
No WebGL context at all, so this does not compete with a backdrop for the one the page is allowed

ember.description: The hot core of a new ember. Orange rather than yellow: a yellow ember on a dark ground reads as a spark from a grinder, which is a different and much more violent thing.

cool.description: What an ember has cooled to by the end of its life. Dark red, close to the ground, so an ember goes out rather than disappearing. Set it closer to the ember colour and the field stops having a direction in time.

count.description: How many embers are alive at once, exactly. Not a spawn rate: a fixed cast with staggered lives is what makes this seekable, and it also means the number you set is the number you get on any machine. This is the whole cost of the effect and it is linear.

rise.description: How far an ember travels in its life, as a share of the host's height. At 1 the longest-lived ones just reach the top, which is usually what you want: embers that stop in the middle of a tall box look like they hit something.

life.description: Seconds an ember lives. Snapped at render time so a whole number of lives fits the period, because a cast part way through a life when the loop comes round is a video that jumps once a cycle. Short lives give a busy fire, long ones give a few sparks drifting.

sway.description: How far an ember wanders sideways, one whole turn over its life. At 0 they go straight up, which reads as a machine rather than as air. Large values turn the rise into a wave and the embers start to look tethered.

size.description: Radius of the largest ember. They are drawn with a halo at three times this, so the lit area is bigger than the number suggests. Past about 5 they stop being embers and become fireflies.

spread.description: How much of the width the embers lift off, centred. Below about 0.3 it is a plume from a single point; at 1 the whole bottom edge is alight, which suits a hero and is too much for a button.

heat.description: Overall brightness. The one control to reach for when the effect is right but loud: it scales alpha rather than count, so the fire thins out instead of thinning down.

seed.description: Seed for the cast: lanes, sizes, sway and the order they go up in. The same seed gives the same embers, so two of these side by side want two seeds.

period.description: Seconds for one cycle. It has to be a whole number of lives and the render rounds `life` to make it so, so this is the figure that actually decides both. Long enough that the repeat is not obvious; a fire that loops every four seconds is a fire you notice looping.

instruction: the embers lift on their own

credit.what: embers lifting off a control, from the Fire Button page. The engine here is a fixed cast with staggered lives rather than a list that grows and shrinks, because a list cannot be seeked
credit.author: Ray Velez

intro:
EmberRise is embers lifting off the bottom edge of an element, cooling and
slowing as they go. It was built for a control that is supposed to look hot, and
it is transparent, so it sits over whatever that control is.

It is a **fixed cast with staggered lives**, not an array of particles, and that
is the most important thing about it.

name: EmbossedText
description: Type pressed into paper rather than extruded off it, with the impression biting unevenly across the line

notes: No canvas and no WebGL. Two text shadows and a colour per character, and getting those right is the whole job

It presses in rather than standing out. The effect this is a recast of extrudes letters towards the viewer with a stack of shadows going down and to the right, which is a sign or a plastic badge. Letterpress leaves the type below the surface: the paper is deformed and what you read is light on the walls of the impression

The dark edge goes on the side the light comes from, because that wall of the impression is turned away from it, and the light edge goes opposite. Reversed, the letter stands up off the page, and that is the most common way this gets written

The impression is uneven across the line. Getting a forme to print evenly is a job with a name, makeready, and before it is done some letters bite harder than others. That unevenness is the difference between a press and a filter

Ink is optional, and a blind emboss with none at all is the best thing here: the letter face is the same paper as the page and the impression is the only thing to read. It needs the `paper` option to match the actual page colour, because the letter face really is painted that colour
The whole line presses at once, because a platen is one surface coming down. The variation is in how hard each letter bites, not in when

The press overshoots and settles, since paper is compressed past where it ends up and pushes some of it back. The curve is divided by its own value at 1 so it finishes at exactly 1 whatever the spring is: without that the last frame of a recording does not match the resting state
Depth and softness are in ems, so an impression looks the same at every size
destroy() puts the original text back, leaving the element as it was found
Two shadows per character, written only when they change. Text shadows are painted rather than composited, so a very long string at a very large size is the case to watch: this is for a heading
No transforms, no filters and no layers. The characters never move, which is what makes it cheap: only their shadows change

paper.description: The sheet. This is not decoration: with no ink the letter face is painted this colour, so it has to match the page the text is actually sitting on, or the heading appears as a block of slightly wrong white and looks like a bug rather than a setting. The default is the house paper. If the page behind the text is a gradient or an image, a blind emboss cannot work at all: put ink on the type instead.

ink.description: The ink on the type, for when there is any. Letterpress ink sits in the bottom of the impression and reads darker than the same colour printed flat, so a softer black than you would normally pick is usually right.

transfer.description: How much ink transferred. 0 is a blind emboss, with no ink at all, and it is the setting worth trying first: it is the one thing this does that nothing else in the library does. Anything between is a light pull, which is a real thing and reads as one.

depth.description: How deep the impression is, in ems, so it holds at any size. Small. A heavy impression is fashionable and it is also what a printer means by punching through the sheet; past about 0.1 this stops being a press and starts being a stamp.

light.description: Where the light comes from, with 0 to the right. Up and to the left is what nearly every photograph of printed matter uses, and it is what the eye reads as recessed rather than raised. Turn it 180 degrees and the same shadows read as embossing instead.

softness.description: How soft the walls of the impression are. At 0 the edges are hard, which is a die cut rather than a press: paper compresses, so the wall of a real impression is a curve.

press.description: Milliseconds for the platen to come down. A press is quick and heavy. Slow it far past a second and it reads as the letters fading in, which is the thing this is trying not to be.

hold.description: Milliseconds before the press comes down. Also how you stagger two of these on one page.

spring.description: How much the paper pushes back. Paper is not clay: it compresses past where it ends up and returns some of that. At 0 the press arrives and stops, which reads as a fade rather than as a strike.

makeready.description: How uneven the impression is across the line. At 0 every letter bites identically, which is a forme that has been made ready properly and, on a screen, is indistinguishable from a CSS filter. The unevenness is the whole tell that something was pressed.

seed.description: Seed for the unevenness. The same seed always gives the same forme, so a recorded video and a live page match letter for letter.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. For a one-shot press this should be a time after it has finished, so the text appears already pressed. That still frame is the whole effect with its one moving part stopped, which costs the viewer nothing here.

instruction: press replay to pull it again
intro:
EmbossedText presses type into paper. A platen comes down, the sheet takes the
impression, and the paper springs back a little.

The effect this is a recast of is called depth text, and it extrudes the letters
towards the viewer in fake 3D with a stack of shadows going down and to the
right. That is a sign, or a plastic badge. Letterpress goes the other way: the
type ends up below the surface, the paper is deformed, and what you read is
light catching the walls of the impression.

So the whole thing is two shadows and a colour, and getting those right is the
entire job.

**A dark edge on the side the light comes from**, because that wall of the
impression is turned away from it, and a light edge opposite. Reverse the two
and the letter stands up off the page instead. Everybody writing a debossed text
shadow does this at least once.

**The impression bites unevenly across the line.** Getting a forme to print
evenly is a job with a name, makeready, and before it is done some letters bite
harder than others. That unevenness is the difference between a press and a CSS
filter, and at `makeready: 0` the two are indistinguishable.

**Ink is optional.** A blind emboss has none at all: the letter face is the same
paper as the page, and the impression is the only thing to read. It is the best
thing this effect does and it is one setting.

The whole line presses at once, because a platen is one surface coming down. The
variation is in how hard each letter bites, not in when.

name: ExpandingTiles
description: A grid of tiles where the pressed one opens out to fill the window, and the rules that bounded its cell travel to the edges of the page with it

notes: Nothing is scaled. The obvious way to grow a box is a transform, and a transform takes the type with it: the title stretches as the tile grows and settles back as it lands, which reads as cheap however well it is eased. The tile is put at its final size immediately and revealed with clip-path: inset(), opening from the cell outwards, so type laid out once at its final size cannot distort

The content is carried rather than left behind. A tile jumped straight to full size has its title wherever the full-size layout puts it, which at the moment of the press is outside the clip: the title would blink out and reappear halfway through. Each child is counter-translated by the distance between where it sits at rest and where it sits open, eased to zero. That distance is measured rather than assumed, because a centred tile moves its title to the middle of the window and a top-left one does not, and a guessed offset gets one of the two wrong

The four rules that bounded the cell travel out to the edges of the window, and they lead the clip slightly. An edge that arrives at the same moment as the thing it bounds reads as a border; an edge that gets there first reads as a movement

Tiles that are links open and then follow their href, which is the whole gesture: the page changes behind a tile that already fills the window. A tile with no href stays open until it is dismissed, so it is never a dead end

Pure in t: the open tile and how far through the gesture it is are folded out of the list of presses each frame, scripted and real presses in the same list, so the recorder can seek anywhere and a live page and a take agree
The grid is laid out by your own CSS. The effect never positions the tiles, it only opens out of them, and the author's own cell borders show through whenever nothing is open

An opened tile is fixed to the window, which takes it out of the grid, and a grid with one fewer item re-places every item after it: the tiles behind the one you pressed shuffle up a cell and the grid's own background shows through the hole. A placeholder sized from the measured cell holds the slot, so nothing behind the open tile moves

One clip-path and one transform per frame while a tile is opening, and nothing at all while the grid is at rest: a still grid writes no styles, because the applied state is compared before anything is set

Layout is read only when the element resizes, never during the gesture. The cells are measured while nothing is open, because an open tile is fixed to the window and no longer reports where its cell was

duration.description: Milliseconds the opening takes. This is a navigation rather than a flourish, so it wants to be short enough that it never stands between the press and the page: past about a second it stops reading as a transition and starts reading as a wait.

closeDuration.description: Milliseconds the closing takes. Shorter than the opening on purpose: opening is the thing you asked for and is worth watching, closing is getting out of the way and should not be.

bleed.description: How far the rules run past the window, as a share of its size. A rule that stops exactly at the edge looks like it was measured to fit; one that runs off reads as a line that carries on past the page.

rule.description: Width of the travelling rules. At 0 none are drawn and the tile simply opens, which is the quieter version and the right one if your grid has no visible lines of its own.

ruleColour.description: Colour of the travelling rules. Match whatever your grid already draws between the cells, because the whole idea is that these are those lines moving.

lead.description: How far ahead of the clip the rules run, as a share of the duration. At 0 the rules arrive with the edge they bound and read as a border; a little ahead and they read as the lines pulling the tile open behind them.

follow.description: Follow the opened tile's href once it has finished opening. Turn it off to use the gesture as a disclosure, where the tile opens over the grid and closes back. A tile with no href stays open whatever this says.

instruction: press a tile
intro:
ExpandingTiles is a grid of tiles where the one you press opens out to fill the
window, and the four rules that bounded its cell travel out to the edges of the
page with it. The grid you were looking at becomes the frame around what you
opened.

Three things carry it, and the first two are what every other version of this
gets wrong.

**Nothing is scaled.** The obvious way to grow a box is a transform, and a
transform takes the type with it: the title stretches as the tile grows and
settles back as it lands, which reads as cheap however well it is eased. Here
the tile is put at its final size immediately and revealed with
`clip-path: inset()`, opening from the cell outwards. Type laid out once at its
final size cannot distort, because nothing ever scales it.

**The content is carried, not left behind.** A tile jumped straight to full size
has its title wherever the full-size layout puts it, which at the moment of the
press is outside the clip: the title would blink out and reappear halfway
through. So each child is counter-translated by the distance between where it
sits at rest and where it sits open, eased to zero.

That distance is measured rather than assumed. A centred tile moves its title to
the middle of the window and a top-left one does not, and a guessed offset gets
one of the two wrong. It is measured once per tile per window size, never during
the gesture.

**The rules lead the clip.** An edge that arrives at the same moment as the
thing it bounds reads as a border. An edge that gets there first reads as the
lines pulling the tile open behind them. That is what `lead` is for, and it is
most of the difference between this looking designed and looking generated.

name: FallingLetters
description: A line of type comes apart and falls, each letter dropping and bouncing once, with every position a closed form in t

notes: Every letter's position is a closed form in t rather than a simulation. A solver steps from the last frame to the next, so frame 200 can only be reached by computing the 199 before it: you cannot seek, you cannot record a loop, and two runs drift apart as soon as one misses a frame. Here the fall is the parabola itself and the bounce is the same parabola reflected and damped, so any t in any order gives the same frame

The letters are measured once and taken out of flow, so nothing reflows. Split a line into spans and animate them in place and every letter that moves changes the line box, so the letters that have not fallen yet shuffle along underneath
The measuring has to finish before any letter is taken out of flow. Do it letter by letter and each removal reflows the rest, so every measurement after the first is of a line that no longer exists

One damped bounce, not none and not five. A letter that falls and stops dead reads as a dropped frame rather than as a thing with weight; five is a rubber ball. One is a piece of lead type landing on a stone
Distances are in line heights rather than pixels, so the same numbers behave at any type size
The original text stays in the accessibility tree as a label on the element, and the per-letter spans are hidden from it. A word split into letters is otherwise read out one letter at a time
destroy() puts the original text back exactly as it was found, including the spaces
One transform per letter per frame while the line is falling, composited, and nothing at all before the first letter goes: a letter that has not started writes no style
No per-frame allocation and no layout reads during the fall. Everything was measured once at build, and the arithmetic is a square root and two multiplications per letter

hold.description: Milliseconds before the first letter goes. Long enough that the line is read as a line first, because the whole gesture depends on it having been intact a moment ago.

stagger.description: Milliseconds between one letter leaving and the next. At 0 the whole line goes at once, which reads as the shelf giving way rather than as the type coming loose.

scatter.description: How scattered the order is. At 0 the letters drop strictly left to right, which reads as mechanical; at 1 the order is unrelated to position, which reads as random. The middle is what looks like something coming apart.

gravity.description: Fall acceleration, in line heights per second squared. In line heights rather than pixels so the same value behaves at any type size.

bounce.description: How much of its speed a letter keeps on the bounce. At 0 it stops dead, which reads as a dropped frame. Past about 0.5 it is a rubber ball rather than a piece of lead type.

drift.description: How far a letter wanders sideways as it falls, in line heights. A little is the difference between type coming loose and a row of counters dropping down a slot.

spin.description: Degrees a letter turns per second while falling, in whichever direction its hash gives it. At 0 the letters stay upright, which is quieter and is the right answer for a line that has to stay readable as it goes.

floor.description: How far below the baseline the letters come to rest, in line heights. Make sure there is room: the element keeps its original height, so anything past the bottom of its container needs the container to allow overflow.

seed.description: Seed for the scatter and the spin directions. The same seed gives the same fall, so a recording and a live page agree letter for letter.

instruction: press replay to drop it again
intro:
FallingLetters takes a line of type apart and drops it, each letter falling,
bouncing once and settling. Pied type: a forme dropped on the way to the press.

Three things carry it, and the first is why this is arithmetic rather than a
physics engine.

**Every letter's position is a closed form in `t`.** A solver steps from the
last frame to the next, which means frame 200 can only be reached by computing
the 199 before it. You cannot seek it, you cannot record a clean loop from it,
and two runs drift apart as soon as one misses a frame. Here the fall is the
parabola itself and the bounce is the same parabola reflected and damped, so
asking for any `t` in any order gives the same frame.

**The letters are measured once and taken out of flow.** Split a line into
spans and animate them in place, and every letter that moves changes the line
box, so the letters that have not fallen yet shuffle along underneath. The
block keeps the height it had and each letter falls from exactly where it was
set.

**One damped bounce.** A letter that falls and stops dead reads as a dropped
frame rather than as a thing with weight. Five bounces is a rubber ball. One is
a piece of lead type landing on a stone, which is what this is.

name: FullscreenMenu
description: A full-viewport index that opens as a real dialog and cascades in

notes: Uses <dialog>.showModal(), so the focus trap, Escape, top layer and focus restoration are the browser's
The fade uses transition-behavior: allow-discrete and @starting-style; where those are unsupported the overlay appears instantly, which is a graceful loss
No focus-trap library, no portal, no scroll-lock package
The stagger is one transition-delay per row, composited
No JavaScript runs per frame

label.description: The trigger's text, and the dialog's accessible name. Keep it a noun. It is read out as the name of the whole overlay.

closeLabel.description: Text on the close control. There is a visible one as well as Escape, because Escape is not discoverable.

open.description: Pass it to control the overlay yourself and listen to onOpenChange. Leave it undefined and the component keeps its own state, which is what you want unless a route change needs to close it.

instruction: open it, then try Escape and Tab
intro:
Contents is a full-viewport index: a small trigger, and an overlay that takes the
whole screen and lists everything in mono with hairline rules between the rows.
The rows cascade in on a 26ms stagger counted across every section, so the reveal
reads as one movement down the page rather than several.

The overlay is a real `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()`. That is the whole
design. The browser then provides the focus trap, Escape, the top layer,
inerting the rest of the page, and returning focus to the trigger on close. Every
one of those is something hand-rolled menus get subtly wrong, and none of them is
our code. There is no focus-trap library, no portal, and no scroll-lock package.

What is left is layout, type, and one transition.

name: GlassNav
description: A bar of glass across the top of a page, clear over a hero and frosted once it has scrolled

notes: The blur is backdrop-filter, which every current browser supports. The refraction is an SVG filter inside backdrop-filter, which only Chromium applies: Safari ignores it and Firefox parses the value, passes an @supports test and then renders nothing, so there is no feature query that tells the truth
What makes a panel read as glass rather than as tinted film is the hairline specular along its top edge, not the blur. Take that one line away and the rest is a grey rectangle

The lens is a signed distance field for the rounded rectangle, computed per pixel into a canvas and handed to feImage. The displacement is the field's gradient weighted towards the edge, which is a bevel rather than a uniform stretch
prefers-reduced-transparency turns the glass opaque and takes the specular with it, because a highlight on something that is not transparent is a lie about the material
forced-colors throws out every background and shadow, so the bar falls back to a border, which is the one thing the mode keeps
A nav landmark, a list, and links. The bar is markup rather than a widget, so the keyboard behaviour is the browser's
The current page is marked with aria-current='page', which is also what the underline styling keys off, so what is announced and what is drawn cannot drift
Contrast is the real risk. Glass over a photograph can put 2:1 text on the page without anybody noticing, which is why the tint comes up as the page scrolls under it rather than staying clear
Scroll is read on a rAF rather than on the event, and the settle value is rounded to two places before it is written, so a style recalculation only happens when something changed
The lens map is drawn once per resize at quarter scale, not per frame. It is a smooth field and feImage resamples it
backdrop-filter is not free: it forces the backdrop into its own layer. One bar on a page is the intended dose

settleOver.description: Pixels of scroll over which the glass goes from clear to frosted. Roughly the height of whatever is behind it at the top of the page.

blur.description: Blur at full settle. Past about 20 it stops reading as glass and starts reading as fog, and it is the setting most likely to cost a user on an old machine their frame rate.

tint.description: How milky it goes once settled. This is the contrast control: glass over a photograph can put 2:1 text on a page without anybody noticing, and this is what stops it.

refract.description: Bend the backdrop as well as blurring it. Chromium only. Everywhere else you get the blur and the edge, which is most of the effect, and nothing looks broken.

refraction.description: How far the rim bends what is behind it, in pixels. Past about 30 the bar stops looking like glass and starts looking like a heat haze.

instruction: scroll the page to settle the glass
intro:
A bar of glass across the top of a page. Nearly clear over a hero, settling into
frosted once the page has scrolled under it.

That settle is the whole design. A bar legible over a photograph and a bar
legible over body copy are not the same bar, and a fixed one has to be the
second, which means it is milky over the thing you most wanted people to see.
Tying the tint to the scroll lets it be clear exactly while there is something
behind it worth looking at.

Underneath it is a nav landmark, a list and links. The current page is marked
with `aria-current="page"`, which is also what the underline keys off, so what a
screen reader announces and what you can see cannot drift apart.

name: GlassSearchBar
description: A search capsule of real glass over a picture, bending and splitting what scrolls behind it

notes: The picture is the host element's own child. It is hidden from sight and left in the document, so the alt text is whatever you wrote and a page with no JavaScript still shows it

This is WebGL rather than CSS because backdrop-filter can blur what is behind an element but cannot bend it, and bending is most of what glass is. The one CSS route that bends, an SVG displacement filter on the backdrop, is Chromium only and fails silently everywhere else
The trade is that the panel owns its backdrop: it refracts the picture it was given rather than arbitrary page content. Anything that has to sit on top goes in the DOM above the canvas
The slab is a signed distance field for a rounded rectangle, and its gradient is analytic rather than sampled, because an approximate normal shows up at once as a wobble along the straight runs
Dispersion is three samples at three offsets along that normal, taken per tap inside the blur so the fringe survives it rather than being averaged away
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes

Legibility is a luminosity compression rather than a tint: the backdrop's brightness is scaled toward a level, so the hue and the detail survive. Mixing toward white measures the same and looks dead, because it desaturates the picture and flattens what the glass is supposed to be bending

The material belongs to the layer floating above content rather than to content itself, which is the rule Apple states for it, so what sits on the panel is a control: a search field, a toolbar, a nav. The demo is a search capsule, inset and low in the frame, which is where a thumb reaches

Legibility is a dimming layer with light labels rather than a milky one with dark labels. A darkened photograph still looks like a photograph because the hue and the tonal relationships survive, and a whitened one does not. It is also what Apple gives its Clear variant, which has no adaptive behaviour of its own

Measured against the brightest tile under the capsule, since white text is hardest where the backdrop is lightest: solid labels come out at 5.3:1 and the secondary ones at 4.79:1. The magnifier, the placeholder and the hint had all been set by eye and all three measured short while the field text passed
Outside the panel it is one texture read per pixel. Everything expensive is inside a branch that most of the frame never takes
Inside: twelve taps on a ring, three channels each, so thirty-six texture reads. That is the cost of frosted glass whose dispersion survives the blur
The image uploads once, on load. Nothing is uploaded per frame

glass.description: The tint the glass leaves and the colour its highlights take. Near white unless the glass is meant to be coloured, because it is multiplied into the picture rather than painted over it.

panelX.description: Centre of the panel across the element.

panelY.description: Centre of the panel down the element.

panelWidth.description: Width of the panel as a share of the element.

panelHeight.description: Height of the panel as a share of the element.

radius.description: Corner radius in CSS pixels, capped at half the shorter side, so a large number gives a capsule rather than an error.

bevel.description: How far in from the edge the bevel reaches. This is the width of the band that bends: the middle of a slab is flat and refracts nothing, which is why the centre stays readable and only the rim distorts.

refraction.description: How far the bevel bends what is behind it, in pixels. At 0 you have frosted glass, and this is the setting that makes it glass rather than a blur.

dispersion.description: How far the three channels separate as they bend. Glass has a different refractive index per wavelength, which is why a real edge fringes, and it is the cheapest thing that stops a shape reading as plastic. Past about 12 it stops being glass and starts being a prism.

frost.description: Frosting, as a blur radius in pixels. Twelve taps on a ring, which is not a Gaussian and does not need to be.

specular.description: How brightly the bevel catches the light. The highlight is lit off a real normal built from the distance field, so it moves round the rim as the light does rather than sitting where it was painted.

shine.description: How tight that catch is. Low is a broad satin sheen along the whole bevel; high is a small hard glint at the point facing the light.

fresnel.description: How much the rim brightens where you are looking through the most glass. This is what gives the edge its thickness.

edge.description: The bright hairline just inside the edge, where the bevel turns over.

tint.description: How much colour the glass leaves on what passes through it. This is also the contrast control if anything is going to be read on top of the panel.

luminosity.description: How far the backdrop's brightness is pulled toward `level` before the glass is drawn. This is what makes anything readable on the panel, and it is a compression rather than a wash: the luminance moves, the hue and the detail do not, so the picture is still a picture. Windows Acrylic calls this the luminosity layer and it is the part that guarantees contrast. At 0 the glass is clear and nothing is safe to put on it.

level.description: The brightness the backdrop is pulled toward. Low dims it, which suits light labels and is how a clear glass control is made legible: dimming a photograph leaves it looking like a photograph, and milking it toward white does not. High milks it, for dark labels. It is the one number that decides which way round the glass works, and the labels have to follow it.

lightX.description: Where the light is, across the panel.

lightY.description: Where the light is, down the panel.

shadow.description: How far the shadow under the slab reaches. Without it the panel is a window cut in the picture rather than an object resting on it.

travel.description: How far the picture travels behind the glass over a full scroll, as a share of the slack the cover fit left. At 0 the picture is fixed and all the glass has to bend is a still.

instruction: scroll the picture behind the glass
intro:
A slab of glass laid on a picture, bending and splitting what scrolls behind it.

Not a blur with a white border. Every part of this is something glass does:

**It bends.** The slab is a signed distance field for a rounded rectangle, and
the direction light bends is that field's gradient, which is the surface normal.
The amount is weighted towards the edge, because the middle of a slab is flat
and only the bevel has an angle to refract through. That is why the centre of
the panel stays readable while the rim distorts.

**It splits.** Glass has a different refractive index per wavelength, so the
three channels bend by slightly different amounts. This is why a real glass edge
fringes, and it is the single cheapest thing that stops a shape reading as
plastic.

**It catches the light.** The 2D gradient plus a height gives a real 3D normal,
so the highlight moves round the bevel as the light moves rather than sitting
where somebody painted it. The rim brightens where you are looking through the
most glass, which is what gives the edge its thickness.

**It sits on something.** There is a shadow under it. Without one the panel is a
window cut in the picture rather than an object resting on it.

name: GlassShatter
description: A plate of glass broken over a picture, cracked along the stress rather than into a honeycomb

notes: Every shattered-glass effect scatters random sites across the plane and gives each pixel to the nearest one. It produces a honeycomb, and a honeycomb is a dry mud flat rather than a broken window

A plate struck at a point breaks along the stress, and the stress is radial and circumferential: cracks run out from the impact and other cracks run round it, crossing the first set. The pieces come out roughly four-sided, small near the impact and growing with distance, because the radial cracks fan apart as they travel

So the lattice is polar rather than square. Sites live in cells of angle by radius, the borders fall along radii and around arcs, and the whole character of real glass comes out of the coordinate system rather than out of any extra work

The radius goes under a square root. A plain radius gives rings of even spacing, and concentric cracks get further apart as they travel; the root also crowds the inner rings together, which is the zone of fine fragments around the impact that any photograph of a broken window has

The sector index is taken modulo the sector count when it is hashed, so the cell on one side of angle zero is the same cell as the one on the other side. Without that there is a seam running out from the impact that no amount of jitter hides. The position uses the unwrapped index, so the distance stays continuous across the join

A site is jittered inside its own cell and capped there, which is the assumption the three by three search rests on. Let a site cross into its neighbour and the nearest site can be two cells away, and the plate tears along the lattice instead of along the cracks
The second nearest site is where the cracks come from. Halfway between two sites the two distances are equal, so their difference falls to zero, and that difference is a distance to the edge for free

Not every crack is the same crack. In a struck plate the radial cracks go first and go deepest, because the plate is in tension around the impact; the circumferential ones are secondary, forming between radials that have already gone, and they are shorter and shallower. Drawn at equal weight you get a spider web, which is a thing built outward from a centre rather than a thing broken from one. Which kind a border is can be read straight off its own normal: a radial crack runs along the radius, so its normal points round, and a circumferential one is the other way about

The picture is sampled a little inside its own edge, because the bend and the drift push the lookup outward and a clamped texture asked past its edge hands back the edge column over and over. At the left and right of the frame that came out as horizontal smears of colour, which reads as a fault in the effect rather than as glass

And not every circumferential crack forms at all. Weighting them down was not enough: a Voronoi diagram partitions the plane, so every cell is ringed by borders and the arcs close into polygons, which is exactly a spider web's architecture and still read as one at a quarter of the weight. Each border is therefore hashed and the circumferential ones only exist if their number comes up. The key is the pair of cells either side of it, taken with a componentwise min and max so both sides agree and a crack does not appear from one shard and not from its neighbour

What turns a dark line into a crack is the bright line beside it. A broken edge is a fresh face of glass and it catches the light, so a crack in a photograph is a dark line with a glint along it. That one term is the biggest single difference between this and a drawn grid

The crack width is in screen pixels, got by dividing the border distance by its own gradient. One lattice unit is a few pixels at the impact and a hundred at the edge of the frame, so a width in lattice units comes out as cracks of wildly uneven thickness. Scaling by fwidth was the first attempt and it is the same mistake in a different hat, because fwidth measures how fast the quantity changes rather than how far away the border is: it gave lines eight pixels thick with a white halo, and the thing came out as a spider web

The picture bends across the crack and the channels come apart as it bends, which is what a wedge of glass does to light passing through it. The bend follows the gradient of the border distance, which points across the crack rather than along it

The shard drift slides the picture inside the shard rather than moving the shard, so it is kept small. Past a fraction of a cell it stops reading as a piece that has shifted and starts reading as the wrong piece of the photograph
The stays in the document, hidden. Its alt text is the accessible version of the picture and a page whose script never runs still shows the photograph
Nine hashes and nine distances per pixel for the polar lattice, then three samples of the picture for the channel split. No list, no sorting, no texture for the sites
Nothing is allocated per frame and the picture is uploaded once
One shot. Once the break has opened the frame stops changing, and the runtime stops the loop when the element leaves the screen

sectors.description: Radial cracks running out from the impact. A prime number by default and for a reason: with an even count the cracks opposite each other line up through the impact and read as a drawn asterisk rather than as a break.

rings.description: Concentric cracks running round the impact, counted along the square root of the radius, so they come out close together near the impact and further apart as they go out. At 1 you have radial cracks only, which is a smashed pane rather than a struck one.

jitter.description: How far a site may sit from the middle of its own cell. At 0 the shards are a perfect polar grid, which is a dartboard. The cap is just under 1 and it is load-bearing: a site that crosses into its neighbour's cell breaks the nine-cell search the whole thing rests on, and the plate tears along the lattice.

crack.description: Width of the dark line, in screen pixels. Thin. A crack in glass is a hairline with light on it, and a fat dark line is a drawing of a crack: that is the single most common way this effect is got wrong.

glint.description: How brightly the fresh edge beside the crack catches the light. The term that does the most work here and the one nobody includes. Set it to 0 once: the cracks stop being cracks and become a grid drawn over the photograph, and no amount of width or refraction brings them back.

gap.description: How far each shard shifts, outward from the impact plus a little of its own. This slides the picture inside the shard rather than moving the shard, so it has to stay small: past about 2.5 the pieces stop reading as shifted and start reading as the wrong part of the photograph.

refract.description: How much the picture bends at a crack. The bend is strongest at the crack and dies away into the middle of the shard, which is where a wedge of glass is thickest and where it is flat.

fringe.description: How far red and blue come apart as the picture bends. It only happens at the cracks, which is the point: a plate of glass is not a prism, but the wedge at a broken edge is.

facet.description: How far a shard may sit out of the plane of the plate, as a share of its brightness. This is what gives the plate thickness: without it the cracks are lines on a flat picture, and with too much of it the shards read as tiles of different colours.

reach.description: How far the damage carries from the impact, measured in short edges of the element. A strike does not break the whole pane: there is a region of cracks around the impact and intact glass past it, and without that the frame is webbed edge to edge at an even density, which is half of why the honeycomb version of this effect never convinces. Above about 1.4 the whole element is inside the break and this stops doing anything.

arcs.description: What share of the circumferential cracks actually form. At 1 every one of them is there, and that is the spider web: a Voronoi diagram partitions the plane, so with a radial crack between each pair of neighbours and an arc joining them the architecture is exactly a web, and weighting the arcs down is not enough to fix it. A break is not a partition of the plane, it is a set of curves with ends. At 0 you have radials only, which is a struck pane that has not finished going.

impactX.description: Where the plate was struck, across the element. Off centre on purpose: a break centred in the frame reads as a graphic, and the whole argument for a polar lattice is that the break has a place it came from.

impactY.description: Where the plate was struck, down the element.

impactAt.description: Seconds of intact glass before it is struck. Worth having at all: the picture whole for half a second is what makes the break an event rather than a texture.

spread.description: Seconds for the break to open. Quick. Glass does not ease: the cracks arrive at something like a kilometre a second, and anything above about 1.5 here reads as the picture slowly developing a fault.

tint.description: The colour of the light on a fresh edge. Slightly cool, because a fresh break in glass is a green-blue line: that is the iron in it, and it is why the cut edge of a float-glass pane looks green end on.

seed.description: Seed for the shards. The same seed gives the same break, which is what makes the take reproducible.

maxDpr.description: Device pixel ratio ceiling. The crack width is in screen pixels, so this changes what the hairlines cost to draw but not how thick they look.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. For a one-shot break this has to be a time after it has opened, so the plate is simply broken. The broken plate is the point; the breaking is how it gets there.

instruction: press replay to break it again. set glint to 0 to see what holds it together

credit.what: Splitting a layer into shards around a set of sites, opening a crack along each border with the next-nearest shard, and bending and colour-splitting the layer across it, from the Shader Effects library's fracture. Their sites are random; the polar lattice here is the answer to what that looks like
credit.author: Shader Effects Inc.

intro:
GlassShatter breaks a plate of glass over a picture and leaves the pieces in
the frame.

Every version of this effect scatters random sites across the plane and gives
each pixel to the nearest one. The result is a honeycomb, and a honeycomb is
what a dry mud flat looks like. It is not what a broken window looks like, and
once you have noticed that you cannot unsee it.

name: GradualBlur
description: A band at the edge of a scrolling area where the content goes progressively out of focus, built from stacked blurs because a masked one does not ramp

notes: The obvious build does not work, and the failure looks like a browser bug rather than a mistake. One element, a backdrop-filter and a gradient mask give a band of fully blurred content whose opacity ramps away: masking a blur fades how much of the blurred layer you can see and does nothing to how blurred it is. The hard edge where the blur starts is not in the mask, so softening the mask will never move it

A blur that ramps has to be several blurs. Each layer blurs twice as hard as the one below it and is masked to its own band, and because a backdrop-filter sees everything painted beneath it, including the previous layers, the blurs compound
The doubling is what makes six layers enough. A linear ramp over the same range needs dozens before the steps stop showing, and each one is another backdrop-filter for the compositor
The bands overlap by one step on each side. Butted up against each other they leave faint but perfectly visible seams, which on a pale page read as printing bands

The wash is a separate layer and is not the same thing as the blur. Haze over a dark photograph wants a little light in it, or the blurred content stays as dark as it was and nothing reads as distance
backdrop-filter needs the content to be painted beneath the band, so this goes on the scrolling element and not on the thing inside it
destroy() removes the band and puts the element's position back
The stack is built once and rebuilt only when something about its shape changes. Per frame there is at most one opacity write, and none at all when `follow` is off

The real cost is the compositor's, not the main thread's: every layer is a backdrop-filter over the same region. Six is a deliberate ceiling, and the doubling is what buys the range without raising it

edge.description: Which edge the haze sits on. The foot of a scrolling panel is the one that earns its keep: it says the text continues. At the top it competes with whatever header is already there.

depth.description: How far the band reaches in from the edge, as a share of the element. A share rather than pixels, so a tall panel gets a long ramp and a short one does not lose a third of itself to haze.

strength.description: Blur at the very edge. This is the end of the ramp, not the whole of it: everything between here and the far side of the band is a fraction of it. Past about 30 the last line is a smear rather than something going out of focus.

layers.description: How many blurs the ramp is built from. Six is enough because each one is twice the last; below about four the steps are visible as bands, and above eight you are paying the compositor for a difference nobody can see.

tint.description: The colour of the wash, if there is one. The page's own paper is the usual answer. Over a photograph a colour taken out of the image reads better than white. `auto` takes it from the page, so the effect adopts whatever it is dropped onto.

wash.description: How strong the wash is at the edge. At 0 there is only blur, which is right on paper. Over a dark photograph it wants some, or the blurred content stays as dark as it was and nothing reads as distance.

follow.description: Bring the haze in as the element is scrolled rather than leaving it always on. For a panel with a top edge this is the honest setting: there is nothing above a list until it has been scrolled, and a haze over nothing is a smudge on the glass.

instruction: the column travels under it
intro:
GradualBlur puts a band at the edge of a scrolling area where the content goes
progressively out of focus before it runs off. Haze, rather than a fade to the
background colour. A fade tells you the text has stopped; a haze tells you it
has not.

The obvious way to build it does not work, and it is worth saying why, because
the failure looks like a bug in the browser rather than a mistake of yours.

One element, a `backdrop-filter` and a gradient mask gives you a band of **fully
blurred** content whose *opacity* ramps away. Masking a blur fades how much of
the blurred layer you can see. It does nothing at all to how blurred it is. So
there is a hard edge where the blur starts, and no amount of softening the mask
will move it, because the edge is not in the mask.

A blur that actually ramps has to be made of several blurs. Each layer here
blurs twice as hard as the one below it and is masked to its own band, and
because a `backdrop-filter` sees everything painted beneath it, including the
previous layers, the blurs compound.

The doubling is what makes six layers enough. A linear ramp over the same range
needs dozens before the steps stop showing, and every one of them is another
backdrop filter for the compositor.

name: GuillocheLines
description: The engine-turned line work off a banknote, printed on paper

notes: WebGL2 for gl_VertexID; there is no WebGL1 fallback and none is planned
The line width is derived from the screen-space derivative of the field, so the engraving stays one pixel wide at any DPR instead of filling in at the centre
Falls back to a still frame under prefers-reduced-motion, handled in the runtime
One full-screen triangle and three line families. No noise, no textures, no render targets
The cheapest effect in the library
Dense line work is the hardest thing in this library for a video codec to encode, so its recording carries a per-item quality override. The effect itself is unaffected

paper.description: The paper the plate is printed on. Match it to your page background. `auto` takes it from the page, so the effect adopts whatever it is dropped onto.

ink.description: The engraving. A desaturated near-black reads as ink; pure black reads as a wireframe. A light-dark() pair picks by the ground it lands on.

accent.description: The second colour, printed over one band of the pattern the way a share certificate prints one guilloche in red over the rest in black. A light-dark() pair picks by the ground it lands on.

scale.description: Size of the whole rosette. Below about 0.5 the lines are finer than the pixels and the plate turns grey.

pitch.description: Lines per unit of radius. Higher is finer engraving, and past about 50 it stops resolving on anything but a retina screen.

lobes.description: Lobes on the first rosette. Whole numbers only: a fractional lobe count gives a curve that never closes, and an open curve reads as a mistake rather than as engraving. The other two families are derived from this and kept coprime to it.

waves.description: Spokes in the family that runs around the circle rather than out from it. This is what turns two ring families into woven guilloche instead of a moire.

depth.description: How far each rosette's radius wobbles. Zero is concentric circles. Past about 0.2 the curves cross themselves and the weave becomes a tangle.

weight.description: Weight of the engraved line. Heavy lines at a high pitch fill in solid, so raise one and lower the other.

accentBand.description: Where the second colour sits, as a radius from the centre. Set it past the corner of the panel to switch the second colour off.

grain.description: Paper tooth. Static by design. Animated grain flickers, and a flicker this fine is what WCAG 2.3.1 exists to prevent.

period.description: Seconds for one turn of the gears. The pattern is exactly periodic over this. Slow on purpose: a backdrop whose cycle you can follow is a backdrop competing with the page, and at a turn every few seconds the eye tracks the rosette instead of reading. 60 is better still and the only reason it is not the default is the preview video, which is fine lines at every scale and the worst thing there is to compress.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. Any time works: a still guilloche is an engraving, which is a finished thing to look at.

instruction: ambient, the gears are turning slowly
intro:
Guilloche is the engine-turned line work off a banknote, a share certificate or
the bezel of a watch, drawn on warm paper.

It is not noise and it is not a gradient. A real rose engine cuts one continuous
line whose radius is modulated by a set of gears, so the result is a family of
curves in a strict harmonic relationship. That is what this draws: three
rosettes, each a circle whose radius wobbles at a whole number of lobes, rendered
as a line field rather than a fill, and multiplied together the way overlapping
ink actually behaves.

The whole-number lobe counts matter. A fractional count gives a curve that never
closes, and an open curve reads as a mistake rather than as engraving. The three
families are kept coprime so their interference takes a long time to repeat and
never settles into a grid.

One band is printed in a second colour, riding the same field, the way a
certificate prints one guilloche in red over the rest in black. It is part of the
engraving rather than a highlight laid on top of it.

One WebGL2 fragment shader on one full-screen triangle. No noise, no textures, no
render targets. It is the cheapest effect in the library.

name: HalftoneBackdrop
description: Two ink plates drift out of registration behind a halftone screen

notes: WebGL2 for gl_VertexID; there is no WebGL1 fallback and none is planned
Falls back to a still frame under prefers-reduced-motion, handled in the runtime
One full-screen triangle, four octaves of value noise, two halftone lookups
No render targets, no textures, no allocations per frame

paper.description: The stock the inks are printed on. An explicit colour rather than `auto`, which adopts the page's own background and is the right default for almost every other item here. A halftone is ink on paper: the dots are a partial covering that lets the stock through, so on a near-black ground there is nothing for them to be a partial covering of and two saturated inks come out muddy. Pass `auto` if you do want it to take the page it is dropped on.

inkA.description: First plate. A desaturated near-black reads as ink; pure black reads as a hole.

inkB.description: Second plate. This is where the colour lives, so change this one first.

scale.description: Size of the ink shapes. Lower is broader and calmer.

screen.description: Halftone frequency. Above about 20 the screen stops reading as a screen and starts reading as noise.

angleA.description: Screen angle of the first plate.

angleB.description: Screen angle of the second plate. Keep it at least 30 degrees from angleA. Closer than that and the two screens beat against each other.

drift.description: Registration error: how far the plates slide apart over a loop. Zero is a clean print and much duller.

coverage.description: Ink density. Past 0.7 the plates flood and the paper stops showing through.

grain.description: Paper tooth. Static by design. Animated grain flickers, and a flicker this fine is what WCAG 2.3.1 exists to prevent.

period.description: Seconds for one full loop. The animation is exactly periodic over this. Slow on purpose: the plates should drift apart over half a minute, which reads as a press settling rather than as something happening.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. Pick one that composes rather than the frame at zero.

instruction: ambient, nothing to do
intro:
Overprint is a full-bleed background that behaves like a two-colour print. Two
ink plates, a desaturated near-black and a burnt orange, are screened into
halftone dots at different angles and multiplied over the paper colour. That is
what a second pass of ink does to the first. Over the loop the plates slide
fractionally out of registration, which is the misprint that makes a risograph
look alive.

It is one WebGL2 fragment shader on one full-screen triangle. No three.js, no
textures, no render targets, no npm dependencies.

It needs a light background. Multiplying ink into black gets you black.

The defaults are tuned to be looked at: dense, plenty of solid ink. If you are
putting text on top, that is too much. Drop `coverage` to about 0.2 and raise
`period` to 15. Do not reach for opacity instead. Opacity greys the paper and
loses the thing that makes it look printed.

name: HalftoneMagnifier
description: A printer's glass on the page: continuous tone until you look closely, then dots

notes: The picture is the host element's own child. It is hidden from sight and left in the document, so the alt text is whatever you wrote and a page with no JavaScript still shows it
The screen ruling belongs to the print rather than to the viewer, so the cell is magnified along with everything else and turning the zoom up makes the dots bigger rather than finer
Four plates at 15, 75, 0 and 45 degrees, with grey component replacement, so what resolves under the glass is a rosette rather than four screens fighting
Nothing is integrated against the previous frame. The glass is exactly where the pointer is, so renderAtTime is pure in t and a scripted path replays identically
No fwidth anywhere. The lens sits inside a branch and derivatives in non-uniform control flow are undefined, so every edge width is worked out from the device pixel ratio instead
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes
Outside the glass it is one texture read per pixel. Everything expensive is inside a branch that most of the frame never takes
Inside the glass: three texture reads for the lateral colour, then four screens each testing nine neighbouring cells. The neighbours are what stop a dot past half a cell being clipped square
The image uploads once, on load. Nothing is uploaded per frame

paper.description: The sheet the picture is printed on. It shows between the dots, so it is most of what you see in the light passages under the glass. `auto` takes it from the page, so the effect adopts whatever it is dropped onto.

yellow.description: The yellow plate. Barely visible on its own, which is why it goes at zero degrees where the interference would show most.

black.description: The black plate, which also tints the barrel. A desaturated near-black reads as ink; pure black reads as a hole.

size.description: Radius of the glass, as a share of the short side, so it keeps its size when the element changes shape. Past about 0.4 it stops being a glass on a picture and becomes a picture with a border.

zoom.description: How much it magnifies. This magnifies the screen as well as the picture, because the ruling belongs to the press: turning it up makes the dots bigger, never finer.

screen.description: The print's screen ruling, as a cell in CSS pixels before magnification. Low is a fine screen and a magazine; high is a coarse one and a newspaper. Below about 2 the rosette is finer than the glass can show and you get tone under the glass as well as outside it, which is the one setting that defeats the whole thing.

bulge.description: How much the magnification eases off towards the rim, the way a real lens does. At 0 the glass magnifies evenly and the edge reads as a hole cut in the picture rather than as something resting on it.

fringe.description: Lateral colour at the rim. Every simple lens has it and every one shows it most at the edge, so a little is what makes the glass read as glass. Past about 0.03 it reads as a broken monitor.

rim.description: How strongly the barrel reads: the ring and the short fall into shade just inside it. This is what makes the glass an object sitting on the page rather than a filter applied to part of it.

grain.description: Paper tooth over the whole thing, inside the glass and out.

instruction: move the cursor over the picture
intro:
A printer's glass laid on the page.

The picture is continuous tone until you look closely, and then it is dots. That
is not a stylisation. It is what a printed photograph is, and it is the one
thing a screen never shows you: away from the glass the halftone is finer than
the eye resolves and reads as tone, which is the entire reason printing works at
all, and under the glass it resolves into four screens at four angles.

So the dots are not drawn at whatever size looks good. They are drawn at
`screen` pixels in the print and magnified along with everything else, which is
why turning `zoom` up makes them bigger rather than finer. A screen ruling
belongs to the press, not to the person looking at it.

The four angles are 15, 75, 0 and 45 degrees, and they are not decoration.
Thirty degrees between the strong plates is what keeps their interference down
to a fine rosette instead of a coarse plaid, and yellow sits at zero because it
is the plate you cannot see anyway. The ink that all three of cyan, magenta and
yellow have in common is pulled out and printed as black instead, which is what
a press does and the reason a shadow in a printed photograph is not a muddy
brown.

One WebGL2 fragment shader on one full-screen triangle. No three.js, no
dependency.

name: HalftoneReveal
description: A picture arriving dot by dot, the way a halftone comes up on press

notes: The picture is the host element's own child. It is hidden from sight and left in the document, so the alt text is whatever you wrote and a page with no JavaScript still shows it

The two tonal orders read the tone at the pixel rather than at each cell centre, which would be nine more texture samples. The difference is sub-cell on a photograph and the ordering is a soft field, so it costs nothing visible
renderAtTime is pure in t, so replaying is a matter of resetting the clock rather than restarting anything
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes
One texture read and one hash per pixel, and a union over the nine cells around it. The neighbours are what stop a dot past half a cell being clipped square
The image uploads once, on load. Nothing is uploaded per frame
The screen is laid out in CSS pixels, so the cost is per pixel and does not change with the cell size

paper.description: Shown wherever a dot has not grown yet, which at the start is the whole frame. Match it to the page behind or the reveal begins as a visible panel. `auto` takes it from the page, so the effect adopts whatever it is dropped onto.

screen.description: Cell size in CSS pixels. Bigger cells are a coarser screen and a more obviously printed arrival. Laid out in pixels rather than in UV so the dots stay round and keep their size when the element changes shape.

angle.description: Screen angle in degrees. 45 is the one a printer reaches for, because a screen on the square reads as a grid and fights whatever is underneath it.

sweep.description: Direction the reveal travels, in degrees. 0 runs left to right. Only visible when scatter is below 1.

scatter.description: 0 is a clean directional sweep, 1 is a random dissolve with no direction at all. Between the two the sweep keeps its direction but its leading edge is ragged, which is the part worth having.

order.description: The queue the cells arrive in. sweep runs across the frame along `sweep`; centre works outward from the middle and edges closes inward from the border; shadows brings the dark areas up first, which is the order a press lays ink down in, and highlights does the reverse, which reads as a picture emerging out of the paper rather than being printed onto it.

shape.description: The shape of the dot. All three are screens a press has actually used: round is the default everywhere, square holds its shape into the shadows instead of merging, which is why newspapers used it, and diamond breaks up the jump at fifty percent where round dots all meet their neighbours at once and the midtone goes abruptly dark.

feather.description: How much of the reveal has cells part way through at any one moment. Low is a hard edge travelling across; high has the whole frame coming up together.

grain.description: Paper tooth over the whole thing.

duration.description: Milliseconds from blank paper to the finished picture.

instruction: press replay to run it again
intro:
A picture arriving the way a printed one does.

Not a fade and not a wipe. The image is screened into halftone cells and each
cell's dot grows from nothing to full. That is how a halftone carries tone in the
first place, so growing the dots is the honest way to bring one in, and it reads
as a press coming up to pressure rather than as opacity being turned up.

The cells do not all start together. Each gets an order, blended between where it
sits along the sweep direction and a hash of its coordinates, so `scatter` runs
from a clean directional sweep at 0 to a random dissolve at 1. Everything useful
is in between: the sweep keeps its direction, but its leading edge is ragged
rather than ruled.

The dots are tested against the whole neighbourhood rather than against their own
cell. A dot only stays a dot while it fits inside its cell, and past half a cell
width a single-cell test clips it against the edges, so the dots grow into
rounded squares and then into plain squares and the whole thing ends up looking
like blocks. Taking the union over the nine cells around each pixel lets them
spill over the boundaries and merge, which is what ink does. The star-shaped
scraps of paper left between merged dots near the end are not an artefact: that
is the shadow-dot stage of a real screen.

One WebGL2 fragment shader on one full-screen triangle. No three.js, no
dependency, no render targets.

name: HighlighterMark
description: Somebody going through a page with a highlighter, marking one phrase at a time, overshooting the ends

notes: It marks the `<mark>` elements already in the text, and that is the whole interface. The browser has had an element for this bit matters since HTML 4 and screen readers announce it, so a page using it reads correctly with the effect off, with CSS off and in a feed reader. Nothing here parses prose, searches for strings or wraps words in spans

Not a CSS background. An animated linear-gradient gets the sweep right and everything else wrong: the band is level, the edges are straight by construction, it stops exactly on the last letter, and the ink is the same everywhere

A hand does none of those. The band has a slight slope, the edges are ragged at the scale of the tip, the stroke overshoots the phrase by a different amount at each end, and the ink doubles where the pen went back over it. The second pass is most of what makes it read as a pen rather than as a fill
