Blended with multiply, because that is what translucent ink on paper does: the glyphs stay on top and darken the ink rather than being covered by it. It is also why this is a paper item and has no dark version. Multiply against a dark ground is black
A phrase that wraps gets one stroke per line, because that is what a person does, and getClientRects already returns exactly those boxes

The geometry is built once and the animation is a clip rectangle widening over it, so a frame costs one attribute per stroke. Rebuilt only on resize or when an option that changes the shape changes, because measuring forces layout

The host is promoted to position: relative if it is static, because the overlay is absolutely positioned inside it, and a static host silently puts every stroke at the top left of the page. Put back on teardown
One SVG, one polygon pair per stroke, and one clip rectangle per stroke resized per frame. There is no per-pixel work at all
Measured with `pnpm budget` at 1280 by 720: 0.0ms, which is to say below the resolution of the timer once style and layout have been forced. The cost of this item is not in its frames
getClientRects is the expensive call and it runs on setup and on resize, not per frame. It is cached against a key built from the options that change the geometry
No canvas and no WebGL context, so this does not compete with a backdrop for the one the page is allowed

selector.description: What to mark, inside the element this is mounted on. The default is the element HTML already has for the job, and using anything else means the page stops saying what it means when the effect is off.

ink.description: The ink. Highlighter yellow is yellow because it is the hue that darkens text least at a given opacity: a blue of the same strength takes a paragraph down to grey. Any colour works, but check the text through it before shipping a dark one.

strength.description: How opaque one pass of the pen is. The second pass goes over the first and multiplies rather than adds, so the middle of a stroke is always darker than this. Past about 0.8 the text underneath starts to struggle, which is a contrast failure rather than a look.

height.description: Band height as a share of the line's height. Under 1 by default, and sat low on the line, because a highlighter covers the body of the text and lets the ascenders out of the top. At 1.2 it is a wide chisel tip and starts to touch the line above.

overshoot.description: How far the stroke runs past the phrase, with a different amount drawn at each end from the seed. Nobody stops exactly on the last letter, and at 0 this reads as a rectangle that happens to be ragged.

tilt.description: Slope of the hand. A degree is enough: it is the difference between a stroke and a highlight, and it is the first thing to turn down if the marks start to look untidy rather than human.

rag.description: How ragged the edges are, at the scale of the pen tip. The two edges are ragged independently, because a soft tip wears differently on each side. At 0 the stroke is a clean polygon, which is a sticker.

duration.description: Milliseconds for one stroke to be drawn, eased out, because a pen is thrown rather than driven. A long duration reads as a machine filling a box; this is somebody moving their wrist once.

stagger.description: Milliseconds between the start of one stroke and the next. Less than the duration, so a reader is still finishing one mark as the next begins, which is what reading with a pen in your hand looks like. At 0 every mark appears at once and the sequence is lost.

hold.description: Milliseconds of stillness before the first stroke. The page should be readable for a moment before anything is marked on it, or the marks arrive before anybody has seen what is being marked.

seed.description: Seed for the hand: the rag on both edges, the slope of each stroke, how far each one overshoots and where the second pass starts and stops. The same seed draws the same strokes every time.

instruction: press Replay to mark it again

credit.what: marking running text with a highlighter rather than a background, from the Highlighter Markup page
credit.author: Ray Velez

intro:
HighlighterMark is somebody going through a page with a highlighter, marking
one phrase at a time and overshooting the ends.

name: ImageGalleryLightbox
description: A contact sheet that opens into a lightbox you can arrow, swipe or play through

notes: Uses <dialog>.showModal(), so the focus trap, Escape, top layer, inerting and focus restoration are the browser's
The fade uses transition-behavior: allow-discrete and @starting-style; where those are unsupported the overlay appears instantly, which is a graceful loss
No carousel library, no focus-trap library, no portal, no scroll-lock package
Swipe is Pointer Events, and is ignored for mouse input, where a small drag is the start of a click rather than a gesture

The space around the plate closes the overlay, as an addition to the close button rather than a replacement: Nielsen Norman find that many readers never discover a click outside and others use it by accident, and a lightbox is the right place for it because a mistake costs one click to reopen

The usual event.target === dialog test does nothing for a full-bleed overlay, because there is no backdrop to click and every pixel is inside the dialog. What the press was not on is the question that survives, so it is a closest() test against the plate and the controls

Press and release, both ends checked, so a drag off the plate or a caption being selected does not throw the overlay away. The listener is on the dialog rather than the stage, so a gesture that starts beside the plate is heard wherever it ends

closedby=any is deliberately not used. Safari has it in preview only, and native light dismiss fires when press and release both land on the dialog, which is what a horizontal swipe beside the plate does: on a phone the gallery would close instead of moving on
No JavaScript runs per frame. The enter is one CSS animation on the image
Thumbnails below the first row are lazy, and the two neighbouring full-size files are decoded while you are looking at the current one
Intrinsic width and height are required on every plate so the sheet reserves its shape and does not reflow as the files arrive

label.description: Accessible name for the sheet and for the overlay. Keep it a noun. It is read out as the name of the whole gallery.

closeLabel.description: Text on the close control. There is a visible one as well as Escape, because Escape is not discoverable and on a touch device it does not exist.

columns.description: Columns at the widest the container gets. The sheet steps down on its own below that, because it fits its container rather than the viewport.

autoplay.description: Seconds between plates once the overlay is open. Zero is off, and off is the default: a gallery that starts moving on its own is rarely what the reader wanted. Any value above zero renders a pause control, and reduced motion turns it off entirely.

playLabel.description: Text on the autoplay control when it is stopped.

pauseLabel.description: Text on the autoplay control when it is running.

instruction: open a plate, then try the arrow keys and Escape
intro:
Plate is a contact sheet that opens into a lightbox. A grid of numbered plates,
and an overlay you move through with the arrow keys, a swipe, the controls, or an
autoplay you have to start yourself.

The overlay is a real `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()`. That is the decision
the rest of it hangs off. The browser then gives you the focus trap, Escape, the
top layer, inerting the page behind, and returning focus to where you came from.
Every one of those is something hand-rolled galleries get subtly wrong, and none
of it is code in this repo or a package in yours. There is no carousel library
here, no focus-trap library, no portal and no scroll-lock.

What is left is the part worth building. Arrow keys and Home and End. A swipe
that is ignored for mouse input, where a small drag is the start of a click
rather than a gesture. Neighbour preload, so the next plate is already decoded
before you ask for it. And a counter, because a gallery with no sense of how far
through you are is a gallery you leave.

The overlay is paper rather than black. A dark lightbox is the convention and it
is the wrong one here: it turns every warm image cold, and it makes the caption
the brightest thing on the screen. A plate in a book sits on the page, with a
margin, which is what this does.

name: InkBleedText
description: Type on paper too absorbent for it, the ink wicking along the fibres

notes: No canvas and no WebGL. One SVG displacement filter, which is the honest mechanism: turbulence supplies the fibre and feDisplacementMap pushes each pixel of the glyph by the amount of fibre under it
Not a blur. A Gaussian softens an edge evenly, which is a lens out of focus rather than ink spreading, and it is what makes most attempts at this look photographic rather than printed
fractalNoise rather than turbulence: turbulence takes the modulus of each octave and leaves hard creases that read as cracks in the letter
The filter region is widened to 150%, because displaced pixels outside it are cut off and a heavily bled letter would come back with its edges sliced square
Each instance gets its own filter, so two bled headings on a page do not share one
Holds 59.8fps at 1440 by 900 at 2x DPR, measured, which is indistinguishable from the same page with no filter on it

That is only true because the turbulence is cached. It is the expensive half, and the fibre of a sheet does not change between frames, so only the displacement scale is set per frame. Setting baseFrequency every frame instead costs a full filter rebuild each time
SVG filters are rasterised on the CPU in some browsers. Use it on a heading, not on a page of body text, and expect the cost to scale with the filtered area

bleed.description: How far the ink creeps, in pixels, at its furthest. Past about 8 the counters of a and e close up and the word stops being readable, which is a real thing badly printed paper does and rarely a thing you want.

floor.description: How far it has crept at its least. Deliberately not zero: a sheet that has taken ink does not give it back, so the letter never returns to a clean edge.

fibre.description: Coarseness of the fibre, as a turbulence base frequency. Lower is a longer, rougher, more absorbent fibre. This is the one to reach for if the bleed looks like noise rather than paper.

detail.description: Layers of fibre. More is a finer, more tangled structure and more work for the filter; the gain above four is hard to see.

period.description: Seconds for one breath of the ink. Driven by a cosine, so it is exactly periodic and the loop closes.

seed.description: Which sheet of paper. Any two seeds give different fibre; the same seed always gives the same sheet.

instruction: ambient, watch the ink creep
intro:
Type printed on paper that is too absorbent for it.

The usual version of this is a CRT wobble: the glyph edges shimmer sideways like
a signal losing lock. Paper has its own way of ruining a letter and it is nothing
like that. Ink wicks along the fibres, so the edge does not move, it grows teeth.
Serifs fill in, counters close up, and the letter gains a fuzz that is irregular
at the scale of the fibre rather than smooth.

An SVG displacement filter is the honest way to draw it. Turbulence supplies the
fibre and `feDisplacementMap` pushes each pixel of the glyph sideways by the
amount of fibre under it, which is exactly the mechanism: the ink goes where the
paper lets it.

It is deliberately **not** a blur. A Gaussian softens an edge evenly, which is a
lens out of focus rather than ink spreading, and it is the thing that makes most
attempts at this look photographic rather than printed.

It also uses `fractalNoise` rather than turbulence proper. Turbulence takes the
modulus of each octave, which leaves hard creases that read as cracks in the
letter rather than as fibre.

No canvas and no WebGL.

name: IrisReveal
description: A camera iris opening on whatever is behind it, with as many sides as it has blades and a swing as it goes

notes: An iris is not a circle growing. A diaphragm is a ring of overlapping blades and the hole they leave is a polygon with as many sides as there are blades: five give a pentagon, nine give something close to a circle but not one. Anybody who has seen an out-of-focus highlight in a photograph has seen this shape, which is why a growing circle reads as a spotlight and a growing heptagon reads as a lens

The blades swing as they open, so the whole opening rotates. On a real lens that is a consequence of the mechanism rather than a decision, and leaving it out is the clearest way to make this look like a mask

The edges bow. A blade is a curved plate, so each side of the hole is a shallow arc bulging inwards. The amount is measured rather than chosen: a polygon's inradius is its circumradius times the cosine of half a blade's angle, so 1/cos minus 1 is exactly how far the middle of a straight edge sits inside the circle it is cutting, and `bow` is the share of that taken back

It reaches past the far corner rather than to the edge. A box's corner is further from the centre than its side and the polygon's own inradius is shorter again, so an opening that stops at 1 leaves slivers in the corners that read as a dirty lens
Drawn with clip-path on the element itself. Nothing is added to the DOM, nothing is drawn, and the content is untouched: it selects, scrolls and reads the whole time, it is simply not all visible yet
The polygon is in percentages, so it follows a resize with no measuring at all
ground is `either` and for once that needs no argument: there is no colour in this item. It clips whatever you put it on, so there is nothing to tune against a background
One clip-path string per frame, built from blades times seven points, and skipped entirely when it comes out the same as the last one
Measured with `pnpm budget` at 1280 by 720: 0.1ms with style and layout forced, which is the cheapest item measured so far
No canvas, no WebGL context and nothing appended to the DOM, so this is free to put on a dozen elements at once
clip-path on a large element is composited rather than repainted in current browsers, but a host with a backdrop-filter inside it is the exception and will repaint

blades.description: How many blades, and so how many sides the opening has. Five is a cheap lens and the shape is unmistakable; nine is an expensive one and reads as nearly round. Past about twelve nobody can tell it from a circle and you have lost the only thing that says lens.

swing.description: Degrees the opening rotates between shut and open. This is the mechanism showing, and at 0 the effect is a polygon being scaled, which is a mask. Large values spin rather than swing and start to read as a shutter on a film projector.

bow.description: How far each edge bows into the hole, as a share of the gap between the straight edge and the circle through the vertices. At 0 the opening is a strict polygon; at 1 it is a circle and the blade count stops mattering. The default is a plate with a gentle curve on it.

from.description: How far open it starts, as a share of the finished opening. A little rather than nothing, because a real diaphragm does not close to a point and a pinhole gives the eye something to track from. At 0 the first frames are an empty box.

duration.description: Milliseconds for the iris to open, eased at both ends because a diaphragm is sprung at both ends of its travel. An ease-out alone makes it look dropped.

hold.description: Milliseconds of stillness before it starts. Short: this is a reveal, and the thing being revealed is what somebody came for.

x.description: Where the centre sits across the element. Off-centre is worth trying when the content has a subject: opening on the face rather than on the middle of the frame is what a camera operator would do.

y.description: Where the centre sits down the element. The reach is measured to the furthest corner from wherever this puts the centre, so an off-centre iris still clears the box.

instruction: press Replay to open it again

credit.what: an aperture cut into the page, from the Recessed Aperture page. The blade geometry here is worked out rather than taken
credit.author: Ray Velez

intro: IrisReveal is a camera iris opening on whatever is behind it.

name: LightShafts
description: Light coming through something and falling across the frame in bands, with the shadow edges going soft as they travel

notes: The whole image comes from one quantity, the angle from the source to the pixel, read against a repeating profile of bars and gaps. That is why the beams fan out from the source rather than running down the frame in parallel, and why pushing the source away straightens them on its own: distance is what turns a fan into parallel lines, and the sun is the limiting case

The shadow edges soften with distance travelled. A shadow is sharp only near the thing that cast it, because the source has width and the half-shadow it throws grows as the shadow runs. One multiplication, and it is the whole difference between a beam of light and a pale triangle

The motes are drawn only inside the beams. Light in clean air is invisible from the side, so the dust is not decoration over the shafts, it is the reason there is anything to see. They drift across the beams rather than along them, because dust in a room is moved by the air and not by the light
The bar pitch is scaled by the distance of the source, so moving the light out to straighten the beams does not also squeeze them into a sliver
There is an ambient term as well as the beams. Without it the unlit bands are flat and the frame reads as two colours rather than as one room
Declared as working on either ground. The default is sun across a pale wall; the same effect with a dark ground is a projector beam, and the dust matters more there
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes

Measured at 0.086 mean absolute change per frame on a 0 to 255 scale, which is in line with MeshGradient at 0.091 and PrismSpectrum at 0.080. Nearly all of it is the band edges sweeping rather than the motes: the motes were the obvious suspect and changing them moved the number by 0.0004

One atan, one exp and two evaluations of value noise per pixel, for the motes. No textures, no render targets and no shadow map: the occluder is a function rather than geometry, which is the whole reason this is cheap
Timed with a readPixels after each draw so the number includes the GPU. At 640 by 360 it came to 0.72ms against 0.88 for MeshGradient and 1.01 for PrismSpectrum measured the same way

ground.description: The surface the light falls on, which is that surface in shadow: the lit bands are added on top of it, so it has to sit below them with room to spare. A ground as pale as the light clips to white across the whole frame, which is the first thing that went wrong here. Set it near black and the same effect is a projector beam in a dark room. `auto` takes it from the page, so the effect adopts whatever it is dropped onto.

light.description: The light itself, added to the ground rather than mixed with it, because light is additive and a shaft that darkens what it crosses is a shaft of paint. Warm, because daylight through a window is warm and a neutral white beam reads as a lightbox.

angle.description: Where the source sits, in degrees around the frame, with 0 to the right. Above and to one side is the one that reads as a window; straight on reads as a torch pointed at the viewer.

distance.description: How far off frame the source is, in frame widths. Near is a lamp and the beams fan hard; far is the sun and they run very nearly parallel. There is no separate setting for parallel beams, because this is what parallel beams are.

bars.description: How many bars the light comes through. A few wide ones read as glazing bars or a door ajar; a great many read as a blind, and past about twenty the frame is a texture rather than a room.

gap.description: The share of each repeat that is open. Think of it as the tilt of a blind: at 0.9 the slats are nearly edge on and the room is bright, at 0.1 they are nearly shut.

softness.description: How soft a shadow edge is where it leaves the bar. This is the near edge only. At 0 the beam starts with a razor edge, which is what a point source does and no real source is.

spread.description: How much softer that edge gets with the distance the shadow has travelled. The detail that makes the light read as light. At 0 the beams are triangles with parallel sides, which is every other version of this effect.

reach.description: How far the light gets across the frame, in frame widths, falling off as it goes. Short is a small window in a large room; long floods the frame and leaves nothing for the beams to be brighter than.

strength.description: Brightness of the light, added to the ground rather than mixed into it. On a pale ground this clips long before it reaches 2, and a quarter is already a bright day: the numbers here are small because the ground is most of the way up the scale before any light arrives.

dust.description: Motes in the air. At 0 the beams are clean bands, which is what light in a vacuum would look like if you could see it, which you could not.

drift.description: Degrees the source swings over one period. Small. The sun moves through about fifteen degrees in an hour, and anything much faster reads as somebody carrying a lamp past the window. It is also the one setting that drives the cost of the animation: a band edge is the highest-contrast thing in the frame, so swinging the light moves a great many pixels. Measured, dropping this from 7 to 4 took the change per frame from 0.151 to 0.086.

period.description: Seconds for one swing and back. Long, because this sits behind something else and a backdrop has to survive being ignored.

instruction: the light swings on its own
intro:
LightShafts is light coming into a room through something, and falling across
the frame in bands. Sun through a blind, through glazing bars, through a door
left ajar.

Every version of this effect anybody ships is a few pale triangles fanned out
from a corner, and they all have the same tell: the beams are solid, their edges
are equally sharp all the way along, and nothing accounts for why they are there
at all. A shaft of light is not a shape. It is the gap in whatever is between
you and the sun.

So this is built the way the thing works.

**There is a source, off frame, at a distance.** Everything is drawn from the
angle to it, which is what makes the beams fan rather than run parallel. Move
the source far enough away and they do run parallel, because that is what
distance does to a fan, and the sun is the limiting case. There is no separate
setting for parallel beams, because this is what parallel beams are.

**There is an occluder.** A repeating profile of bars and gaps, crossed by the
rays. The bright bands are the gaps, not the bars.

**The edges go soft with distance.** A shadow edge is sharp only near the thing
that cast it, because the source has width and the half-shadow it throws grows
as the shadow travels. This one multiplication is the whole difference between a
beam of light and a triangle.

**The beam is visible because of what is in the air.** Light in clean air cannot
be seen from the side, so the motes are not decoration over the top of the
shafts: they are the reason there is anything to see, and they are drawn only
inside the beams.

name: LightningVein
description: A discharge branching across a dark sky, built by recursive displacement and deliberately flashing far slower than the real thing

notes: Canvas 2D rather than a shader, because the subject is a path. A branching polyline is a handful of line segments to a canvas and a signed distance field to a fragment shader, which would be hundreds of distance tests per pixel for a shape that is mostly empty space

The path is built by recursive midpoint displacement: one segment, push the midpoint along its normal, repeat on both halves with half the push. That gives kinks at every scale, which is what a discharge looks like. A wobble applied per step has detail at one scale only and reads as a scribble
The push is along the segment normal rather than along x. Pushing along x gives a bolt that is only ever ragged left and right, which reads as a flag rather than as electricity
Branches leave the channel and never rejoin it. They start below the head, because a branch off the very top has nothing above it to have come from

Flashing is bounded on purpose and this is the one number not to raise. WCAG 2.3.1 is Level A and wants nothing flashing more than three times a second; real lightning flickers far faster. A strike here brightens at most twice and the next is a `period` away, which at the default is two brightenings in nine seconds

Nothing is random at render time. The strike index comes from `t` by division, the bolt is built from a generator seeded on that index, and the same `t` always gives the same bolt. That is what lets the recorder seek and what closes the loop
The glow is three strokes of increasing width rather than shadowBlur. shadowBlur on a path of a thousand points is the slowest thing a canvas can be asked to do, and the falloff is indistinguishable
Built for a dark ground and declared as one. A discharge is light, and on a pale ground there is nothing for it to be brighter than
The path is built once per strike and kept, not rebuilt per frame. Six passes over a growing array is a few thousand points of arithmetic for a shape that does not change while the strike burns
Most frames draw nothing at all. Between strikes the envelope is under a thousandth and the renderer returns after clearing, so the resting cost of this backdrop is one fill

Zero WebGL contexts, which is the quiet advantage of doing this in 2D. The one context budget is for the page as a whole, and a storm behind your content does not spend any of it, so a WebGL item elsewhere on the page is unaffected

sky.description: The sky behind it. `auto` takes it from the page, which is almost always right: the strike should sit in your page rather than bring its own rectangle of night.

bolt.description: The channel itself. Near white with a little blue in it reads as hot; pure white reads as a drawn line.

halo.description: The glow around the channel. Cooler and dimmer than the bolt, because air lit from the side scatters blue.

period.description: Seconds from one strike to the next. Exactly periodic over this, and the lower bound is held well above anything WCAG 2.3.1 would count.

lean.description: How far the strike wanders off vertical overall, as a share of the width. At 0 it falls straight down and looks drawn.

jitter.description: The first displacement, as a share of the width. Every pass after it is half the one before, so this sets the character of the whole path.

detail.description: How many times the path is subdivided. Six is sixty-four segments. Above seven the extra kinks are smaller than a pixel and cost without showing.

branches.description: Limbs thrown off the main channel. At 0 it is a single stroke, which reads as a crack rather than a discharge.

weight.description: Width of the main channel. The glow is drawn from this, so raising it thickens everything rather than only the core.

afterglow.description: How long the channel stays faintly lit once the flash is over. This is most of what makes it read as a discharge rather than as a line that was switched off.

seed.description: Changes every bolt in the sequence without changing anything else about them.

instruction: it strikes on its own
intro:
LightningVein is a discharge branching across a dark sky. A strike arrives,
throws a few limbs, burns for a fraction of a second and leaves the channel
glowing faintly behind it. Then nothing happens for several seconds.

Three things carry it, and the first is what separates this from a jagged line
with a glow on it.

**The path is built by recursive displacement.** Start with one segment, push
its midpoint sideways, then do the same to both halves with half the push, and
again. That gives kinks at every scale: a lean across the whole strike, bends
within the lean, and a tremble on the short runs. A wobble applied per step has
detail at one scale only, which is why it reads as a scribble rather than as
electricity finding its way down.

**The push is along the segment normal, not along x.** Pushing along x gives a
bolt that is ragged left and right wherever it is pointing, which reads as a
flag. Along the normal, the kinks stay perpendicular to the run of the channel.

**The flicker is bounded, and that is a requirement rather than a preference.**
Real lightning flickers many times a second. WCAG 2.3.1 is Level A and wants
nothing flashing more than three times a second, so this does not imitate one:
a strike brightens at most twice, and the next strike is a whole `period` away.
At the default that is two brightenings in nine seconds. It still reads as
lightning, because the shape is doing the work rather than the strobing.

name: MagneticButton
description: An element that leans towards the cursor before the cursor arrives

notes: No canvas and no WebGL. One CSS transform
Reads the pointer at window scope, because the point is reacting to a cursor that is still outside the element
The easing is a CSS transition rather than a per-frame spring, so nothing integrates and renderAtTime stays pure
Composited transform only
One getBoundingClientRect per frame while the cursor is in range, and none when it is not

reach.description: How far outside the element the pull starts, as a multiple of its own size. 1 is one element-width of empty space around it. Large values on a small button make it twitch at things happening on the other side of the page.

strength.description: How far the element travels towards the cursor, as a fraction of the gap. Above 0.6 the cursor can never catch it, which is funny once and annoying afterwards.

maxShift.description: Cap on the travel, whatever the strength works out to. This is what stops a wide element sliding out of its own layout.

scale.description: Scale at full pull. 1 is no growth.

rotate.description: Degrees of lean at full pull, following the cursor left and right. Off by default: on text it reads as a wobble rather than a lean.

ease.description: How long it takes to follow the cursor, and to let go. Low is a rubber band; high is treacle. The release matters more than the catch.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. At rest there is no pointer, so this draws the element unmoved, which is the right answer.

instruction: move the cursor near the button, not onto it
intro:
Magnet leans an element towards the cursor before the cursor gets there, and lets
go once it has passed. One CSS transform. No canvas, no WebGL, no npm dependency.

It reads the pointer at window scope rather than element scope, because the whole
point is reacting to a cursor that is still outside. The runtime reports
element-relative coordinates that go past 0 and 1, so "one and a half element
widths away, up and to the right" is a number rather than a guess.

The easing is a CSS transition, not a per-frame spring. Nothing integrates
against the previous frame, so `renderAtTime` stays pure and the recorder can
scrub it. The release is what people actually notice, and a transition handles
the release better than most springs do.

`destroy()` clears every style it set.

name: MarbledPaper
description: Ink floated on size, dropped and then raked, the way marbled endpapers are made

notes: Every marbling operation has a closed-form inverse, so each pixel runs the session backwards instead of the tray being simulated forwards. One pass, no render targets, no feedback
The drop loop runs backwards and stops at the first drop that contains the point, so raising the count costs much less than it looks like it should

Each pixel is sampled four times on a rotated grid and averaged. The edge you see is a circle dragged through two combs and through every drop laid after it, so it reaches the screen at an arbitrary angle, and there is no analytic width to smoothstep against: fwidth() of the distance would be a derivative taken inside a loop that breaks per pixel, which is undefined in non-uniform control flow
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes

Measured 0.45ms at one drop, 2.25ms at the default sixty and 2.63ms at seventy-two, at 1440 by 900 on an RTX 3080, timed with a readPixels sync because without one you are timing the dispatch rather than the shader

Four of those milliseconds in five are the four samples per pixel. Whether a point is inside a drop is a yes or no question, so one sample can only produce two answers and every boundary arrives as a staircase. The samples sit on a rotated grid, which is what 4x MSAA uses and for the same reason

Cost rises with the drop count but far less than linearly: the loop breaks the moment a drop claims the point, so most pixels walk only the last few. The pixels that walk the whole list are the paper margins
One inverse-drop per step, which is a dot product and a square root. Nothing is uploaded per frame and only uniforms change

paper.description: The size in the tray, and what shows wherever no ink reached. Match it to the page behind or the margins read as a panel. `auto` takes it from the page, so the effect adopts whatever it is dropped onto.

ink.description: The main ink. Roughly two thirds of the drops are this, or this thinned toward the paper, which is what a second pass of one colour looks like once the first has spread.

accent.description: The second ink, on roughly a third of the drops.

drops.description: How many drops go into the tray. Each one pushes every earlier one outward, so this sets the density of the rings rather than just the amount of ink.

scale.description: How large the pattern reads. Higher zooms in on fewer, bigger shapes; lower pulls back and shows more of the tray, down to the paper margin round the edge of the ink.

spread.description: How far the drops are scattered. Low stacks them into a single rosette, which is the stone pattern; high covers the tray.

size.description: How big each drop is before anything pushes it. The ink conserves area, so the patch it finally covers is the sum of the drop areas: halving this and quadrupling the count gives the same coverage at four times the detail, which is the knob you actually want.

rake.description: How far the comb pulls the ink across. Zero leaves the drops as plain rings, which is a stone marble and a perfectly good thing to stop at.

comb.description: Teeth per unit across the comb. Higher is a finer comb and a tighter zigzag.

swirl.description: A second comb drawn at right angles to the first. Two passes crossed is how a gel-git pattern is made; leave it at zero for a single-direction nonpareil.

grain.description: Paper tooth over the whole thing.

period.description: Seconds for one pass of the comb. Both combs run whole multiples of the same angle, so the pattern returns to exactly where it started and the loop is seamless. Slow on purpose: a comb you can watch crossing the tray is the loudest thing on the page.

instruction: ambient, watch the comb draw through
intro:
Ink floated on size, dropped, and then raked. The pattern on a marbled endpaper,
made the way the endpaper was.

This is not noise dressed up as marbling. Every operation a marbler performs on a
tray has a closed-form inverse, and that single fact is what the whole effect
rests on. A drop of ink pushes everything already floating outward by an exact
amount, conserving area. A comb drawn through displaces points along its own
direction by an amount that depends only on how far from it they sit, so the
displacement never changes the quantity the displacement was computed from. Both
undo in one step, with no iteration and no search.

So the tray is never simulated forwards. Each pixel runs the session backwards:
undo the combs, then undo the drops one at a time from the last to the first, and
the moment the point falls inside a drop you know which ink it was. That is the
colour. One pass, no render targets, no feedback, no history, and the result is
exact rather than approximated.

It gives the rings away for free, too. A drop laid down later pushes an earlier
one into an annulus around itself, and walking the operations backwards
reproduces that instead of having to draw it.

Measured at 0.42ms for one drop and 0.64ms for seventy-two, at 1440 by 900 on an
RTX 3080. The count costs far less than it looks like it should, because the loop
stops at the first drop that claims the point.

One WebGL2 fragment shader on one full-screen triangle. No three.js, no
dependency.

name: MaskedHeading
description: A heading uncovered by a sheet sliding off it, with the edge of that sheet torn rather than cut

notes: A straight-edged mask crossing a heading is a wipe, and a wipe reads as a machine because nothing in the physical world has an edge that straight. The whole item is in the edge

A deckle edge, the untrimmed side of a handmade sheet, has structure at two scales: a slow wander where the pulp ran thin against the deckle, and a fine fray of fibres on top. One scale alone gives either a gentle curve or a saw blade, and neither reads as paper

The tear is built once and keeps its shape as it travels, because a torn edge does not re-tear itself while the sheet is being pulled away. Regenerating it per frame is the quickest way to turn paper into a flame

It is a clip-path polygon and nothing else, so the text is never taken apart: it selects, wraps, translates and reads exactly as before. This and SplitFountainText are the only two effects here that leave the DOM alone
The clip is composited, so a heading being uncovered costs a transform rather than a repaint

The polygon closes across the side that stays uncovered, and the corners sit outside the box. Closing it the other way round clips the half you meant to keep, which looks like the animation running backwards
The travel goes past the end by the overshoot, so the torn edge clears the type rather than coming to rest somewhere across it

The travel starts and ends entirely off the element, by the depth of the tear at each end. Starting at exactly 0 looks like a bug rather than a sheet: the parts of the tear that poke forwards are already inside the box, so a sheet supposedly at rest leaks slivers of the heading through its own edge
One string built and one property written per frame, and only when the string has changed. The polygon is `points` plus two corners, so 48 points is a 50-point path
Nothing is created after mount and nothing is measured. The tear is sampled once per seed

direction.description: Which way the uncovered area grows. Up is a sheet lifted off, and it is the one that reads as paper rather than as a transition; the sideways ones read as a sheet being slid, which is also a real thing but a busier one on a wide heading.

duration.description: Milliseconds for the sheet to come away, eased so it arrives rather than stops. Quick: somebody pulling a sheet off a print does it in about a second, and anything slower reads as a curtain in a theatre.

hold.description: Milliseconds before it starts, and how you stagger two blocks on one page.

tear.description: How far the slow wander of the edge reaches, as a share of the element. This is the large structure: where the pulp ran thin. At 0 the edge is straight and you have a wipe.

fray.description: How far the fine fray reaches. The fibres, on top of the wander. Raise it past about 0.05 and the edge stops being torn paper and becomes a saw blade.

points.description: Points along the edge. More is a finer tear and a longer path: below about twenty the fray has nowhere to happen and the edge reads as a gentle curve, and past a hundred you are paying for detail smaller than a pixel.

overshoot.description: How far past the end the sheet travels, so the torn edge clears the type. At 0 it comes to rest exactly at the far side, which on a tear means a few fibres are still lying across the last line.

seed.description: Seed for the tear. The same seed gives the same sheet, so a recording and a live page match. Give two blocks on one page different seeds, or they are uncovered by the same torn sheet twice.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. For a one-shot reveal this should be a time after the sheet has gone, so the heading is simply there and unclipped.

instruction: press replay to uncover it again
intro:
MaskedHeading uncovers a heading by sliding a sheet off it, and the edge of that
sheet is torn rather than cut.

A straight-edged mask crossing a heading is a wipe, and a wipe reads as a
machine, because nothing in the physical world has an edge that straight. The
whole of this item is in the edge.

A **deckle edge** is the untrimmed side of a handmade sheet, where the pulp ran
thin against the frame. It has structure at two scales: a slow wander over a
third of the sheet, and a fine fray of fibres on top of it. One scale alone
gives either a gentle curve or a saw blade, and neither reads as paper. Both are
here.

The tear is built once and **keeps its shape as it travels**, because a torn
edge does not re-tear itself while you pull the sheet away. Regenerating it per
frame is the quickest way to turn paper into a flame.

name: MeshGradient
description: The soft flowing colour field behind half the software marketing on the web, lit by its own slope

notes: Three ingredients and nothing else: layered waves for scale, a domain warp so the bands bend around each other rather than staying parallel stripes, and shading taken from the slope of the same field

The shading is the part most versions of this leave out. On the original the plane is a mesh whose vertices are displaced, so the light follows the displacement; here the same derivative that would have moved a vertex lights the result instead. Without it the whole thing flattens into wallpaper
The diagonal edge people associate with this effect is not in the shader and should not be. On the original it is the container, skewed with CSS and clipped, which is two lines and is in the recipe

Every moving term is a sum of waves whose time coefficients are whole numbers of turns over the period, so the loop closes exactly. Noise advanced by time never returns to its first frame and the recorder needs it to
The warp is frozen while the layers drift through it. Warping the warp as well doubles the measured change per frame for something that reads as the whole image sliding
Declared as working on either ground. The default palette is warm paper with pastel layers; the same effect with dark colours over a dark base is the version everybody else ships
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes
Five fields of four waves each, so forty sines and forty cosines per pixel, and no textures, noise lookups or render targets
The cost is the pixel count rather than the shader, so a full-screen canvas at 2x device pixel ratio is the thing to watch

base.description: What the colour layers are laid over, and what shows wherever none of them reaches. Usually the palest of the four, because it is doing the job the paper does in print. `auto` takes it from the page, so the effect adopts whatever it is dropped onto.

one.description: The first colour layer, laid over the base. Keep the three within reach of each other on the wheel and mind what they make where they overlap: the first palette here had a peach under a cornflower, and peach under blue is tan, so the frame had a patch of mud in it that neither colour explains.

two.description: The second layer, over the first.

three.description: The third, and the one that shows least, because it is only drawn where its own field is high.

scale.description: Size of the shapes. Lower is fewer and larger, which is what a hero wants: the shapes should be bigger than the headline sitting on them, not a texture behind it.

warp.description: How far the field is bent before it is read. At 0 the layers are parallel bands, which is the single thing that gives away most attempts at this effect.

softness.description: Width of the transition between one layer and the next. This is the control that decides whether the result reads as a gradient or as a map of three countries.

relief.description: How much the field is lit by its own slope. Small, and the thing that makes it look like a surface being folded rather than a picture being blurred. At 0 it is wallpaper.

grain.description: Grain, which on a field this smooth is doing real work: it breaks the banding that eight bit colour leaves across a slow gradient. Static rather than crawling.

period.description: Seconds for one full cycle, and the pace control. Long on purpose: this sits behind a headline, and a backdrop has to survive being ignored.

instruction: it drifts on its own
intro:
The soft flowing colour field that sits behind half the software marketing on
the web, and behind Stripe's home page in particular.

It is worth being precise about what that effect is, because the usual
description is wrong in a way that matters. It is not a CSS gradient with more
stops, and it is not a blurred photograph of some blobs. The original is a plane
cut into a grid of a few hundred vertices, each pushed around by layered noise,
with three or four colour layers blended over each other by more noise.

Three ingredients, and this has all three:

**Layered waves.** Several octaves, each finer and weaker than the last. That is
what gives the field its sense of scale: broad shapes with detail inside them,
rather than one smooth blob or one busy texture.

**A domain warp.** The field is read at a position pushed sideways by another
field, which is what bends the bands around each other. At `warp` 0 you get
parallel stripes, and parallel stripes are the single thing that gives away most
attempts at this effect.

**Shading from the slope.** This is the one most copies leave out. On the
original the mesh is displaced, so the light follows the displacement; here the
same derivative that would have moved a vertex lights the result instead. Set
`relief` to 0 and the whole thing flattens into wallpaper. It is the difference
between a surface being folded and a picture being blurred.

name: MetaballField
description: Blobs that merge and part, raymarched from a distance field rather than modelled

notes: There is no geometry. The scene is a function that answers how far the nearest surface is, and the picture is made by stepping a ray forward by exactly that much. That is why the blobs can merge at all: two meshes cannot flow into one another without somebody rebuilding the mesh, while two distance fields merge by taking the smaller of the two

The softening of that minimum is the whole item. A plain min gives two spheres that interpenetrate with a visible crease; blending over a band leaves a fillet, and the neck and pinch it produces are what read as liquid

The ray skips straight to a bounding sphere around the swarm and a ray that misses it is abandoned on the spot. On a backdrop most of the frame is empty, and without this every one of those pixels runs the full march to find nothing
The march breaks on a hit rather than running to the step count. Sphere tracing converges quickly once it is close, so a typical hit costs a dozen steps where the ceiling is fifty
Normals come from the tetrahedron trick, four samples rather than the six a central difference would take. On a surface this smooth there is nothing to see in the difference
Blob paths are circles with whole numbers of turns per period, so the loop closes exactly and nothing is integrated between frames

Built for a dark ground and declared as one. The blobs are lit against the page, and on paper the background fill would have to become the page colour, at which point the rim light has nothing to separate it from

The hit threshold grows with distance, because a pixel does. A ray is a cone and the patch of world one pixel covers widens along it, so a constant epsilon fails exactly the rays that graze a silhouette: the march crawls towards a surface it never formally reaches and draws a thin dark splinter along the edge of a lobe. Twice the step count only made it smaller; scaling the threshold takes it to a hairline for nothing

The march steps three quarters of what the field reports, because a smooth minimum is not a true lower bound on the distance: it rounds the join outwards, so near a fillet the value overestimates how far there is to go

The most expensive shape of item here, because a raymarcher pays per pixel for every step and every blob, and yet it measures cheap: 1.1ms for a draw and a forced flush at 1280 by 720, against WaterCaustics at 1.00 and DustMotes at 1.20 on the same run. The bounding sphere is why. Most of a backdrop is empty, and a ray that misses the swarm is finished in a few instructions rather than fifty steps

0.360 mean absolute change per frame on a 0 to 255 scale, worst 0.448, against WaterCaustics at 0.222 and DustMotes at 0.016. Large smooth shapes moving slowly, so it reads calmer than the figure suggests, but it is not a quiet item. `period` is the dial and the change is close to linear in it
Cost is linear in `count` and in the steps actually taken, which is well under `detail` for most rays

background.description: Behind the blobs. Nothing is drawn there, so it is a flat fill, and it is also what the body colour is mixed towards in shadow.

body.description: The body, seen where a surface faces the camera. Keep it close to the background in value: the shape is carried by the rim and the highlight, and a body that is much lighter flattens both.

light.description: The light, seen in the rim and the highlight. Warm against a cool body is what gives the surface somewhere to turn through.

count.description: How many blobs. Along with detail, this is the cost: the distance function asks about every one of them at every step of every ray.

radius.description: Blob radius in scene units, where the swarm is about two units across. Large enough and they never part, which loses the thing worth watching.

blend.description: Width of the fillet where two blobs meet. At 0 they interpenetrate with a visible crease and read as two balls at the same address. Past about 1 they are one lump that never separates.

orbit.description: How far the blobs travel from the centre. This and radius together decide whether they ever actually part.

detail.description: Ceiling on raymarching steps. The thin necks between separating blobs are the first thing to go when this is low, and they are the part worth keeping. Most rays finish well short of the ceiling.

shine.description: How hard the highlight is. At 0 the surface is matte and reads as clay rather than as liquid.

period.description: Seconds for one cycle. Every blob travels a whole number of turns in it, so they are all exactly where they started and the loop has no join.

seed.description: Seed for the orbits and phases. Two of these side by side want two seeds.

instruction: the blobs move on their own
intro:
MetaballField is a handful of blobs that merge and part, raymarched.

There is no geometry in it. The scene is a function: hand it a point in space
and it returns the distance to the nearest surface. The picture is made by
walking a ray forward by whatever that function says is safe, over and over,
until it arrives at something. That is sphere tracing.

It is done this way because of what it buys. Two meshes cannot flow into one
another without somebody rebuilding the mesh; two distance fields merge by
taking the smaller of the two, which is one line. Soften that minimum and the
join becomes a fillet, and the neck and pinch you get out of it are the whole
reason this reads as something liquid rather than as spheres parked in the same
place.

`blend` is that softening. At 0 the blobs interpenetrate with a visible crease
where they cross and the illusion is gone.

name: MisprintText
description: A printing plate slipping out of register, so the word prints twice in two inks

notes: No canvas and no WebGL. Three stacked copies of the text, moved with transforms
The offset plates use mix-blend-mode: multiply, because overlapping ink is darker than either colour. A channel split goes brighter where the channels meet, which is light rather than ink
The in-register plate stays in normal flow and is the one that can be selected. The other two are aria-hidden and pointer-events: none
Offsets are in em, so one setting works at every type size
Two transforms per frame, composited. Nothing is measured and nothing reflows
The text is split once, not per frame. Rebuilding it would throw away the layout and make it unselectable

ink.description: The plate that is in register. This is the one in normal flow and the one a mouse can select; the other two are decoration.

accent.description: The first plate that is not in register.

second.description: The second plate that is not. Two is what makes it read as a press rather than as a drop shadow.

slip.description: How far a plate slips, in em, so it tracks the type size rather than needing a different number at every heading level. Past about 0.12 the words separate and you are reading three of them.

hold.description: Seconds a plate holds its position before being knocked. Registration does not drift: a plate sits wrong for a whole run and then moves, so this is a step rather than a speed.

chance.description: Share of runs where the plates are actually out. A press that is always wrong is not a press that is nearly right, and at 1 the text never settles.

skew.description: How far a slipped plate also turns, in degrees. Small: a plate that is out by a whole degree is a plate that has fallen off.

seed.description: Which runs slip and how far. Change it for a different sequence; the same seed always gives the same one.

instruction: ambient, watch the plates go in and out
intro:
A printing plate slipping out of register, so the word prints twice in two inks.

The usual version of this splits the red and blue channels apart and calls it a
glitch. That is a television fault: an analogue signal arriving at the wrong
time. Paper has its own version of the same idea and it looks quite different. A
press lays one plate per ink, and if a plate is a fraction out of position its
colour prints beside the others rather than on top of them.

So this is three copies of the same text, two of them coloured and offset, and
the stack **multiplies** rather than composites, because that is what overlapping
ink does. The overlap going darker is the whole tell. A channel split goes
brighter where the channels meet, which is light, not ink, and it is the thing
that makes the usual version read as a screen rather than as a page.

Registration does not drift, either. A plate sits wrong for a whole run and then
gets knocked, so the offset holds still and then jumps. Easing it would turn a
press into a wobble, and a wobble is a very different and much less interesting
fault.

No canvas and no WebGL. Three stacked spans and two transforms per frame.

name: MoireScreens
description: Two halftone screens laid over each other at a small angle, with the fringes left to emerge rather than drawn

notes: Nothing in the shader draws a fringe or knows where one is. There are two regular screens and the interference is what comes out, which is why the fringes behave correctly when the angle changes: the spacing of the beat goes as the pitch over twice the sine of half the angle, so it runs away towards infinity as the screens line up

The anti-aliasing is load-bearing rather than a polish pass. A regular screen at this frequency aliases against the pixel grid, and that aliasing is itself a moire, so the fringes would be partly the screens beating with the display rather than with each other and the effect would be a rendering artefact wearing the costume of an optical one. Each screen's coverage is computed analytically and softened by exactly one pixel's footprint, measured with fwidth

The inks multiply rather than add, because that is what ink does: two transparent layers pass the product of what each passes. Added instead, the overlaps saturate and the fringes flatten at the dark end, which is the difference between reading as print and reading as two gels on a lightbox
Element size is derived from coverage properly, through the area of a disc in a square cell for dots and half the covered width for lines, so `coverage` means the same thing in both modes

This is a printing fault induced on purpose, and the reason process colour is screened at 15, 45, 75 and 105 degrees is to avoid it. Set `separation` to 30 for the industry's answer and 4 for the thing every printer has had to explain to a client

The drift is a sine rather than a continuous turn, so the loop closes. A screen turning continuously passes through the angles where the beat vanishes and comes out the other side, which is a busier effect and a different one
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes

Measured at 0.103 mean absolute change per frame on a 0 to 255 scale at the default drift, which is in line with MeshGradient at 0.091, and 1.1ms at 640 by 360. The change per frame is exactly linear in the drift, so halving one halves the other
Two rotations, two fract calls and two smoothsteps per pixel, plus the derivative fwidth needs. No textures, no noise and no render targets
The derivative is the only unusual cost and it is a hardware instruction. It is also not optional: without it the screens alias and the effect is measuring the monitor

Shipping this is the real constraint, not drawing it. A full-frame dot screen is nearly all high-frequency detail and every dot edge moves as the screens drift, so a codec has nothing to predict: at pitch 10, 30fps and crf 26 one aspect ratio came to 18.5MB against a 3.5MB budget, and at 15fps with crf 36 it was still 5.3MB. Coarsening the pitch to 14 is what actually fixed it, because it is the dot count that costs, and it reads better as a screen into the bargain

paper.description: The sheet both screens are printed on, and what shows where neither covers.

first.description: The first screen's ink. Since the two multiply, this is the colour the sheet takes where only this screen covers.

second.description: The second screen's ink. Two different inks make the fringes read as colour as well as tone, which is what makes the beat visible at low coverage. The same colour twice is the purer demonstration and the duller picture.

pitch.description: Distance between screen elements, in CSS pixels. Fine pitches give large fringes for a given angle and read as an optical event; coarse ones read as two patterns you can see individually. It is also the one setting that decides what this costs to ship: a screen is high-frequency detail across the whole frame, so halving the pitch roughly quadruples the dot count and the video with it. At 10 the take would not fit in the repo's budget at any frame rate worth watching; at 14 it does, and the dots read more clearly as dots. Below about 3 the screen is at the limit of what a display can resolve and the effect starts depending on the device.

coverage.description: Share of the sheet each screen covers. The fringes are strongest near a half, because that is where a small change in overlap makes the biggest difference to how much paper is left. At the extremes there is either nothing to overlap or nothing left uncovered.

separation.description: The angle between the two screens, and the control that matters. It sets the fringe spacing through the pitch over twice the sine of half of it, so the relationship is violently non-linear: 10 degrees gives a tight rosette, 2 gives fringes the size of the frame, and 0 gives no beat at all because the screens are in register.

angle.description: How the first screen is set in the frame. It does not affect the beat at all, only which way the whole thing is turned. 15 is where a printer would put the first screen of a four-colour job.

drift.description: Degrees the second screen turns over one period, and the one setting that decides how busy this is. Tiny numbers are enough, because the fringe spacing depends so sharply on the angle that a degree sweeps the fringes right across the frame. It is also exactly linear in the change per frame: measured at 0.0514, 0.1028 and 0.2055 for 0.4, 0.8 and 1.6 degrees, so this is the dial to turn if it is too much. At 0 it is a still image, which is a perfectly good way to use this.

lines.description: Fine lines rather than dots. A line screen beats in one axis only, so the fringes are bands rather than a rosette, which is the version you see when a striped shirt is photographed. Dots are the print version.

detune.description: Difference in pitch between the two screens, as a share of the first. The other way to make a beat: two screens at the same angle but slightly different pitch give straight fringes rather than turned ones. A little of both is more interesting than either alone.

period.description: Seconds for one cycle of the drift. Long, because the fringes move much faster than the angle does and a backdrop has to survive being ignored.

instruction: the second screen drifts on its own
intro:
MoireScreens lays two halftone screens over each other at a small angle and
lets them beat.

The fringes are not drawn. Nothing in the shader draws a fringe or knows where
one is: there are two regular screens, and the interference is what comes out.
That is the point of building it this way rather than drawing the pattern, and
it is why the fringes behave correctly when the angle changes. The spacing of
the beat is the pitch over twice the sine of half the angle, so it runs away
towards infinity as the screens line up: ten degrees gives a tight rosette, two
gives fringes the size of the frame, and zero gives nothing at all.

This is a printing fault, induced on purpose. It is the reason process colour is
screened at fifteen, forty-five, seventy-five and a hundred and five degrees:
those angles are chosen so four screens do not do this. Set `separation` to 30
and you have the industry's answer. Set it to 4 and you have the thing every
printer has had to explain to a client.

name: OdometerNumber
description: A number on wheels, where a wheel only turns while the one below it goes from nine round to nought

notes: The carry is the whole difference between this and ten independent spinners, and it is one line of arithmetic. A wheel is driven by the one to its right and turns only while that one is going from nine round to nought, so the tens wheel sits perfectly still for most of the units wheel's revolution and then turns all at once

You can see it on any petrol pump: the pence wheel is a blur, the pounds wheel steps, and the tens of pounds wheel has not moved all day. Get it wrong and every wheel turns at its own steady speed, which is a fruit machine

`carry` chooses the mechanism. Narrow is a geneva drive and snaps, so every figure sits squarely in its window. 1 is a straight gear train, and that one has a consequence: a continuously geared counter never shows clean figures except at exact multiples, which is why a gas meter is read to the last settled digit. The demo shows both, because they look nothing alike
Each strip carries nought to nine and then nought again. Without the repeat a wheel rolling off nine has nothing to roll on to and snaps back through the whole drum
The figures near the edge of the window are shaded, because they are on the curve of the wheel and going out of sight. Flat instead, they slide past as though printed on a belt
The window is an em tall, so it follows the type. Only the pixel value for the transform is read from the layout, and only on resize
A screen reader is given the value as a number, once, in a hidden label. A column of digits read aloud is not a number
Pure in t: each wheel's position is arithmetic on the value and the value is arithmetic on the clock
One transform and one filter per wheel per frame, both written only when they change. Six wheels is six composited transforms
Nothing is measured per frame. The strips are built once per digit count

from.description: Where the count starts. A real odometer starts wherever it was left, so this is also how you show a figure that is already high and only moves a little.

to.description: Where it ends. The distance between the two decides how much rolling there is to watch: a change of twelve on a six-wheel counter moves one wheel and nudges a second.

duration.description: Milliseconds for the whole travel, eased so it arrives rather than stops. Longer than a count-up wants to be, because the mechanism is the point and a fast roll is a blur.

hold.description: Milliseconds before it starts. A moment of the starting figure is what tells you the wheels were somewhere before they moved.

digits.description: Fewest wheels to show, padded with leading figures. Six is a car. The leading noughts are not decoration: a counter with a fixed number of wheels is what makes it a counter rather than a number, and it stops the layout changing width as the value grows.

group.description: What goes between groups of three, as furniture between the wheels. Empty by default, because a mechanical counter has no separators: the wheels are all the same and nothing sits between them. Set a comma if the figure is money rather than mileage.

carry.description: How much of a wheel's travel the wheel above it moves during, and the one setting that decides what machine this is. 0.12 is a geneva drive: the upper wheel is still until the lower one is nearly round, then snaps, and every figure sits squarely in its window. 1 is a straight gear train, where every wheel turns all the time, and it has a consequence worth knowing: such a counter never shows clean figures at all except at exact multiples, which is why a gas meter is read to the last settled digit. Anything between is a gear train with slack in it.

drum.description: How much a wheel darkens as it turns, because the figure coming into the window is on the curve of the drum. At 0 the figures slide past as though printed on a flat belt, which is the other thing this could be and a much less interesting one.

seed.description: Unused by the maths, and here so that two counters on a page can be told apart in a config. Nothing about an odometer is random: that is rather the point of one.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. For a one-shot count this should be a time after it has finished, so the final figure is simply there. A counter is read, not watched.

instruction: press replay to run it again
intro:
OdometerNumber is a number on wheels. Each digit is a strip of figures behind a
window, and the strips roll.

The whole difference between this and ten independent spinners is the **carry**,
and it is one line of arithmetic. A wheel does not move on its own: it is driven
by the one to its right, and it only turns while that one is going from nine
round to nought. So the tens wheel sits perfectly still for most of the units
wheel's revolution and then turns all at once, and the hundreds wheel is still
for most of that.

You can see it on any petrol pump. The pence wheel is a blur, the pounds wheel
steps, and the tens of pounds wheel has not moved all day. Get it wrong and
every wheel turns at its own steady speed, which is a fruit machine.

name: PanelGauge
description: A moving-coil gauge with a scale that lights to the reading and a needle that is never quite still

notes: The scale is not symmetrical about the top. A panel meter sweeps about 250 degrees from the lower left, because that is where the stops are, and the dead sector at the bottom is where the movement lives. A scale that starts at twelve o'clock and runs clockwise is a progress ring

Majors and minors are not the same tick. The minors between two majors are what make the eye read a position as a value rather than as an angle, and the ticks below the reading are lit while the ones above are not, which is how a scale carries the value as well as the needle does

The reading hunts. A real one moves by a fraction of a division because what is being measured is not still either, and a needle frozen at exactly 0.62 reads as a picture of a gauge. Two sines of different periods, so it does not tick like a metronome, and both complete whole turns in a period so the needle comes home

There is no overshoot, and that is a loss taken deliberately. A moving coil arrives at a reading by passing it, which is the most characterful thing a needle does, but it is a response to a change and therefore state between frames. The first version drove a closed-form damped oscillator from t: the needle swept up from zero and settled, which reads beautifully and does not loop, because frame zero was at the bottom of the scale and the last frame was at the reading
2D rather than WebGL. An instrument is something you want four of on a page, and the budget is one WebGL context
Built for a dark ground and declared as one. The face is painted, so the item supplies its own ground and only the area outside the dial shows the page
One filled circle, one arc, thirty-ish ticks and a four-point needle. The tick loop is the whole cost and it is linear in majors times minors

Measured with `pnpm budget` at 1280 by 720: 1.7ms for a draw and a forced flush, against DustMotes at 1.6 on the same run, and 0.016 mean absolute change per frame on a 0 to 255 scale, worst 0.026. A dial that barely moves is the point: the hunt is a fraction of a division
No canvas and no WebGL context held between frames beyond the one it draws into, so this does not compete with a backdrop for the page's context

face.description: The dial face. Painted rather than left transparent, because a gauge is a thing with a face on it and the alternative is ticks floating on your page.

ink.description: Unlit ticks and the boss at the centre. Grey rather than white: the unlit half of the scale is there to be read past, not read.

needle.description: The pointer. The one thing on the dial that should be found without looking, so it wants to be the only saturated colour in the frame apart from the lit arc it belongs to.

lit.description: The arc and the ticks below the reading. Usually the needle's colour, because they are telling you the same thing; set them apart only if the arc is reporting something the needle is not.

value.description: Where the needle sits on the scale. Drive this through update() to make the gauge report something real; the hunt is applied on top of whatever you set.

hunt.description: How far the reading wanders either side, as a share of the scale. Small. At 0 the needle is frozen and the gauge stops reading as something connected to anything; past about 0.12 it is a fault rather than a reading.

sweep.description: Degrees of arc the scale covers, centred on twelve o'clock with the dead sector at the bottom. 250 is what a panel meter does, because that is where its stops are. At 320 there is nowhere for the movement to go and it reads as a ring.

majors.description: Major divisions, the ones a real dial numbers. Few: a scale you can count at a glance is the point of a dial, and past about ten you are reading a ruler.

minors.description: Minor divisions between each pair of majors. These are what let the eye read a needle between two numbers as a value. At 0 the dial can only say which division it is in.

period.description: Seconds for one cycle of the hunt. Both sines complete whole turns in it, so the needle is in the same place at the start and the end.

seed.description: Seed for the hunt's phase. Two gauges side by side want two seeds, or they wander in step and read as one instrument drawn twice.

instruction: the reading hunts on its own

credit.what: the lit scale and the live readings on the front panel in the Machine Front Panel Page
credit.author: Ray Velez

intro:
PanelGauge is a moving-coil gauge: a painted dial face, a scale that lights up
to the reading, and a needle that is never quite still.

name: PaperGrain
description: The surface of a sheet of paper with nothing on it, lit by its own roughness

notes: The image is a lighting calculation rather than a pattern. One noise field becomes a height, the height is differenced into a normal, and the normal meets one low light. Drawn as tone instead, the same field is a grey cloud that could be anything

Which field goes into the height and which goes into the tone is the whole shape of this rather than a detail. Only the fibre is surface. Formation is a density, so it changes how much light comes back and not which way the sheet faces, and it belongs in the tone: put both in the height, which is the obvious way to write it, and the broad field contributes almost nothing while the fine fibre dominates the derivative. The first version of this was rough-cast plaster

The fibre is stretched along the machine direction, because stock runs in a direction on a paper machine and the fibres lie along it. Isotropic noise is the single thing that stops a paper texture reading as paper: the sheets that really are isotropic are the handmade ones, and they look like felt

The tooth is smaller than a pixel, so it is in neither the height nor the tone. It is a flicker added to the light and weighted by how much the light rakes, because roughness you cannot resolve only shows as sparkle in grazing light. Raise `light` towards overhead and it goes flat, which is what happens to real paper under a ceiling light

Nothing in the paper moves. The light swings through a few degrees and back. Grain that crawls is film grain, which is a different effect and a far noisier one: measured at 0.013 mean absolute change per frame on a 0 to 255 scale, this is the quietest thing in the library by a factor of several

The normal is differenced over exactly one CSS pixel and divided by that step, so it is a slope rather than a difference and `relief` means the same thing at every canvas size. A shorter step samples detail the screen cannot resolve, which comes back as sparkle that changes when the canvas is resized
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes

Four evaluations of four-octave value noise per pixel: three of the fibre, for the height and the two differences, and one of the much broader formation field. That is the cost of lighting something rather than drawing it, and it is the whole reason it reads as a surface

Timed with a readPixels after each draw so the number includes the GPU. At 640 by 360 it came to 0.31ms against 0.88 for MeshGradient and 1.01 for PrismSpectrum measured the same way, which makes it the cheapest backdrop in the library
No textures, no render targets and no feedback buffer. The cost is the pixel count, so a full-screen canvas at 2x device pixel ratio is the thing to watch

paper.description: The stock. A warm white, because a true white sheet is a thing almost nobody prints on: it is bleached, it is colder than the ink wants, and on a screen it leaves the lighting nowhere to go above it.

fibre.description: What the sheet is tinted towards where the fibre lies thickest. Close to the stock on purpose. The difference between the two is doing the same job as the difference between two whites in a real sheet, which is to say it should be almost nothing.

scale.description: Fibres across the short side. Higher is a finer, harder sheet; lower is closer to a heavy rag paper, where the fibre is visible as fibre rather than as texture.

direction.description: The machine direction: the axis the fibre lies along, and the axis a sheet tears cleanly down. Slightly off square is better than square, for the same reason a halftone screen is set at an angle.

stretch.description: How far the fibre is drawn out along that axis. At 1 there is no direction at all, which is a handmade sheet, and handmade sheets read as felt rather than as paper.

formation.description: Strength of the cloud: the uneven spread of fibre you see when a sheet is held up to a window. Papermakers judge stock by it. It works on the tone rather than on the surface, because it is a density and not a shape. At 0 the sheet is perfectly even, which no sheet is.

tooth.description: The micro-roughness that takes the ink, which is what a printer means by the tooth of a paper. It is in the light rather than in the surface, so it fades as the light rises: that is not a shortcut, it is what grazing light does to a rough surface.

light.description: Height of the light. 0 rakes along the surface and 1 is straight down on it. Low, always: this is a flat sheet, and the only thing that can make a flat sheet interesting is light arriving across it rather than onto it.

relief.description: How strongly the surface is lit by its own slope. Past about 1.5 the sheet stops being paper and becomes hammered metal, which is a real effect and not this one.

sweep.description: Degrees the light swings over one period, and the only moving thing here. At 0 it is a still image, which is a perfectly good way to use this and the quietest thing in the library.

shive.description: Specks of fibre the beater did not break down. Papermakers call it shive, and it is the one thing here that is a mark rather than a surface. Sparse on purpose: a sheet with visible shive all over it is a sheet nobody bought.

period.description: Seconds for one swing of the light and back. Long, because this sits behind something else and a backdrop has to survive being ignored.

instruction: the light swings on its own
intro:
PaperGrain is the surface of a sheet of paper, with nothing on it. Not a pattern laid
over a background: the paper is the subject, and what you are looking at is
light falling across its own roughness.

Three things make a surface read as paper rather than as noise, and leaving any
one of them out gives you grey static.

**Fibre.** A sheet is a mat of fibres, and on a machine-made sheet they lie more
along one axis than the other, because the stock runs in a direction. So the
noise is stretched along that axis rather than isotropic. This is the machine
direction, and it is why a sheet tears cleanly one way and raggedly the other.

**Formation.** Hold a sheet up to a window and you see cloud: the fibre is not
spread evenly, and the patches are far larger than the fibres themselves.
Papermakers call it formation, or look-through, and it is what separates good
stock from newsprint.

**PaperGrain.** The micro-roughness that takes the ink, and the thing the effect is
named after. Too small to see as shape, so it shows only as a flicker in the
light, and only where the light is raking.

Which of those goes into the surface and which goes into the tone is the whole
shape of this effect rather than a detail of it. Only the fibre is surface: it
is differenced into a normal and lit. Formation is a density, so it changes how
much light comes back rather than which way the sheet faces, and it belongs in
the tone. The tooth is smaller than a pixel, so it is in neither, and it is
added to the light.
