Get that wrong and no amount of tuning will save it. The first version of this
put both fields in the height, which is the obvious way to write it, and the
result was rough-cast plaster: the broad field contributed nothing, because a
broad field has almost no slope, and the fine fibre dominated the derivative.

name: PointSwell
description: A sea of glowing points rolling toward you, with the camera diving into it as the page scrolls

notes: Travelling waves, not scrolling noise. The usual way to build this is two octaves of simplex with the sample point sliding forward each frame, which looks right and cannot loop: simplex is not periodic in any direction, so a field that slides forward never returns. It also cannot be driven by renderAtTime, because sliding forward means accumulating and the surface then depends on how it got there rather than on the clock

Each mode is a sine of k dot x minus omega t, which is a closed form in t, and every omega is a whole number of turns per period, so the sea is exactly where it started when the period comes round. The waves travel toward the camera because that is what a positive omega against a forward wavevector does: the streaming is the physics rather than an offset added to a sample point
Eighteen modes, because a sum of a few plane waves is quasi-periodic and lays itself out in a visible lattice however it is weighted. The count is what stops it reading as a pattern

The headings fan about straight-on rather than spreading over the full circle. A real swell has a direction; waves arriving from everywhere average into chop, and what reads as a sea rolling toward you is a narrow fan with a little disagreement in it
Deep-water dispersion, so a long wave runs faster than a short one as the root of the wavelength, rounded to whole turns because that is what closes the loop

No bloom pass. The glow is tens of thousands of additively blended points overlapping, which is where the brightness in this kind of scene actually comes from. A composer stack buys a halo for three full-screen render targets and a second pair of passes, and this is a backdrop that sits behind a page rather than being the page

A grid, not a reshaped sphere. Scenes of this kind often start from a SphereGeometry and throw the shape away in the vertex shader, which works and leaves the point spacing bunched at the poles of a sphere nobody can see
The grid is jittered off its lattice. A perfectly regular sheet of points shows its rows as moire at a shallow angle, and a shallow angle is the only one this is ever seen at
The cursor parts the surface sideways along the ground plane rather than lifting it. A sea that bulges towards whoever is looking at it is the wrong physical story and a much louder one
Built for a dark ground and declared as one. Additive points on a near-black fill is the whole idea, and added light on paper is invisible
A single draw of the sheet, with the surface solved in the vertex shader

background.description: Behind the sea. Nothing is drawn there, so it is a flat fill, and it wants to be near black: the points are additive, so every bit of brightness in the fill is brightness the crests cannot add to.

colorLow.description: The troughs. Close to the background, because a trough is the part of the sea with no light on it.

colorHigh.description: The crests. The whole range of the sea lies between this and colorLow, so the distance between the two is the contrast of the item.

density.description: Points across the sheet. The count goes as the square of it, so this is the whole cost. Below about 120 the sea stops being a surface and becomes a scatter.

pointSize.description: Point size at the near edge, falling off with distance. Large enough and the crests fuse into a solid ribbon, which loses the thing that makes it points.

opacity.description: How much light each point adds. They are additive, so this compounds where they overlap: the crests are bright because many dim points are stacked there, not because any one of them is.

swell.description: Height of the swell in scene units. At 0 it is a flat sheet of points, which is a different and quieter item. Past about 3 the crests reach the camera at the near edge.

scale.description: Waves across the sheet, for the longest one. The rest of the spectrum is built up from it, so this sets the size of the whole sea.

waves.description: Modes in the surface. The one that decides whether it reads as water: below about twelve the sum is quasi-periodic and the swell arranges itself on a visible lattice however the rest is tuned.

dive.description: How much of the camera's descent the scroll performs. At 0 the view stays high and the item is a sea seen from above; at 1 it finishes skimming the surface. Eased over the first third of the travel, because the interesting part of the move is the arrival.

parallax.description: How far the pointer moves the camera, in scene units. The pointer does not touch the water: it moves the viewer. Parting the surface under the cursor was tried first and reads as the sea noticing you, where moving the camera reads as leaning over it, which is what somebody looking at a sea is doing. The move is instant rather than eased, because easing means keeping the last position and moving a fraction of the way each frame, and that is an accumulator: it would make the frame depend on the frames before it and renderAtTime could no longer be seeked.

period.description: Seconds for one cycle. Every mode completes a whole number of turns in it, so the sea returns exactly and the loop has no join.

seed.description: Seed for the headings and phases. Two of these side by side want two seeds, or they are the same sea twice.

instruction: scroll to dive in, and the cursor parts the surface

name: PointerFilings
description: Iron filings aligning to a magnetic field, with the cursor as the magnet

notes: The real dipole expression, not spokes radiating from a point. Filings align with the field rather than pointing at the magnet, and a dipole field loops: out of one pole, round, and back into the other
The field is sampled once per filing rather than per pixel. Per pixel each segment bends into a curve, which no single filing does
Window pointer scope, so the filings have begun to turn before the cursor reaches the element
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes
Nine cells per pixel, each one dipole evaluation and one segment distance
Nothing is uploaded per frame. Only uniforms change
Cost is flat: every cell does the same work wherever the magnet is
Thousands of small hard-edged marks are difficult for a video codec, so the recording carries a per-item quality override. The effect itself is unaffected

paper.description: The tray the filings are scattered on. `auto` takes it from the page, so the effect adopts whatever it is dropped onto.

ink.description: A filing lying flat, out where the field is weak. A light-dark() pair picks by the ground it lands on.

accent.description: A filing standing up in a strong field. The pattern reads as much from this change in tone as from the alignment. A light-dark() pair picks by the ground it lands on.

pitch.description: Cell size in CSS pixels. There is one filing per cell, so this is how thickly they are scattered.

length.description: Length of a filing where the field is strongest, measured in cells. Past about 0.9 they overlap into continuous lines, which is a field diagram rather than a tray of filings.

weight.description: Half the thickness of a filing, in cells.

reach.description: How far the magnet reaches before the filings stop caring. The falloff saturates rather than multiplying, so close to the magnet the marks stand fully up instead of running away to a few enormous ones.

jitter.description: How far each filing is thrown off the centre of its cell. At 0 the grid they are organised by becomes visible, which no scattered tray has.

tilt.description: Angle of the bar magnet in degrees. Turns the whole pattern, the way turning the magnet on the bench would.

instruction: move the cursor across it
intro:
Iron filings scattered over a magnet, and the magnet is the cursor.

Filings do not point at a magnet. That is the thing most versions of this get
wrong, and it is why most of them look like a starburst rather than like a
physics demonstration. Filings align with the **field**, and the field of a
dipole loops: out of one pole, round through the space beside it, and back into
the other. Spokes radiating from a point are what a single charge gives, and a
single magnetic charge is not a thing that exists.

So this evaluates the real expression. For a moment **m** at displacement **r**
the field runs along `3(m · r̂)r̂ − m`, and every mark is a short segment laid
along it. The loops are a consequence of the maths rather than something drawn.

The field is sampled once per filing, at the filing, not per pixel. Sampling per
pixel bends each segment into a little curve, which no single filing does: a
filing is a rigid sliver of iron and it can only be straight.

Near the magnet the dipole expression runs away to infinity, so the falloff is a
ratio rather than a product. It saturates at 1 instead of producing a handful of
enormous marks on top of each other at the centre.

One WebGL2 fragment shader on one full-screen triangle. No three.js, no
dependency.

name: PointerLitBusts
description: Three helmeted busts in a dark room, lit by the cursor carrying the only lamp

notes: The forms are generated rather than loaded. A prompt here hands over source, and a decimated head scan is several megabytes of binary nobody can read, review or tune. A lathe profile and three primitives is a few hundred numbers and every part of it can be changed by somebody who has never opened a 3D tool

The light moves in the world, on a plane in front of the busts, rather than in screen space. A light pinned to the cursor in two dimensions lights everything from the same angle wherever it goes, so the shading never changes and the scene reads as a flat image with a bright patch on it
There is always a little rim light. On a dark ground an unlit form is not subtle, it is absent, and a reader who moves the cursor somewhere empty concludes the page is broken

No shadow maps. A moving light and three solids is the case where real shadows look obvious and cost a second render pass every frame, and at this scale the shading says most of what a shadow would have
One render pass, three lathes and a few primitives, no shadow map and no post

lamp.description: Brightness of the lamp the cursor carries.

lampColour.description: Colour of the lamp. Warm, so it reads as a lamp rather than as a screen.

reach.description: How far in front of the busts the lamp sits.

sweep.description: How far the lamp travels across the scene.

rim.description: The edge that keeps a form present when the lamp is elsewhere.

rimColour.description: Colour of the rim, which is the room rather than the lamp.

room.description: The ground the busts stand in.

parallax.description: How far the camera drifts against the cursor. Zero holds it still.

polish.description: How polished the shell is. Low is stone, high is lacquer.

instruction: move the cursor to light them
intro:
PointerLitBusts is three helmeted busts in a dark room where the cursor
carries the only lamp. Move it and the forms turn: a cheekbone catches, a
visor goes black, the one at the back comes out of the dark for a moment and
goes again.

Three things carry it, and the first is what separates this from a torch
cursor.

**The lamp moves through the world**, on a plane in front of the busts, not in
screen space. A light pinned to the cursor in two dimensions lights everything
from the same angle wherever it goes, so the shading never changes and the
scene reads as a flat image with a bright patch travelling over it. Moving the
light through the scene is what makes a form turn: the same cheek is lit from
the left, then from below, then not at all.

**There is always a little rim light.** On a dark ground an unlit form is not
subtle, it is absent, and a reader who moves the cursor into an empty corner
concludes the page is broken. A faint cool edge keeps all three present and
makes the lamp read as a lamp rather than as the only thing that exists.

**There are no shadow maps.** A moving light and three solids is exactly the
case where real shadows look obvious, and they cost a second render pass every
frame. The forms read from shading alone, which at this scale says most of
what a shadow would have.

name: PointerRippleGrid
description: A field of matte forms on paper, rippling around the cursor

notes: three.js must already be a dependency of the project. It is not bundled
One InstancedMesh, so 324 forms cost one draw call and one shadow pass
The ripple is a standing wave centred on the cursor, not a propagating one with memory. renderAtTime has to be pure in t, and a wave with history is not
324 instance matrices composed per frame in JavaScript, then one upload
The shadow map is the cost, not the geometry. Drop count to 16 before touching anything else

paper.description: The paper the field stands on. Match it to your page background or the panel reads as a pasted-in rectangle. `auto` takes it from the page, so the effect adopts whatever it is dropped onto.

stone.description: The forms at rest. Slightly lighter than the paper is what makes them read as objects standing on it. A light-dark() pair picks by the ground it lands on.

accent.description: The forms at the crest of the ripple. The colour is what makes the wave legible in a still frame, so do not set it to the same value as stone. A light-dark() pair picks by the ground it lands on.

count.description: Forms per side. 18 is 324 of them. Past 30 the forms are narrower than their own shadows and the field turns to fur.

form.description: Shape of each form. Cylinders read as softer and hide the grid; boxes keep the rows visible, which suits a lower count.

thickness.description: Width of each form as a fraction of its cell. Above 0.9 neighbours touch and the field becomes a surface.

base.description: Height of a form at rest. Low is a floor that rises; high is a forest that sways.

amplitude.description: How far the crest rises above the base.

frequency.description: Rings per unit of distance. Above about 5 the rings are finer than the grid and it aliases into noise.

falloff.description: How quickly the ripple fades away from the cursor. Low spreads across the whole field; high is a tight pool underneath it.

elevation.description: Sun height above the horizon. Low throws long shadows between the forms, which is most of what gives the field depth.

shadow.description: How dark the shadows fall on the paper. The paper is never lit, so this is the only thing drawn on it.

softness.description: Shadow edge softness. Zero is a hard midday edge, one is heavy overcast.

tilt.description: Camera height. Zero is eye level with the paper, one looks straight down. Low is dramatic and hides the ripple; high shows the pattern and flattens the forms.

zoom.description: How much of the frame the field fills.

period.description: Seconds for one loop of the idle swell, the motion used when no pointer is present. Exactly periodic, so the loop closes.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. Pick a time where the idle swell has some variation across the field rather than one where it is flat.

instruction: move the cursor across the field
intro:
Swell is a field of matte forms standing on paper, rippling around the cursor.
324 of them by default, drawn as one instanced mesh, lit by a single sun with a
real shadow map. Same family as Sundial: matte forms, warm paper, shadows doing
the work.

The ripple is a standing wave centred on the pointer rather than a propagating
one with memory. That is a deliberate constraint. A wave with history integrates
against the previous frame, and `renderAtTime` has to be pure in `t` or the
effect cannot be recorded or scrubbed. A standing wave that follows the cursor is
indistinguishable at a glance and reproducible to the pixel.

With no pointer the field keeps a slow diagonal swell of its own, so it is alive
before anyone touches it and the loop still closes.

The crest is tinted towards the accent colour. That is what makes the wave
legible in a still frame, which matters for the poster, for reduced motion, and
for anybody who arrives on a touch screen.

name: PointerSmoke
description: Smoke off the cursor, spreading and thinning as it drifts

notes: An older puff is wider and fainter than a new one, because nothing holds smoke together. That is the opposite of a particle trail, where older means smaller
The puffs multiply rather than compositing, so two that overlap are denser than either

Every puff carries its own age in seconds rather than taking it from its place in the list. The list version worked out to one puff per frame, which left a third of a second of smoke on a 60Hz display and a sixth on a 120Hz one

A trail needs history, which is not a function of t. When pointerPath is set the whole track is known in advance and the trail is read backwards off it instead of accumulated, so a recorded take is identical however the frames are asked for. A live pointer keeps its own stamps
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes
One distance and one smoothstep per puff per pixel, and the loop stops at the number of puffs actually held
The puff positions and ages are two array uniforms, uploaded once per frame
Cost scales with the puff count rather than with how far the cursor has moved

paper.description: The paper the smoke drifts over. `auto` takes it from the page, so the effect adopts whatever it is dropped onto.

smoke.description: The body of it, once it has spread. Keep it close to the paper: smoke is the absence of a clear view, not a dark shape, and a strong colour here reads as paint. A light-dark() pair picks by the ground it lands on.

accent.description: What warmth the freshest smoke carries, at the head of the trail. Only a little of the trail is ever this, so a saturated colour shows up as a bead following the cursor. A light-dark() pair picks by the ground it lands on.

marks.description: How many puffs the trail holds. The shader has room for 28; asking for more silently gives you 28, because the array is a fixed size and growing it means editing the shader as well.

size.description: Radius of a fresh puff, as a share of the short side, so it keeps its proportion when the element changes shape.

spread.description: How much wider a puff gets by the end of its life. Nothing holds smoke together, so this is the main thing that makes it read as smoke rather than as a cursor with a tail. At 0 you get a row of identical discs.

fade.description: How quickly a puff gives up. Higher is a shorter trail with a cleaner end; lower leaves a tail that hangs about.

edge.description: How much of a puff is its soft shoulder rather than its body. Smoke has no edge at all, so this wants to be near 1; at 0 you get plates of grey.

life.description: Seconds a puff lasts, which is the length of the trail. This is measured in time rather than in frames, so the same gesture leaves the same trail on a 60Hz display and a 144Hz one. Past about a second the smoke starts to read as something heavy being dragged behind the cursor.

instruction: move the cursor across it
intro:
Smoke off the cursor, spreading and thinning as it drifts.

Not a comet and not a glow. A puff of smoke does two things while it hangs
there. It **widens**, because nothing is holding it together. And it **thins**,
because the same amount of it is spread over more room. So an older puff is
bigger and fainter than a new one, which is the opposite of a particle trail,
where older means smaller, and it is the single thing that makes this read as
smoke rather than as a cursor with a tail.

The puffs multiply rather than compositing, so two that overlap are denser than
either. What warmth there is sits at the head, where the smoke has not yet had
room to spread.

One WebGL2 fragment shader on one full-screen triangle. No three.js, no
dependency.

name: PrismSpectrum
description: A beam of white light through a turning prism, split into a spectrum by tracing it rather than drawing it

notes: Built for a dark ground and declared as one. This is light on a ground rather than a pattern on a surface
The fan is traced, not drawn: sixteen wavelengths, each refracted at the entry face, carried through the glass and refracted again on the way out, each cast as its own ray

The index comes from Cauchy's equation, n = A + B over lambda squared, which is the two-term fit every glass catalogue starts with. Red bends least and violet most because the index rises towards the blue end, so the ordering is a consequence rather than a choice: reverse the dispersion constant and the spectrum reverses
The fan is narrow on purpose. A real 60 degree prism in crown glass spreads the visible band by about a degree, which is why a prism throws a long thin spectrum rather than a wide one
Total internal reflection is handled rather than papered over: where a wavelength cannot leave the second face, no ray is drawn for it, which is a real thing a prism does

The tints are the CIE 1931 colour matching functions converted to linear sRGB and evaluated at build time. Several are outside the gamut and clamp, which is unavoidable: a monitor cannot show a spectral green, and desaturating the whole spectrum to make it fit would be worse

The prism rocks rather than spins. A whole turn spends most of its time with the beam missing the glass or leaving by the face it came in through, and the pass through minimum deviation goes by in a moment
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes

Two ray-triangle intersections for the beam itself, then sixteen refractions and sixteen distance-to-ray tests per pixel. No textures, no noise lookups, no render targets. Measured at 0.57ms for a 960 by 540 canvas, timed with a readPixels after each draw so the number includes the GPU, which makes this the most expensive backdrop in the library and still well inside a frame
Which face the beam leaves by is worked out once with the middle of the band rather than per wavelength, because the rays inside the glass arrive within a pixel of each other

background.description: The room behind it. Dark, because everything drawn here is light being added to it: on a pale ground the beams have nothing to be brighter than.

apex.description: Apex angle of the prism. 60 is the one in every textbook and the one that spreads the band usefully; a shallow prism barely splits the light, and past about 75 degrees most of the beam is lost to total internal reflection.

incidence.description: The angle the beam arrives at. Together with the sway this decides how near the pass is to minimum deviation, which is where the fan is tightest and brightest.

tilt.description: How the prism is set in the frame. This is the aim: it decides where the spectrum lands and how much of the canvas it crosses, and together with incidence it sets how near the pass is to minimum deviation.

index.description: Cauchy's A, which is roughly the refractive index in the middle of the visible band. 1.52 is crown glass, 1.46 fused silica, 2.42 diamond.

dispersion.description: Cauchy's B, in micrometres squared, and the dispersion itself. 0.0045 is about right for crown glass; flint glass is two or three times that, which is why it is what you cut a chandelier from. At 0 the glass still bends the beam and no longer splits it.

size.description: How large the prism is, as a share of the short side of the frame. Larger glass means a longer path inside it and a wider fan on the way out.

spread.description: Width of the beams. This is the one number here that is a drawing decision rather than an optical one: a real beam is as wide as its source, and this is how wide you want it to read.

brightness.description: Strength of the light. A soft shoulder keeps the crossings from clipping, so a high value goes white where the rays overlap the way a photograph does rather than flattening into a hard patch.

glass.description: How visible the prism itself is. Low on purpose: the light is the subject, and a prism drawn as a solid object in front of its own spectrum is a paperweight.

sway.description: How far the prism rocks, in radians, over one cycle. At 0 it is a still composition, which is a legitimate way to use this and the quietest thing in the library.

grain.description: The sensor noise of a long exposure. Static rather than crawling: film grain that moves is a different effect and a far noisier one.

period.description: Seconds for one full cycle, and the pace control. Long on purpose: a backdrop has to survive being ignored, and a spectrum sweeping across a page is about as distracting as a backdrop can be.

instruction: it rocks on its own
intro:
A beam of white light through a slowly turning prism, on a dark ground.

The fan is **traced, not drawn**. Sixteen wavelengths, each with its own
refractive index, each refracted at the entry face, carried through the glass
and refracted again on the way out, each cast as its own ray.

That matters because everything people recognise about a prism then falls out
of it rather than being arranged:

**Red bends least and violet most**, because the refractive index of glass rises
towards the blue end. The ordering is not a choice here. Reverse `dispersion`
and the spectrum reverses, as it would in a material with anomalous dispersion.

**The fan is narrow.** A real 60 degree prism in crown glass spreads the visible
band by about one degree. That is why a prism throws a long thin spectrum rather
than a wide one, and why the picture everybody has in mind is of a spectrum cast
several metres away.

**The spread changes as it turns**, and it is tightest near minimum deviation,
where the beam passes through symmetrically. That is the one moment in the cycle
when the fan narrows and brightens, and it is the detail that says this is being
worked out rather than painted.

**Some wavelengths do not get out.** Where the angle inside the glass is past
the critical angle the ray is totally internally reflected and no line is drawn
for it, which is a real thing a prism does and not a case to paper over.

name: RelightImage
description: A lamp moved across a printed photograph, finding the relief in the impression

notes: The picture is the host element's own child. It is hidden from sight and left in the document, so the alt text is whatever you wrote and a page with no JavaScript still shows it

This lights the print rather than the scene. There is no depth in a photograph and no honest way to get one out of a single frame, so the height field is the picture's own luminance and what the lamp finds is relief in the sheet

Known limit, and the reason the modelling is laid over the picture rather than replacing it: lighting already in the photograph becomes relief, so a cast shadow across a wall turns into a step in the paper. A flat-lit image is the one this flatters most
The gradient is taken across several pixels rather than one, which low-passes the height field on the way and is what keeps sensor noise and compression blocks out of the normal
Nothing is integrated against the previous frame. The lamp is exactly where the pointer is, so renderAtTime is pure in t and a scripted path replays identically
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes
Five texture reads per pixel: one for the picture and four for the central differences the normal is built from
No second pass and no render target. The normal is computed where it is used rather than baked, which costs four reads and saves a framebuffer
The image uploads once, on load. Nothing is uploaded per frame

light.description: Colour of the lamp. Keep it close to white, warm or cool. It is painted over the picture as a sheen rather than mixed into it, so a saturated colour tints the highlights rather than reading as illumination.

height.description: How far above the sheet the lamp is held, as a share of the frame's height. Low is a raking light that finds every ridge in the impression; high is a lamp overhead that finds almost none. This is the first dial to reach for and most of the character is in it.

relief.description: How much relief the impression has. At 0 the sheet is flat and all you have is a soft gradient moving about. Past about 15 the paper stops reading as paper and starts reading as hammered metal.

smooth.description: Pixels either side the gradient is taken across. Low-passes the height field on the way, so this is the difference between lighting the shape of the impression and lighting the noise in the file. Below about 1.5 you are mostly lighting JPEG blocks.

strength.description: How much modelling the lamp lays over the picture. The photograph is exactly itself at the midpoint of the light, so this opens the gradient out either side of it rather than re-exposing anything.

ambient.description: How much light the room has already, which is the point either side of which the lamp works. The light a lamp delivers across a frame averages nothing like a half, so leaving the neutral at a half dims the whole picture before it lights anything. Near the average gives you a gradient; at 0 the lamp only ever adds.

gloss.description: How much the ink catches the light that the paper does not. This is the part that says the dark areas are ink rather than dark paper, and it is what separates this from a gradient.

shine.description: How tight that catch is. Low is a broad satin sheen; high is a small hard glint that only appears where a ridge faces the lamp exactly.

reach.description: How far the lamp throws, as a share of the frame's height. Small is a reading lamp held close with the corners falling away; large is a window on the far side of the room.

grain.description: Paper tooth over the whole thing.

instruction: move the cursor over the picture
intro:
A lamp moved across a printed photograph.

It does not relight the scene. There is no depth in a photograph and no honest
way to get one out of a single frame, so anything that claims to move the sun
around inside a picture is guessing at a shape it cannot see. What this lights
is the print: the sheet the picture is on, which has relief wherever the
impression is heavy, and a raking light finds that relief the way a raking light
finds any other surface.

Height is the picture's own luminance. A shadow in the photograph is a hollow in
the sheet and a highlight stands proud, and the normal is the gradient of that
height taken across a few pixels rather than one, because a one-pixel difference
is mostly sensor noise and compression blocks.

There is one thing the lamp adds that a gradient cannot, and it is the thing
worth having: ink has a sheen that paper does not. The specular is what says the
dark passages are ink sitting on a surface rather than dark paper, and without
it this is a soft blob moving about.

One WebGL2 fragment shader on one full-screen triangle. No three.js, no
dependency, no depth map to author or ship.

name: RotatingWords
description: One word in a sentence swaps for another on a loop, in a box sized to the longest so the line never moves

notes: The box is sized to the longest word before anything moves. A list of words of different lengths swapped in place changes the width of its own line on every swap, so everything after it slides back and forth for as long as the page is open. It is the most common fault in this effect and it is entirely avoidable

The sizing needs no measurement. Every word is placed in the same cell of an inline-grid, so the cell is as wide as the longest and as tall as the tallest, and it stays that size whichever word is showing. Nothing to recompute on resize and nothing that can be wrong before a font has loaded

The words are the author's markup and are never replaced. Passing a list of strings and building spans means the text is invisible to anything reading the page before the script runs, and it puts copy inside a configuration object where nobody will think to translate it

Only the first word is in the accessibility tree; the rest are aria-hidden and the element is aria-live off. A screen reader meeting eight alternatives in a row would otherwise read the sentence eight times, and a live region would announce a change nobody asked for every two seconds
Pure in t: which word is showing and how far through its handover are arithmetic on the clock, so the recorder can seek anywhere and a live page and a take agree
Only the arriving and leaving words are touched. Everything else is parked with no transform to compute, so twelve words cost the same per frame as two
Two transforms and two opacities per frame during a handover, and nothing at all between them: the applied state is compared before anything is written, so a word being held writes no styles
A blur of 0 is left off entirely rather than written as blur(0px), because a filter costs a compositing layer whether or not it does anything

interval.description: Milliseconds each word is held, including its handover. This sets the length of the whole loop, which is the interval times the number of words, so four words at 2200ms is an 8.8 second cycle and that is what a recording has to span.

swap.description: Milliseconds the handover takes, clamped to the interval so one word cannot still be leaving when the next starts. Around a quarter of the interval reads as a deliberate change rather than as a flicker.

rise.description: How far a word travels as it goes, as a share of its own line height. At 0 the words cross-fade in place, which is quieter and is the right answer inside running text.

tilt.description: Degrees the moving words tip. Zero by default because a tilted word in the middle of a sentence reads as a mistake; it earns its place in a large display line and almost nowhere else.

blur.description: Blur on a word in motion. Zero is crisper and cheaper, and a filter costs a compositing layer whether or not it does anything, so a value of 0 is left off rather than written as blur(0px).

instruction: the word changes on its own
intro:
RotatingWords swaps one word in a sentence for another on a loop. "Printed by
letterpress, by lithography, by screen print."

Three things carry it, and the first is why most versions of this are
unpleasant to look at without anyone being able to say why.

**The box is sized to the longest word before anything moves.** A list of words
of different lengths, swapped in place, changes the width of its own line on
every swap, so everything after it slides back and forth for as long as the
page is open. It is the most common fault in this effect and it is entirely
avoidable.

The sizing needs no measurement. Every word is placed in the same cell of an
`inline-grid`, so the cell is as wide as the longest and as tall as the
tallest, and it stays that size whichever word is showing. Nothing to recompute
on resize, and nothing that can be wrong before a font has loaded.

**The words are your markup and are never replaced.** Passing a list of strings
and building spans makes the text invisible to anything reading the page before
the script runs, and puts copy inside a configuration object where nobody will
think to translate it.

**It is pure in `t`.** Which word is showing, and how far through its handover,
are arithmetic on the clock.

name: ScrambleText
description: Type set one character at a time, in the order you choose

notes: No canvas and no WebGL. It splits the text already in the element and animates the pieces
The original string stays in the accessibility tree as one label, so a screen reader does not read sixty separate characters
destroy() puts the original text back, leaving the element as it was found
One transform and one opacity per piece, composited
The blur is dropped the moment a piece lands, because a permanent blur(0px) keeps every piece on its own layer

split.description: What each animated piece is. Characters are grouped inside their word so the text still wraps.

order.description: The order pieces arrive in. `centre` starts in the middle and works outwards. `random` keeps every piece in its place in the sentence and only changes its turn.

stagger.description: Milliseconds between one piece and the next. On a long heading this multiplies fast: 40ms across 60 characters is a two and a half second wait.

duration.description: Milliseconds each piece takes on its own.

rise.description: How far each piece travels. Negative falls from above instead of rising from below.

blur.description: Blur each piece starts at. Zero is cheaper and often better at small sizes, where the blur just reads as a smudge.

scale.description: Scale each piece starts at. 1 is no scaling, which is usually right for text.

seed.description: Seed for the random order. The same seed always gives the same order, so a recorded video and a live page match.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. For a one-shot reveal this should be a time after the animation has finished, so the text simply appears.

instruction: press replay to set it again
intro:
Sort sets type one piece at a time. A sort is a single piece of metal type, and
that is what each animated fragment here is: a character, a word or a whole line,
arriving on a stagger.

It takes an element that already contains text, splits it, and animates the
pieces. There is no canvas, no WebGL and no npm dependency.

Two things it does that most text-splitters do not. Characters are grouped inside
their word, so the text still wraps at the right places. And the original string
stays in the accessibility tree as one label, so a screen reader reads a sentence
rather than sixty separate characters.

`destroy()` puts the original text back. The element is left as it was found.

name: ScrollMarquee
description: A strip of content running sideways for ever, leaning with the scroll and reversing when it does

notes: No canvas and no WebGL. The strip is the author's own markup, moved into a track and transformed, so links keep working and images that have loaded stay loaded

Pure in t, which is the part that takes care. A marquee written the obvious way accumulates an offset every frame, and an effect that integrates against its own last frame cannot be recorded, cannot be seeked and drifts on a dropped frame. The position here is a function of the clock and the scroll position and nothing else
The content is duplicated once so the wrap is seamless, and the clone is aria-hidden with every focusable inside it given tabindex -1. A duplicate of the content is a duplicate to a screen reader too

The lean is scroll velocity, normalised and clipped. A trackpad reports an order of magnitude more than a wheel, and without a ceiling the strip lies flat on its side the first time somebody flicks the page
One transform on one element per frame, which is a composited property, so this does no layout work at all
One transform write per frame on a single element. Both properties are composited, so there is no layout and no paint
The content width is measured on mount and on resize rather than per frame

period.description: Seconds for the strip to travel exactly one copy of its content, which is also the loop. Longer content at the same period runs faster, because the distance is longer: this is a pace rather than a speed.

direction.description: Which way it runs when the page is still. 1 is leftwards, which is the direction text is read away from and the one that feels like it is going somewhere.

drag.description: How far the scroll drags it, in copies of the content per full scroll of the element through the viewport. This is what makes it reverse when you scroll back up. At 0 it runs at a constant pace and ignores the page.

skew.description: Degrees of lean at full scroll speed. This is the whole character of the effect: it is what makes the strip feel like it has mass and is being dragged rather than playing beside the page. Past about 15 it reads as a glitch.

stretch.description: How much it stretches along its travel at full scroll speed. Keep it small on a strip of type: this is a scaleX, so it widens the letterforms rather than moving them, and 12 per cent of that is enough to read as the font changing width mid-sentence. A row of logos or images takes far more of it happily, which is what the upper end of the range is for.

reference.description: The scroll speed that counts as full, in screens per second. 1.2 is about a brisk flick, so an ordinary scroll leans the strip a few degrees and a hard one leans it fully. Too low and a single wheel click pins it at maximum, which loses the difference between a nudge and a flick.

gap.description: Space between the end of one copy of the content and the start of the next. It is applied inside the copy, so it is part of the width the wrap is measured against: a gap added between the copies instead would make the loop a fraction longer than the thing it is wrapping, and the strip would stutter once per cycle.

instruction: scroll the page
intro:
A strip of content running sideways for ever, which leans when the page is
scrolled and reverses when the scroll does.

No canvas and no WebGL. The strip is your own markup, moved into a track and
transformed, so the links keep working and the images that have loaded stay
loaded.

Three things separate it from a 1996 `<marquee>`:

**It never stops.** The content is duplicated and the transform wraps at exactly
one copy's width, so there is no jump to find and no gap at the end.

**It leans with the scroll.** The skew comes from scroll velocity, which is what
makes the strip feel like it has mass: it is being dragged by the page rather
than playing beside it.

**It reverses.** Scrolling up pushes it the other way, because the same scroll
that skews it is added to its travel.

name: ScrollRevealRows
description: Children arrive on a stagger, held until the container is on screen

notes: No canvas and no WebGL. It moves the children already in the element
No IntersectionObserver of its own: the runtime already holds the loop until the element is on screen
destroy() clears every style it set, leaving the children as they were found
One transform and one opacity per child, composited
Nothing here reads layout, so it cannot cause a synchronous reflow

select.description: CSS selector for the children to animate, scoped to the container. Empty means every direct child, which is what you want most of the time.

order.description: The order children arrive in. `centre` starts in the middle and works outwards, which suits a row of three or five.

stagger.description: Milliseconds between one child and the next. Past about 150 a list of eight takes over a second to finish and people start scrolling away from it.

duration.description: Milliseconds each child takes on its own.

rise.description: How far each child travels. Negative falls from above. Large values read as a page that has not finished loading.

scale.description: Scale each child starts at. 1 is no scaling. Anything below 0.9 makes text resample and look soft on the way in.

blur.description: Blur each child starts at. Off by default: on a card with an image inside, a blur costs far more than the transform does.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. For a one-shot reveal this should be a time after the animation has finished, so the content simply appears.

instruction: press replay to bring them in again
intro:
Riser brings a container's children in on a stagger. It is the plainest thing in
this library and the one most pages actually need.

There is no canvas, no WebGL and no npm dependency. It takes a container, finds
the children, and moves them.

There is no `IntersectionObserver` in it either, which is the part worth knowing.
The runtime already has one: it holds the loop until the element is on screen. So
calling `start()` on mount gives you a scroll-triggered reveal, and adding your
own observer on top would only fight it.

`destroy()` clears every style it set. The children are left as they were found.

name: ScrollSlideshow
description: A slideshow the page scroll runs, on a web that drags and fringes as it moves

notes: The images are the host element's own children. They are hidden from sight and left in the document, so the alt text and source order are whatever you wrote, and a page with no JavaScript still shows the pictures
At rest nothing is distorted. The whole effect is a function of scroll velocity, so a reader who has stopped scrolling is looking at a photograph
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes
Textures are CLAMP_TO_EDGE. The bow samples past the edge of the image and a repeating wrap would tile the opposite side of the picture into the gap
Two texture reads per channel per pixel while crossfading, three channels, so six taps. It is fill rate and nothing else
Images upload once, on load. Nothing is uploaded per frame
Scroll velocity is measured on the scroll event and decayed in the frame loop. A per-frame difference reads zero on most frames, because scroll events do not fire every frame, and the effect stutters

paper.description: Shown wherever the web has pulled the image away from the edge of the frame. Match it to the page behind, or the gap reads as a border that appears only while scrolling. `auto` takes it from the page, so the effect adopts whatever it is dropped onto.

bend.description: How hard the sides lag behind the middle. Off by default: the bow is the loudest thing the press does and it competes with the picture, which is the thing you are actually showing. Turn it up to around 0.09 for the full press. Past about 0.12 it stops being a press and starts being a fisheye.

slip.description: How far the whole web slides against the direction of travel, the way anything with mass does when it is pulled. Small: this is the part you feel rather than see.

fringe.description: Separation between the colour channels at the edges while moving. A press running colour work strikes one plate per ink, and a moving web lands them a fraction apart. Keep it under about 0.01 or it reads as a broken monitor.

grain.description: Paper tooth over the image. Fixed per slide rather than per frame, because grain that crawls is a screen artefact and grain that sits still is paper.

reference.description: The scroll velocity that counts as full speed, in screens per second. Above it the effect stops growing. Lower makes the web bow more readily; too low and an ordinary wheel click maxes it out.

crossfade.description: Fraction of each slide's travel spent crossing to the next. Low holds each picture still and then cuts; 1 never stops dissolving.

instruction: scroll the page, then stop and watch it settle flat
intro:
A slideshow the page scroll runs, printed on a web rather than on sheets.

A web press does not feed sheets. It feeds one continuous ribbon of paper off a
reel, and everything this does follows from that: the ribbon has mass, so it
drags against the direction of travel, and a press running colour work strikes
one plate per ink, so a moving web lands them a fraction apart.

That is the whole behaviour. At rest this draws an undistorted photograph and
nothing else. The distortion is a function of scroll velocity, not of time and
not of position, so a reader who has stopped scrolling is looking at the picture
rather than at an effect. Most WebGL sliders warp continuously and end up reading
as a filter laid over the content. This one only exists while it is being pulled.

There is a third thing the press does, and it is off by default. At speed the
ribbon bows between the rollers, the sides lagging behind the middle. It is a
good effect and it is the loudest thing here by some distance, which is why
`bend` starts at zero: a slideshow is for showing the pictures, and a picture
that bends every time somebody scrolls past it is being shown second. Set `bend`
to about 0.09 if you want the press rather than the pictures. ScrollWarpImage is
the one that is actually about the distortion.

One WebGL2 fragment shader on one full-screen triangle. No three.js, no
dependency, no render targets.

name: ScrollWarpImage
description: A sheet drawn through its own frame by the scroll, leading in the middle and level again when it stops

notes: The picture is the host element's own child. It is hidden from sight and left in the document, so the alt text is whatever you wrote and a page with no JavaScript still shows it

One arc across the width, sin(pi x), so the sides hold back and the middle goes the way the page is going. The sign is the difference between a sheet being drawn through its frame and one sagging in it, and only the first reads as travel

The sheet is a rectangle inset from the frame and the drag carries its boundary with its contents, so the edges curve rather than staying square. Nothing is done to the horizontal axis: a sideways bend has no edge to run along and reads as the picture breathing
At rest nothing is distorted. The whole effect is a function of scroll velocity, so a reader who has stopped scrolling is looking at a photograph
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes
Three texture reads per pixel, one per channel, because the colour fringe evaluates the bow three times
The image uploads once, on load. Nothing is uploaded per frame
Scroll velocity is measured on the scroll event and decayed in the frame loop. A per-frame difference reads zero on most frames, because scroll events do not fire every frame, and the effect stutters

paper.description: Shown wherever the warp has pulled the sheet away from the frame. Match it to the page behind, or a border appears out of nowhere as soon as anyone scrolls. `auto` takes it from the page, so the effect adopts whatever it is dropped onto.

bend.description: How far the middle of the sheet runs ahead of its sides. This is the arc, and it is the option you came for: half a period of a sine across the width, nothing at the edges and everything in the span between them. Keep it and slip together under about inset x (1 - 2 x inset), or a hard flick pushes the bent edge off the frame.

slip.description: How far the whole sheet slides against the direction of travel, flat across its width, the way anything with mass does when it is pulled. Small: this is the part you feel rather than see, and it is kept apart from the bend so either can be turned off.

fringe.description: Separation between the colour channels while the sheet is moving. A press strikes one plate per ink and a moving web lands them a fraction apart. Keep it under about 0.01 or it reads as a broken monitor.

inset.description: How far the sheet sits in from every edge of the frame, as a share of the frame. The margin is what the bend happens in: at 0 the bent edge runs off the canvas and is chopped square, which reads as clipping rather than as paper. Measured in the frame rather than in the picture, so a photograph of any shape is inset by the same amount on all four sides.

reference.description: The scroll velocity that counts as full speed, in screens per second. Above it the effect stops growing. Lower makes the sheet bow more readily; too low and an ordinary wheel click maxes it out.

instruction: scroll the page, then stop and watch it settle flat
intro:
A photograph on a sheet drawn through its own frame by the scroll.

One arc across the width. The sides hold back, the middle goes the way the page
is going, and it comes level the moment the scroll stops. Scroll down, the page
travels up past you and the middle leads it up; scroll back and the curve turns
over. At rest there is no effect at all, which is the point: a reader who has
stopped scrolling is looking at a photograph rather than at a filter.

**The shape is the whole thing**, and it is worth saying what it is, because
there are two curves you could draw here and only one of them is a sheet.

```glsl
uv.y += velocity * bend * sin(uv.x * PI);
```

Half a period of a sine: zero at both sides, one in the middle, one smooth curve
with nothing in it to catch the eye.

**The sign is not a detail.** Both of them give you the same arc and they are
different effects. This one sends the middle the way the page is going, so the
sheet reads as being drawn through its frame while the sides hold back. Subtract
instead and the middle lags: the sheet sags, and it reads as weight rather than
as travel, which looks tired rather than pulled. Try both on your own picture
before you settle, and if it looks wrong rather than weak, this is the line to
change.

The sign follows the scroll rather than being fixed, so the curve turns over
when you scroll back up. A sheet that bent the same way whichever way you went
is a sheet nothing is pulling.

The other *curve* is the distance from the centre, squared, which is what this
effect used to do. It pins the middle and throws the sides about, and reads as
the frame wobbling rather than the picture moving. It also used to bend both
axes at once. A sideways bend has no edge to run along, so all it does is muddle
the shape, and taking it out is most of what makes the arc read.

The edges deform with the picture. The sheet is a rectangle inset from the
frame, the drag carries its boundary and its contents together, and whatever
falls outside is paper, so the edges curve rather than staying square. There is
no geometry here beyond one triangle: the shape of the sheet is a by-product of
the sampling rather than a mesh.

One WebGL2 fragment shader. No three.js, no dependency, no render targets.

name: SheenButton
description: The action pill: mono, uppercase, with a slow band of light crossing it

notes: Uses color-mix(); Chrome 111+, Safari 16.2+, Firefox 113+. Older browsers get the base colour with no hover shift, which is a graceful loss
No JavaScript animation at all. The motion is two CSS transitions
Composited transform and opacity only; nothing here triggers layout

tone.description: `solid` is the accent pill and is for the one action on the page that matters. `quiet` is the outlined secondary. If a screen has two solid SheenButtons on it, one of them is wrong.

href.description: Given an href it renders an <a>. Without one it renders a <button type="button">. Do not fake a link with a click handler. Keyboard users and screen readers both notice.

disabled.description: Button form only. An anchor cannot be disabled, so the anchor form sets aria-disabled instead and you must stop the navigation yourself.

instruction: hover, then tab to it
intro:
SheenButton is the action pill: mono, uppercase, 100px radius, with one slow band of
light crossing its face on hover. It is the one piece of the library that is
deliberately ordinary. The surprising things are meant to be the effects. This is
the thing you press to get one.

Two tones. `solid` is the accent pill and belongs to the single most important
action on a screen. `quiet` is the outlined secondary. If a page has two solid
SheenButtons on it, one of them is wrong.

It renders a `<button>` by default and an `<a>` when given an `href`. A thing
that navigates should be a link and a thing that acts should be a button. There
is no `as` prop and no polymorphic generic: the distinction is small enough to
make by hand and important enough not to get wrong.

The hover state darkens. The accent sits near the top of its range already, and
lifting it drops white lettering below 4.5:1. The direction most libraries go is
the one that fails.

name: SphereCluster
description: A hundred and one lit spheres that fly in, settle, breathe, and open where you point

notes: One InstancedMesh rather than a mesh each: the same geometry at the same tessellation, one draw call and one matrix per sphere instead of a hundred and one draw calls.

frustumCulled is off. An InstancedMesh computes its bounding sphere once and keeps it, and the first frame of the entrance has every sphere below the frame, so the cached bounds sit off screen and every later frame is culled against them. That records as a take of empty background with no error anywhere.

Which sphere the cursor is over is a real ray-sphere intersection against the displaced centres, not the nearest centre on the ground plane. The plane version picks the wrong sphere wherever the cluster is deep under the cursor, which is most of it: the nearest in x and y can be well behind the one whose surface you can see.

The entrance is a closed form in t rather than a timeline, so it can be seeked. The disturbance cannot be, and carries state; it is identically zero until the pointer touches it, which is why a take is still a pure function of t.
A hundred and one spheres at sixty-four segments square is about eight hundred thousand triangles, affordable exactly once because every instance shares the one geometry.

The collision pass is every pair, five thousand distance tests, and it runs only while something is actually out of place. It is what spreads the disturbance rather than what prevents overlaps, so it cannot be dropped: without it the interaction is one sphere twitching. Measured with pnpm gputime at 0.21ms a frame and about 1ms on a frame where the cluster is being pushed.

background.description: Behind the cluster. The near-white the hero sits on in the page this came from; the spheres are a pale blush and need a light ground to be pale against.

body.description: The spheres' own colour, before the light and the glow reach them. A dusty rose, which with a pure red glow over it is what gives the cluster its colour from every angle.

glow.description: The glow every sphere carries regardless of the light. This is the emissive, and it is doing more for the colour than the body is: an emissive is not lit, so it survives into the shadow side where the diffuse has gone, which is why the cluster reads warm all over rather than warm on one side. The scene this came from sets it to pure red. On r128's colour pipeline that renders as a blush; on a current one it saturates the red channel completely, which stops the bright side clipping to white and leaves every sphere a flat coral. A darker red puts the highlights back.

light.description: The key light, which does the modelling.

keyStrength.description: How bright the key is. Half the flat light, which is the balance the scene was lit at: the flat light is most of what you see and the key only has to say where the form is.

ambient.description: The flat light that reaches every surface whichever way it faces.

ambientStrength.description: How bright the flat light is. At full strength, as the scene has it, which is why the cluster is evenly lit and the shapes are carried by the silhouette rather than by shading.

distance.description: How far the camera sits from the cluster, in scene units. It is pulled back further on a narrow frame so the cluster still fits, which matters on a phone: at that aspect it otherwise runs off both sides.

intro.description: Seconds the entrance takes for one sphere, before the stagger. At 0 the cluster starts settled, which is what a backdrop behind a page that is already open wants.

stagger.description: Seconds between one sphere setting off and the next. The whole entrance therefore lasts the intro plus a hundred of these, so at the default it is finished a little after four and a half seconds.

drop.description: How far below the frame the spheres start, in scene units. Far enough that none of them is in shot before it sets off.

overshoot.description: How far past its resting place each sphere flies before falling back, and how far it bulges towards the camera on the way. The bulge is a half sine over each stage, so it returns to the resting depth exactly.

breathe.description: How far each sphere drifts once settled: a sine in height against a cosine in depth at half the amplitude. At 0 the settled cluster is still.

breatheSpeed.description: How fast it breathes, in radians a second. Each sphere is a fifth of a radian behind the one before it, which is what makes the cluster shimmer rather than pulse as one body.

part.description: The size of the shove a hovered sphere is given, along the normal at the point the cursor ray met its surface, which is a point on the side facing you. It is delivered over about a second rather than at once, and the collision pass carries it outward into the neighbours, so sweeping the cursor pushes the whole cluster about and it drifts home afterwards.

partRadius.description: How far along the cursor ray a sphere can be and still be hovered, as a multiple of itself. It exists only to stop a ray that has left the cluster entirely from catching something behind it.

instruction: you can push the swarm around with the cursor

credit.what: The whole scene: the hundred and one hand-placed sphere positions and radii, the dusty rose body under a red emissive, the three light intensities, the twenty-five degree camera, and the staggered three-stage entrance. The arrangement is placed rather than generated and that is most of why it reads as composed, so it is carried across as his rather than replaced with a hash. What could not come across is the physics: its pointer force decays frame to frame and its collision pass tests every pair, and both are accumulators that would stop renderAtTime being seekable.
credit.author: Ray Velez

name: SplitFlapText
description: A departure board, built as hinged leaves that have to pass through the strip to reach their letter

notes: No canvas and no WebGL. Each character becomes four layers: the top half of the glyph arriving and the bottom half of the one leaving, both still, and two leaves over them that fall and rise

The leaves go through the strip in order. A cell cannot jump from A to R, it has to pass through everything between, which is why a real board lands its letters in the order the alphabet puts them rather than left to right. Nothing about that was designed: it falls out of modelling the strip, and it is the most recognisable thing about the object
A character that is not on the strip stops at position 0, the blank. A board cannot show what it does not carry, and inventing a leaf for it would be the one dishonest thing in here

Every cell is the width of the widest glyph on the strip, measured once in the real face. The flaps on a board are all the same size because they are the same part, and a board whose cells breathe is not a board

A falling leaf darkens as it turns away from the light. It is the only shading in the effect and it is doing a lot: without it the two leaves are flat shapes sliding over each other and the cell reads as a wipe
Pure in t. Which leaf a cell is on and how far through its fall are both arithmetic on the clock, so the recorder can seek it and a dropped frame costs nothing
The original string stays in the accessibility tree as one label. A board read leaf by leaf is a stream of nonsense
destroy() puts the original text back, leaving the element as it was found

Four layers of DOM per character, two of them transformed every frame. That is the cost of building the mechanism rather than suggesting it, and it is the reason this is for a board and not for a paragraph: keep it under about forty characters
Both moving leaves are composited transforms and a filter. The text of a leaf is only written when it changes, which is once per flap rather than once per frame

strip.description: The leaves, in the order they are stacked. Position 0 is what a cell shows at rest, and a blank there is why a board starts empty. The order is the mechanism: a cell has to pass through every leaf between where it is and where it is going, so putting the digits after the letters is what makes a time take longer to land than a word.

flap.description: Milliseconds for one leaf to fall. This multiplies: a cell showing Z has to drop twenty six leaves to get there, so 52ms is already more than a second of travel for the back half of the alphabet. That is what a board does, and it is why they are satisfying.

stagger.description: Milliseconds between one cell starting and the next. At 0 the whole board starts together, which is what a board does when the schedule changes, and the letters still land in alphabetical order because the strip decides that, not this.

hold.description: Milliseconds before the first cell starts. A board sits blank for a moment before it runs, and that moment is what tells you it is a board rather than a label that happens to be animating.

face.description: The face of a leaf. Dark, because that is what they are: these are painted metal or plastic tiles, and a pale one reads as a card being turned rather than a flap falling.

ink.description: The type printed on the leaf. Off white rather than white, which is both what the real thing looks like after a few years and what keeps it from glaring out of a paper page.

seam.description: How dark the line across the middle of a cell is. It is drawn as a line rather than a gap, because on a board it is two leaves meeting and not a space between them. At 0 the cell reads as one tile and the mechanism disappears.

depth.description: Perspective applied to the fall. At 0 it is a flat fold, which looks like a sheet of paper creasing; low numbers are a strong perspective and read as a leaf that has thickness. Too low and the leaf swings past the front of the cell.

shade.description: How much a falling leaf darkens as it turns away from the light. At 0 the two leaves are flat shapes sliding over each other and the cell reads as a wipe rather than as something hinged.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. For a one-shot reveal this should be a time after the board has finished, so the text simply appears, set in its cells and still.

instruction: press replay to set it again
intro:
SplitFlapText is a departure board. Each character is a split-flap cell: a stack
of hinged leaves, each carrying half a glyph, dropping one at a time until the
right one is showing.

The mechanism is the effect, so it is built rather than suggested. Four layers
per cell:

- the top half of the glyph arriving, sitting still behind everything
- the bottom half of the glyph leaving, likewise
- a leaf over the top half, carrying the upper half of the leaving glyph,
  falling from upright to edge on
- a leaf over the bottom half, carrying the lower half of the arriving glyph,
  rising from edge on to upright

Two things follow from that and neither had to be designed.

**The leaves go through the strip in order.** A cell cannot jump from A to R. It
has to pass through everything between, one leaf at a time, which is why a real
board lands its letters in the order the alphabet puts them rather than left to
right, and why a time takes longer to arrive than a word. That is the single
most recognisable thing about the object, and it falls straight out of modelling
the strip.

**A character that is not on the strip stops at the blank.** A board cannot show
what it does not carry. Inventing a leaf for it would be the one dishonest thing
in here.

It is pure in `t`: which leaf a cell is on, and how far through its fall, are
both arithmetic on the clock.

name: SplitFountainText
description: Two or three inks in the same duct, blended by the rollers, with the gradient belonging to the sheet rather than to the letters

notes: The gradient belongs to the sheet, not to the letters, and that is what makes it a split fountain rather than gradient text. One pass of ink across the whole forme: a word near the left is in one ink, a word near the right is in another, and the heading between them is caught in the blend

That falls out of mounting it on the sheet. background-clip on a container clips its background to every piece of text inside, however deeply nested, so one gradient inks a whole page in register. Put the gradient on each element instead and every heading gets the same little rainbow

It is the only text effect here that does not take the text apart. No spans, no splitting, no hidden label: the text is the text the browser already had, so it selects, wraps, translates, searches and reads exactly as before. Nothing else in this library can say that

The blend is built from several stops per ink rather than one, so its boundary can be nudged. A duct is filled by hand and the rollers do not mix evenly, so the line where two inks meet is never straight; one stop per ink is a CSS gradient and not a press
The stops are sorted before they are written. A CSS gradient quietly clamps any stop that falls before the one in front of it, which turns a wobble into a hard edge
-webkit-text-fill-color is set as well as color. Without it WebKit paints the text in its own colour over the clipped background and the effect does nothing at all
Pure in t: the whole gradient is arithmetic on the clock and a hash of the seed

One string built and one style written per frame, and only when the string has changed. The cost is the repaint of the text, which is why this wants to be a sheet of headings rather than a page of body copy
No elements are created and nothing is measured. The DOM is untouched

first.description: The ink at the start of the duct. Split fountains are at their best with inks that make something worth seeing where they meet: two that mix to mud give a sheet with a dead band across the middle.

second.description: The ink in the middle. Set it to the same value as one of its neighbours and you have a two-ink fountain, which is what most presses actually run.

third.description: The ink at the far end.

angle.description: Which way the duct runs across the sheet. A real fountain runs across the press, so the gradient is square to the sheet; a degree or two off square is the honest amount, and it stops the blend lining up with the lines of type.

blend.description: How wide the mixing zone is. Narrow is a press just started, with the inks still separate; wide is one that has been running, with the colours walked well into each other. Both are real points in a run and they look quite different.

wobble.description: How uneven the blend is. At 0 it is a perfectly even ramp, which is to say a CSS gradient. The unevenness is the whole tell that ink was involved.

walk.description: How far the whole fountain walks over one period. On a press the inks creep along the duct as the run goes on, so the boundary moves and never comes back. Here it returns, because a loop has to; keep it small enough that it reads as creep rather than as a sweep.

seed.description: Seed for the unevenness. The same seed gives the same sheet, so a recording and a live page match.

period.description: Seconds for one cycle of the walk. Long: this is the colour of the page, and the colour of a page should not be something you can watch changing.

instruction: the fountain walks on its own
intro:
SplitFountainText is a split fountain. Two or three inks go into the same duct
on the press, the rollers blend them where they meet, and every sheet comes off
with a gradient running across it.

What makes it a split fountain rather than gradient text is that **the gradient
belongs to the sheet, not to the letters**. One pass of ink across the whole
forme: a word near the left is in one ink, a word near the right is in another,
and the heading between them is caught in the blend. A heading that wraps starts
its second line back in the first ink, because the ink depends on where you are
on the sheet and not where you are in the string.

Put the gradient on each element instead, which is what every version of this
does, and every element gets its own little rainbow, every heading has the same
colours in the same places, and the whole point is gone.

That falls out of **mounting it on the sheet rather than on the text**.
`background-clip: text` on a container clips its background to every piece of
text inside it, however deeply nested, so one gradient inks a whole page in
register.

name: SpotlightCard
description: A card under a desk lamp, lit across the face and bright on the near edge

notes: No canvas and no WebGL. One added span whose background and box-shadow are painted by CSS from the pointer position
Two layers rather than one: a wide weak sheen across the face, and a hard highlight on whichever edge is turned toward the light. Paper is matte, so it scatters rather than reflecting a bright spot

Light and shade together. Lifting the face alone is what the physics says and what nothing in a light room can see, so the far side darkens as the near side brightens. Painted normally rather than screened, because screening cannot darken anything
Window pointer scope, so the sheen moves before the cursor reaches the card
Two style writes per frame on one composited element. Nothing is measured and nothing reflows
The layer is added once, at setup, and removed on destroy

light.description: Colour of the lamp. Warm, unless the room is not. It is screened over the card rather than painted on it, so a saturated colour tints the whole face.

sheen.description: How much the face lifts under the lamp. Paper scatters, so this wants to stay low and wide: a tight bright spot is a light source sitting on the card rather than a card being lit.

spread.description: How wide the lift is, as a share of the card. Large and weak reads as a lamp; small and strong reads as a torch.

edge.description: How brightly the edge facing the lamp catches. This is the part that sells it: a glow with no lit edge reads as something emitting light, and a card does not emit anything.

shade.description: How far the side away from the lamp falls into shade. This is what makes it read at all. A near white card lifted a few percent looks like a near white card; what you see when something is lit is the gradient across it, and half of that gradient is the dark half.

ease.description: How fast the lamp catches up with the cursor, as a fraction of the remaining distance per frame. At 1 it is welded to the pointer and reads as a rectangle following the mouse.

instruction: move the cursor over the card
intro:
A card under a desk lamp, with the cursor as the lamp.

The usual version of this puts a bright radial glow on a dark card and calls it a
spotlight. That is a light source sitting on the surface, which is not what a
lamp does to paper. Paper is matte: it scatters. Move a lamp across a card and
what you see is a broad, low-contrast lift across the face, a hard bright line on
whichever edge is turned toward the light, and the far side falling away into
shade.

All three are here, and the third one is the one that makes it work. The first
version of this lifted the face and nothing else, which is what the physics says
and what nothing in a light room can actually see: a near-white card lifted a few
percent is indistinguishable from a near-white card. What you read when something
is lit is the **gradient** across it, and half of that gradient is the dark half.

The edge matters too. A glow with no lit edge reads as something emitting light,
and a card does not emit anything.

No canvas and no WebGL. One added span whose background and box-shadow are
repainted from the pointer position.

name: SquircleKeycap
description: A key drawn as a superellipse and extruded, which travels when you press it

notes: The shape is the point. A border-radius is a rectangle with circular arcs stuck on the corners, and the join between the straight edge and the arc is continuous in position and direction but not in curvature: it jumps from zero to one over the radius, instantly. A superellipse has no join at all, because it is one equation the whole way round

Walked as a path rather than approximated, so the exponent is a real control: 2 is an ellipse, 4 is the shape everybody means, and by 12 it is a rectangle with a suggestion of a corner. No value of border-radius lands on any of them

The exponent is applied to the absolute value of the cosine and the sign put back, because a fractional power of a negative number is not a number and the left half of the shape would simply not be drawn

The travel is a closed form of the time since the press, so renderAtTime is pure in t. A key is state between frames by nature, which is the one thing this library will not have: the resolution is to keep the list of presses rather than the position and work the displacement out from the clock. Seeking backwards unpresses the key, which a spring integrated frame by frame can never do
An attack and a decay, not a spring. A keycap does not oscillate: it goes down against a stop, fast and ending abruptly, and comes back on a rubber dome, slower and settling without overshoot

The side is drawn as its own extrusion rather than as a drop shadow, which is the difference between a key and a sticker. It is also what makes the travel legible: the side gets shorter as the key goes down, and that is the part anyone actually reads
The top is dished rather than domed. A keycap is concave so a fingertip sits in it, and what reports that is a soft dark edge at the top of the face, not a highlight in the middle
A press anywhere on the element counts rather than only inside the drawn shape. A click two pixels outside the edge is a click the reader believes they made
2D rather than WebGL. A key is something you want several of on a page, and the budget is one WebGL context
It is a drawing of a control, not a control. There is no role, no focus and no keyboard handling, because a canvas cannot carry them. Put it behind a real button if it is going to do something
Two filled paths of a hundred and twenty points, a clipped gradient and one glyph

plate.description: The surface the key sits on. Slightly darker than the cap, because a key is lighter than the thing it is set into and that difference is most of what says it stands up.

side.description: The sides, which are what makes it a solid rather than a sticker. It wants to be a clear step darker than the cap: this is a facet turned away from the light, not a shadow.

ink.description: The legend, and the contact shadow under the key.

legend.description: What is printed on the key. One or two characters: it is set at under a third of the key's width, and a word at that size is a label on a key rather than a key.

corner.description: The superellipse exponent. 2 is an ellipse, 4 is the shape everybody means by a squircle, and by 12 it is a rectangle with a hint of a corner. The useful range is narrow and the difference inside it is the whole item.

size.description: How much of the shorter side of the element the key takes up.

depth.description: How tall the key stands, as a share of its width. This is the thing the press has to eat into, so a flat key has nowhere to travel and reads as a flicker.

travel.description: How far down it goes when pressed, as a share of its height. At 1 it bottoms out flush with the plate, which reads as broken rather than as pressed.

snap.description: Seconds the key takes to come back up. The way down is fixed and fast, because that is a key hitting a stop; this is the rubber dome, and it is the only half with any character in it.

instruction: press the key
intro:
SquircleKeycap is a key you can press: a superellipse, extruded, that travels
when you push it and comes back on a rubber dome.

name: StippleField
