description: A stipple drawing where tone is how many marks there are, and the cursor works it up

notes: Tone is carried by the number of marks rather than their size, which is what separates a stipple from a halftone: an engraver has one nib, so darker means more marks rather than fatter ones
Each mark is tested against the nine surrounding cells, because a mark thrown off centre crosses into its neighbour and testing only its own cell would slice it at the boundary
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes

The cursor raises the tone it is over, which adds marks rather than enlarging them. It is a plain function of the pointer position with nothing integrated, so a scripted path replays identically and renderAtTime stays pure
Nine cell tests per pixel, each a hash and a distance, plus four octaves of value noise for the tone field
Most cells fail the tone test and cost one hash, so the lighter the field the cheaper it is
Nothing is uploaded per frame. Only uniforms change

paper.description: The paper behind the marks. `auto` takes it from the page, so the effect adopts whatever it is dropped onto.

ink.description: The nib. A light-dark() pair picks by the ground it lands on.

accent.description: A second nib, on a small share of the marks. A light-dark() pair picks by the ground it lands on.

pitch.description: Cell size in CSS pixels. There is at most one mark per cell, so this is the spacing of the stipple rather than its weight. Laid out in pixels so the marks keep their size whatever shape the element is.

jitter.description: How far each mark is thrown off the centre of its cell. At 0 the marks sit on a grid and it stops being a stipple; at 1 they are anywhere in their cell and the grid is undetectable.

scale.description: Size of the tone field the marks follow. Lower is broader country with slower changes in density.

weight.description: Radius of a mark, measured in cells. Every mark is the same size, which is the point: an engraver has one nib. Past about 0.4 they touch at full density and it becomes a solid.

contrast.description: How hard the tone field pushes away from the midtone. Applied about 0.5, so raising it opens the field out rather than dragging the whole thing dark.

accentShare.description: Share of marks that take the second nib. Small: this is a second pass over a drawing, not a second drawing.

touch.description: How much tone the cursor works up under itself. Tone is how many marks there are, so this is the hand adding marks, not a light being shone on the drawing. Zero leaves the field ambient.

reach.description: How far the hand reaches, as a share of the short side. The falloff is a Gaussian and has no edge to find, so this is where it has mostly faded rather than where it stops.

period.description: Seconds for one loop of the drift. The tone field travels a closed circle through noise space, so it returns to exactly where it began and the loop is seamless. Slow on purpose: the marks should seem to be settling rather than moving.

instruction: move the cursor across it
intro:
A stipple drawing. Tone is carried by how many marks there are, not how big they
are.

That is the whole distinction from a halftone, and it is worth being exact about,
because the two look superficially alike and the difference is the entire reason
this exists alongside HalftoneBackdrop. A halftone puts a dot in the middle of
every cell of a regular grid and varies its size: the count is fixed and the area
does the work. A stipple engraver has one nib. Every mark is the same size, and
darker means more marks, closer together.

So the grid here is only a way of avoiding a sort. Each cell holds at most one
mark, thrown off the centre by a hash, and whether it exists at all comes from
comparing a second hash against the tone wanted at that point. Off-grid positions
and a population that thins out is what reads as a hand rather than as a screen.

Each pixel is tested against the nine cells around it rather than only its own. A
mark thrown off centre crosses into its neighbour, and testing one cell would
slice it at the boundary: the jitter would then read as marks being cut rather
than as marks being scattered.

The tone field drifts on a closed orbit through noise space, so the loop returns
to exactly where it started rather than being crossfaded.

One WebGL2 fragment shader on one full-screen triangle. No three.js, no
dependency.

name: StrokeText
description: Hollow letters that fill with ink from the foot up, with the stroke outside the letterform where it belongs

notes: -webkit-text-stroke centres the stroke on the letterform, so half of it is painted inside the glyph. On a light weight that half eats the counters: the inside of an o closes up, an e fills in, and the setting goes muddy at exactly the widths where an outline is worth having. A face designed as an inline puts the stroke outside the letter

The fix needs no new CSS and works everywhere. The text is drawn twice: behind, a stroke of twice the width asked for, centred, so it reaches the right distance outside the letter; in front, the same text filled, painting over the inner half. What is left is an outside-only stroke of exactly the width given, with the counters intact

The animated thing is the ink. The front layer is a gradient clipped to the text with a hard edge in it, so below the edge the letter is solid and above it the letter is paper. Moving the edge fills the type from the foot up, which is what inking a block looks like
The ink line tilts and has a small wobble, because a roller is not level. A dead horizontal edge across a line of type reads as a mask rather than as a surface of ink

`paper` has to match the page behind the element. It is not decoration: it is the colour that covers the inner half of the stroke, so if it is wrong the hollow of every letter is wrong and the outline looks twice as thick as it is
The stroked copy is the one in the flow and the one a screen reader reaches. The filled copy on top is marked hidden, because the text underneath is the real text and the layer over it is paint
-webkit-text-fill-color is set as well as color on the front layer. Without it WebKit paints the text over the clipped background and the fill never shows at all
Two copies of the text and one gradient string per frame, written only when it changes. Text strokes and background-clip are both painted rather than composited, so this wants to be a heading
Nothing is created after mount and nothing is measured

outline.description: The outline. It carries the whole letterform while the ink is still low, so it wants enough contrast against the paper to be read on its own.

ink.description: The ink that fills the letters. A second colour is worth having: ink the same colour as the outline gives a letter that simply goes solid, and the point is to watch it fill.

paper.description: What the hollow of a letter shows, and it must match the page behind the element. Load-bearing rather than decorative: this is the colour that paints over the inner half of the stroke, so if it is wrong every counter is wrong and the outline looks twice as thick as it is.

width.description: Width of the outline, in ems, so it holds at any size. This is the real outside width: the stroke actually drawn is twice this and the inner half is covered. Past about 0.05 the outline starts closing the counters from the outside instead, which no trick can fix.

level.description: How full the letters are when the run has finished. 1 fills them completely and ends on solid type. Around 0.6 leaves them half inked, which is the more interesting place to stop and reads as a block that has been rolled once.

duration.description: Milliseconds for the ink to rise, eased so it arrives rather than stops. Slow enough to watch: the rise is the effect and the outline is only where it starts.

hold.description: Milliseconds of empty outline before the ink starts. Worth having: it is the moment that tells you the letters were hollow to begin with.

tilt.description: How far the ink line is off level. A roller is not level, and a dead horizontal edge across a line of type reads as a mask. Two or three degrees is enough to be felt without being seen.

wobble.description: How uneven the height of the ink is. Small, and fixed by the seed rather than moving: a roller lays an uneven line, it does not lay a wavy one.

seed.description: Seed for the unevenness. The same seed gives the same pull, so a recording and a live page match.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. For a one-shot rise this should be a time after it has finished, so the letters are inked to the level set. Setting it to 0 instead gives the hollow outline, which is also a perfectly good still.

instruction: press replay to ink it again
intro:
StrokeText sets hollow letters and fills them with ink from the foot up. An
inline face being inked, rather than an outline for its own sake.

Two problems, and the first is why most outlined text on the web looks wrong.

**`-webkit-text-stroke` centres the stroke on the letterform**, so half of it is
painted inside the glyph. On a light weight that half eats the counters: the
inside of an o closes up, an e fills in, and the setting goes muddy at exactly
the widths where an outline is worth having. A typeface designed as an inline
puts the stroke outside the letter, where it belongs.

The fix needs no new CSS and works everywhere. The text is drawn twice. Behind,
a stroke of **twice** the width you asked for, centred, so it reaches the right
distance outside the letter and an equal distance inside. In front, the same
text filled, painting over the inner half. What is left is an outside-only
stroke of exactly the width given, with the counters intact.

**The second problem is what to animate**, and the answer is the ink. The front
layer is a gradient clipped to the text with a hard edge in it: below the edge
the letter is solid, above it the letter is paper. Move the edge and the type
fills from the foot up.

The edge tilts and has a small wobble, because a roller is not level. A dead
horizontal line across a setting reads as a mask rather than as a surface of
ink.

name: TerrainRelief
description: A topographic relief on paper, printed with its own contour lines

notes: three.js must already be a dependency of the project. It is not bundled
The displacement runs in the vertex shader, so a 160 square grid is one upload and costs memory rather than frame time
The same displacement is injected into a custom depth material. Without that the land casts the shadow of a flat plane and the relief detaches from its own shading
25,600 vertices, four octaves of noise each, twice: once for the surface and once for the shadow pass
Nothing is uploaded per frame. Only uniforms change

paper.description: The paper behind the land. Match it to your page background or the horizon reads as a hard edge. `auto` takes it from the page, so the effect adopts whatever it is dropped onto.

land.description: The land itself. Keep it close to the paper but not identical, or the horizon disappears entirely. A light-dark() pair picks by the ground it lands on.

ink.description: The contour lines. A warm grey reads as print; pure black reads as a wireframe. A light-dark() pair picks by the ground it lands on.

indexInk.description: Every fifth line is an index contour, the one a real map would label. This is the obvious place for your own colour. A light-dark() pair picks by the ground it lands on.

relief.description: Height of the land. Past about 3 the ridges are steeper than the sun can light and the far side goes black.

scale.description: Size of the landforms. Lower is broader country with fewer, longer ridges.

density.description: Contour lines per unit of height. More lines reads as steeper country. Past about 8 the lines are closer than the pixels and the map turns grey.

weight.description: Weight of the lines. Zero is bare land with no map printed on it, which is a perfectly good backdrop in its own right.

elevation.description: Sun height above the horizon. Low rakes the ridges and is most of where the depth comes from. High flattens the whole thing into a map.

azimuth.description: Sun direction around the compass. Convention on a printed map is light from the north west, which is about 315.

tilt.description: Camera height. Zero is down on the deck with a horizon, one looks straight down at a map. The interesting ground is in between.

zoom.description: How much of the frame the land fills.

drift.description: How far the land travels through noise space on its circuit. Separate from how fast it travels, and the one that matters behind a heading: a slow period still moves the same ground the same distance, and distance is what the eye catches. At 0 the land is fixed and the only thing that moves is nothing.

period.description: Seconds for one loop of the morph. The land travels a closed orbit through noise space and returns exactly. Slow on purpose: ground that visibly moves behind a heading is the fastest way to lose a reader.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. Any time works here: a still relief is a map, which is a finished thing to look at.

instruction: ambient, watch the land breathe
intro:
Contour is a topographic relief on paper: matte land, one low sun, and contour
lines printed on the surface at fixed height intervals. Every fifth line is an
index contour, the one a real map would label, drawn in a second colour.

It is a real three.js scene, and the displacement runs in the vertex shader
rather than in JavaScript. A 160 square grid is 25,600 vertices uploaded once,
after which the resolution costs memory and not frame time.

The part worth knowing about is the shadow. three renders the shadow pass with a
different material, which knows nothing about a displacement written into the
surface shader, so the land would cast the shadow of a flat plane and the whole
relief would detach from its own shading. The same terrain function is therefore
injected into a custom depth material as well. That is the step most terrain
demos skip, and it is why theirs look painted on.

The height field is ridged rather than smooth. Taking the absolute value of each
octave and inverting it turns rolling hills into ridges and valleys, which is
what makes contour lines worth drawing at all: smooth noise gives you concentric
blobs.

The land morphs along a closed orbit through noise space, so the loop returns to
its start exactly and any span of `period` seconds joins back on itself.

name: TiltCard
description: A panel that leans towards the cursor, with a sheen raking across it

notes: No canvas and no WebGL. One CSS transform and one radial gradient
The easing is a CSS transition rather than a per-frame spring, so nothing integrates and renderAtTime stays pure
The sheen uses mix-blend-mode: soft-light, which is unsupported below Safari 15.4 and simply does not paint there
Composited transform and opacity only
The gradient string is rebuilt each frame; the paint is cheap, the string is cheaper

maxTilt.description: How far it leans at the corners. Past about 16 the text on the card starts to distort and people read it as a bug rather than a bevel.

perspective.description: Perspective distance. Lower is a wider, more theatrical lens; higher flattens the lean into something closer to a skew.

scale.description: Scale while the pointer is over it. 1 is no lift. Above 1.06 the card starts covering its neighbours.

sheen.description: Strength of the light pool following the cursor. Zero switches the overlay off entirely.

sheenColor.description: Colour of the sheen. On paper a warm white reads as light falling on the card. A cool white reads as glass, which is a different product.

sheenSize.description: How wide the light pool is, as a fraction of the panel. Small and bright reads as a torch; wide and faint reads as a window.

ease.description: How long the panel takes to follow the cursor and to settle back. Zero locks it to the pointer, which feels precise and slightly cheap.

invert.description: Tip away from the cursor rather than towards it. Reads as pushing the card rather than lifting it.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. At rest there is no pointer, so this draws the panel flat and unmodified, which is the right answer.

instruction: move the cursor across the card
intro:
Tilt leans a panel towards the cursor and rakes a pool of light across it as it
goes. One CSS transform and one radial gradient. No canvas, no WebGL, no npm
dependency.

The easing is a CSS transition rather than a per-frame spring. That is a
deliberate choice: nothing integrates against the previous frame, so
`renderAtTime` stays pure and the recorder scrubs the smoothing along with
everything else. A spring would look almost the same and would make the effect
impossible to record.

The sheen is a warm white by default, not a cool one. Cool white on a panel reads
as glass. Warm white reads as light falling on paper, which is the library this
belongs to.

`destroy()` removes the sheen and clears every style it set.

name: TranslucentSheets
description: A drifting stack of translucent paper that goes darker where the sheets cross

notes: three.js must already be a dependency of the project. It is not bundled
The sheets multiply rather than composite, which is order-independent, so the whole pile is one InstancedMesh and there is no transparency sorting to get wrong
Nothing in the scene can be brighter than the paper. A multiply has no way to add light, so there is no specular highlight and there cannot be one
No shadow map. Nothing here is opaque enough to cast one

Known limitation: with the grain on and the pile moving, a tenth of a millisecond of movement changes about a fifth of the frame. It is fizz rather than motion and it scales with the sheet count, measured at 0.12 mean for one sheet, 0.66 for four and 2.08 for the default twelve. fibre at 0 removes it, and so does drift at 0. Hashing the grain in screen space instead does not
One draw call whatever the sheet count. Two triangles each
The instance matrices are rebuilt on the CPU each frame, which is fourteen compose calls into pre-allocated scratch
Fill rate rather than geometry is the cost. A stack of large sheets covering the viewport several times over is the worst case
Paper fibre is grain, and grain is the hardest thing for a video codec to compress, so the recording carries a per-item quality override. The effect itself is unaffected

paper.description: The paper behind the stack. Everything else multiplies down from here, so this is the lightest value in the scene. `auto` takes it from the page, so the effect adopts whatever it is dropped onto.

ink.description: What each sheet multiplies the paper by. Most of the stack is this. A warm grey reads as tracing paper; push it green and it becomes drafting film.

accent.description: Roughly one sheet in five is printed in this instead. Never the first, so the accent always has something crossing it.

sheets.description: How many sheets. Changing it rebuilds the pile, which is the one option here that is not free. Depth is by index, so a new sheet lands on top rather than shuffling the stack.

density.description: How dark one sheet is on its own. The stack compounds from here, so small numbers go a long way: fourteen sheets at 0.3 is a solid brown blot in the middle where they all cross. Behind content, come down rather than reaching for opacity.

spread.description: How far the sheets are scattered. Low is a neat pile with heavy overlap, high is a table strewn with them.

radius.description: Corner radius of a sheet. Real vellum is guillotined rather than die-cut, so keep it small. It exists so the corners do not read as a hard polygon.

sheen.description: How much a sheet lifts toward the light as it turns into it. Within a multiply this can only mean less tint, never more light, which is what paper catching a lamp actually looks like.

fibre.description: Paper fibre. At zero the sheets are film rather than paper.

elevation.description: Light height above the horizon, degrees.

azimuth.description: Light direction around the compass, degrees.

tilt.description: Camera height. 0 is edge on to the pile, which is mostly cut edges. 1 looks straight down at it.

zoom.description: How much of the frame the stack fills.

drift.description: How far each sheet travels on its circuit. Separate from how fast it travels, and the one that matters behind a heading: slowing the period alone moves the same sheets across the same gap. At 0 the pile is still and you have a static collage, which is a perfectly good backdrop.

period.description: Seconds for one loop of the drift. Every sheet travels a closed circle, so the pile returns to exactly where it started and the loop is seamless. Slow on purpose: sheets that settle over half a minute read as paper, and sheets that cross the frame in ten seconds read as an animation.

instruction: ambient, watch the overlaps build
intro:
A loose stack of translucent paper, drifting. Where two sheets cross the paper
goes darker, and you can read the order of the pile by how dark it gets.

The blend mode is the whole design. These sheets multiply rather than composite:
the result is destination times source, which is what a diffusing sheet laid over
another one actually does. More usefully, multiplying is order-independent. Two
sheets crossing give the same answer whichever is drawn first.

That matters more than it sounds. Ordinary alpha-blended transparency has to be
sorted back to front, and there is no way to sort inside a single InstancedMesh,
so stacked-plane scenes usually either flicker as the sort order flips or give up
on instancing and take a draw call per sheet. Multiplying sidesteps the problem
rather than solving it. Fourteen sheets draw in one call, in any order, and the
picture is the same.

The cost is real and worth stating. Nothing here can be brighter than the paper.
A multiply has no way to add light, so there is no specular highlight and there
cannot be one. Where a sheet turns into the light it fades toward no tint at all,
which within a multiply is the only direction "brighter" exists in, and which
happens to be what paper catching a lamp looks like anyway.

There is no shadow map either. Nothing in the scene is opaque enough to cast one,
and a translucent sheet throwing a hard shadow is the tell that gives these scenes
away. The overlaps are the depth cue.

Concept credit: [Infinite Liquid Glass
Grid](https://tympanus.net/codrops/), Codrops, September 2026, for the idea that
the glass can be faked in the shader with no refraction pass at all. Written from
scratch, and recast from glass to paper.

name: TruchetMaze
description: Quarter-circle tiles flipped at random in a square lattice, joining into one continuous maze that breathes along a diagonal

notes: The arcs are distance fields rather than drawn strokes. Distance to a circle is one length() and a subtraction, so a tile is two of those and a minimum, and the stroke is a band around the zero set. Line width is therefore a number rather than a resolution, and nothing aliases as the cells get small

fwidth measures one pixel in lattice units, which is what keeps the edge the same softness at every cell count and every rotation. A constant would be a different number of pixels each time the lattice is scaled

The tile hash is the multiply-and-stir kind rather than fract(sin(x) * 43758.0). The argument is a cell index that grows without bound as the lattice is rotated or the cell count raised, and the sine of a large number is a different value on a different driver

One hash, two length() calls, a minimum and a smoothstep per pixel. No noise, no loops, no textures and no render targets: this is among the cheapest effects in the library and it is meant to be, because a backdrop that costs a tenth of a frame is a backdrop that still works on a machine already doing something else
Measured with pnpm gputime rather than by timing the draw call, which returns as soon as the command is queued and says nothing about what the GPU then does

ground.description: The ground the maze is drawn on. Near-black with a trace of violet in it rather than a true black, so the darkest part of the ramp still has somewhere to go.

near.description: Line colour at the near end of the ramp.

mid.description: Line colour through the middle. This is the stop that matters: between two colours you get one hue and a tint of it, and passing through a third is what makes a ramp read as light falling across something rather than as a fade.

far.description: Line colour at the far end.

cells.description: Tiles across the short edge of the frame. Few and large reads as architecture; many and small reads as a textile, and past about twenty the curves are too short to follow and it becomes a texture rather than a maze.

thickness.description: Line width as a fraction of a cell, so it holds when the cell count changes. At 0.5 neighbouring arcs meet and the maze fills in solid, which is a different and also usable look.

rotation.description: Rotation of the lattice in degrees. Only ninety are worth having: a square lattice of symmetric tiles is unchanged by a quarter turn.

softness.description: Softness of the line edge, on top of the one pixel of antialiasing that is always there. At 0 the line is as crisp as the display allows; high values turn the maze into a glow of itself.

seed.description: Which tiles are flipped. Changes the maze and nothing else, and every value is as good as every other, which is the pleasant thing about a Truchet tiling.

breathe.description: How much the line weight swells and thins as the wave passes. At 0 the maze is a still image, which is a legitimate way to use this and costs nothing to draw.

wave.description: Cells between one crest of the breathing wave and the next. Short wavelengths make neighbouring tiles disagree and read as noise; long ones move the whole frame together and read as a tide.

tilt.description: Direction of the colour ramp. 0 runs it up the frame, 1 runs it across, and between the two it runs on a diagonal, which is where it crosses the most curves.

period.description: Seconds for one cycle of the breathing wave. The loop closes exactly on it, because the phase advances a whole turn in that time.

instruction: the maze breathes along a diagonal

credit.what: The parameter set: cells, thickness, rotation, softness and seed turned out to be the right five knobs for a quarter-circle Truchet tiling, and there was no reason to invent different ones. The tiling itself is Sebastien Truchet's, from 1704. The code here is this repo's own.
credit.author: Shader Effects Inc.

name: TumblingBlocks
description: A rhombille tiling lit as stacked cubes, with the light going round rather than the geometry moving

notes: The three internal edges of a hexagon are rays from its centre, not lines through it. A line at one of those angles also passes through the opposite vertex, so measuring distance to lines draws six spokes and splits each rhombus into two triangles. Behind the ray the nearest point on it is the centre, so the distance there is the length.
A hexagonal lattice is two rectangular lattices offset by half a cell, so the nearest centre is found by measuring against both and keeping the closer. No trigonometry and no loop.
fwidth measures one pixel in lattice units, which keeps the line the same weight at every cell count and every rotation.
One hash, one atan, a three-step loop over the spokes and a smoothstep per pixel. Measured with pnpm gputime rather than by timing the draw call.

near.description: The lighter cube colour, and the one a cube starts from.

far.description: The other cube colour, mixed in per cube so the wall is not one tone. The variation is in hue only: see `relief`.

line.description: The lattice lines, between cubes and across each one. A near-black with some of the cube hue still in it, because a true black line over a coloured face reads as a gap rather than as an edge.

cells.description: Cubes across the short edge. Few and large reads as architecture; past about fifteen the faces are too small to carry their own shading and the illusion goes with them.

rotation.description: Rotation of the lattice in degrees. Only sixty are worth having: a rhombille is unchanged by a third of a turn, and the three faces simply exchange roles.

thickness.description: Line width in lattice units. At 0 there are no lines and the cubes are held apart by their shading alone, which works and is quieter.

softness.description: Softness of the line edge, on top of the one pixel of antialiasing that is always there.

variation.description: How far the cube colour wanders from cube to cube. Kept low on purpose. The variation is in hue and the shading is identical on every cube, because agreement about where the light is coming from is the only thing telling the eye these are solids; push this up and a dark-hued cube's lit face ends up darker than a light-hued one's shadowed face, which is enough to flatten the whole wall into a pattern of diamonds.

relief.description: How far the three faces separate in tone. This is the illusion and almost nothing else is: at 0 the faces match, the solids flatten, and what is left is a pattern of diamonds. The shading is identical on every cube in the field on purpose, because agreement about where the light is coming from is the only thing telling the eye these are solids.

seed.description: Which cubes take which colour. Changes nothing else.

period.description: Seconds for one turn of the light. The loop closes exactly on it, because a whole turn of the light is the same light.

instruction: the light goes round the blocks

credit.what: The parameter set, and the choice of a rhombille tiling read as cubes. Their IsometricCubes names cells, thickness, rotation, softness and a per-cube colour variation, which is the right set. The tiling is a rhombille and the illusion is older than photography. The code here is this repo's own.
credit.author: Shader Effects Inc.

name: TypewriterText
description: Text typed on a machine with type bars: an uneven hand, a breath at the punctuation, and every letter struck a little off square

notes: No canvas and no WebGL. The string is already in the element and the untyped part is hidden rather than absent, so the line boxes are final from the first frame and a paragraph typing itself in the middle of a page does not push the page about
The rhythm is uneven. Each character takes its own interval from a hash, spread around the mean rather than added to it, so raising the unevenness does not also slow the whole thing down

It takes a breath at the punctuation: a full stop costs the full pause, a comma a third of it, a space an eighth. That pause is most of what makes typing sound like language rather than like a machine gun, and it is the one thing an even timer can never give you

Every letter is struck rather than placed. It lands a fraction off the baseline, a fraction off square, and with more or less ink depending on how it was hit. All three come off one hash of the letter's index, so the same string always types the same way and the recorder gets the same frames
The caret is solid while typing and blinks once it stops, which is what a caret does. The blink runs on its own clock rather than on the typing one, so it does not stutter when the rhythm does
One caret element for the whole string, moved to the cell the next character will land in. A caret per character is 2N elements for something only one of them is ever doing
The schedule is built from the text rather than from the clock, so seeking to the middle of a run costs one scan and the effect is pure in t
The original string stays in the accessibility tree as one label. The alternative is a label that grows a character at a time, which is a live region nobody asked for
destroy() puts the original text back, leaving the element as it was found

Only the letters whose state changed are touched, so typing writes about one style per frame rather than one per character per frame. On three hundred characters that is the difference between one frame and several
One offset read per frame, for the caret. Everything else is a composited transform and an opacity

pace.description: Average milliseconds between one character and the next. It multiplies by the length of the string, so a sentence at 62ms is about four seconds and a paragraph at 62ms is a minute. Heading slow, body fast: about 90 for a line somebody is meant to watch and about 25 for copy they are meant to read.

rhythm.description: How uneven the hand is. At 0 it is a machine, and an even typewriter is the single thing that gives away every version of this effect. Spread around the mean rather than added to it, so this does not change how long the run takes.

pause.description: Extra milliseconds after a full stop. A comma takes a third of it and a space an eighth. This is the setting that makes it read as somebody writing: at 0 the punctuation goes by at the same speed as the letters and the whole thing flattens.

hold.description: Milliseconds before the first character. Also how you stagger two of these: give the paragraph a hold long enough to let the heading finish.

jitter.description: How far off the baseline a letter lands, in ems, so it holds at any size. Small. A type bar is a mechanism with slack in it, not a drunk.

skew.description: How far off square a letter lands. Past about three degrees it stops reading as a machine with slack and starts reading as a ransom note.

ribbon.description: How much the ribbon varies: the ink a strike leaves. A worn ribbon gives an uneven page, and this is the difference between type that was struck and type that was set.

caret.description: Width of the caret, in ems. A real typewriter has no caret at all, so 0 is the historically honest setting and the one to use when the effect is standing in for a printed page rather than for a screen.

blink.description: Milliseconds for one blink, once typing has stopped. It runs on its own clock rather than on the typing one. Keep it slow: a fast blink is the fastest way to make a block of text hard to sit with.

seed.description: Seed for the rhythm and the strikes. The same seed always gives the same hand, so a recorded video and a live page match letter for letter. Change it to give two blocks of text on the same page two different typists.

reducedMotionTime.description: The single frame shown when the user prefers reduced motion. For a one-shot reveal this should be a time after the typing has finished, so the text simply appears. The strikes are still there in that frame, which is the nice part: the page looks typed rather than set.

instruction: press replay to type it again
intro:
TypewriterText types text one character at a time, on a machine with type bars
rather than a cursor that reveals a string.

The usual implementation animates the width of a box, or appends to a string on
a timer, and both have the same two faults: the rhythm is perfectly even, which
no typist has managed, and every letter lands exactly in place, which no
typewriter has managed either. The result is a progress bar made of letters.

Four things here instead, and all four are cheap.

**The rhythm is uneven.** Each character takes its own interval from a hash,
spread around the mean rather than added to it, so turning the unevenness up
does not also slow the run down.

**It takes a breath at the punctuation.** A full stop costs the full pause, a
comma a third of it, a space an eighth. This is most of what makes typing sound
like language rather than like a machine gun, and it is the one thing an even
timer can never give you.

**Each letter is struck rather than placed.** It lands a fraction off the
baseline, a fraction off square, and with more or less ink depending on how it
was hit. All three come off one hash of the letter's index, so the same string
always types the same way.

**The caret is solid while typing and blinks once it stops**, which is what a
caret does, on its own clock rather than on the typing one.

Nothing reflows. The whole string is in the element from the start and the
untyped part is hidden rather than absent, so a paragraph typing itself in the
middle of a page does not push the page about. The letters are invisible either
way, so it looks the same, and the layout is the one it will finish at.

name: VariableWeightText
description: Type that puts on weight under the cursor, on a line that does not move while it does

notes: Needs a variable font with the axis being driven. A static face ignores font-variation-settings without complaining, which is the one way this fails silently: the effect mounts, runs, and does nothing visible

The line does not move, and that is the whole item. A weight axis changes the advance width of every glyph it touches, so a line of individually weighted letters reflows continuously as the cursor crosses it: characters shuffle sideways, the line end breathes, and anything laid out after it moves too. That is why most versions of this only ever appear on a single centred word

Each character is measured once at the heaviest value the axis will reach, which is the widest it can ever be, and held in a box that wide with the letter centred in it. One measuring pass, and it is the difference between an effect you can put on a paragraph and one you can put on a word
The falloff has a shoulder rather than being linear. Pressure does not fall off in a straight line from a nib, and a linear ramp reads as a triangle of bold sliding along the line
The axis is a setting rather than a constant. Weight is the obvious one and the default, but a face with a width or a slant axis will do this just as well and only three strings change
The value is written to one decimal place. A weight axis quantised to a tenth is finer than any face resolves, and it stops the style being rewritten every frame for a change nothing can draw
Like every pointer effect here it eases against its own last frame, so it is deliberately not pure in t, and the recorder drives it from the scripted path in this file
The original string stays in the accessibility tree as one label, so a screen reader reads the sentence rather than the characters

One rect read and at most one style write per character per frame. The rects are the cost: they are read live so that a wrapped paragraph knows where its characters actually are, which is also what lets this work on more than one line
Keep it to a heading or a short paragraph. Three hundred characters is three hundred rects a frame, and at that length the effect is a smudge following the cursor anyway

axis.description: The variation axis to drive, spelled as the font declares it. Four lower-case letters for a registered axis: wght for weight, wdth for width, slnt for slant, opsz for optical size. A custom axis is upper case. Name one the face does not have and nothing happens, with no error anywhere.

rest.description: Where the axis sits with the cursor far away, which is to say what the text looks like to everybody who never moves a mouse over it. It should be the weight you would have set anyway.

peak.description: Where the axis goes directly under the cursor. Stay inside the range the face actually has: asking for 900 of a 400 to 700 font clamps to 700, so the effect quietly gets weaker as the cursor arrives rather than stronger.

reach.description: How far the hand reaches, as a share of the element's width. Relative, so the same setting works on a heading and on a column. Wide reaches read as the whole line breathing; narrow ones as a finger pressing on one letter.

shoulder.description: Shape of the falloff. 1 is linear, which reads as a triangle of bold sliding along the line and is the giveaway of every version of this. Higher keeps the peak tight and lets it fall away quickly, which is what pressure from a nib actually does.

ease.description: How fast the letters follow the hand, per frame. At 1 they are welded to the cursor, which looks like a bug rather than like ink. Paper takes a moment to give.

steady.description: Hold each character in a box as wide as its heaviest form. On, always, unless the face has no width change across the axis: a slant axis does not need it, and a weight axis absolutely does. Turn it off once on a paragraph to see why it is here.

tracking.description: Extra tracking. A little room stops the heaviest letters touching their neighbours, since every box is as wide as its own character needs and not as wide as the pair does.

instruction: move the pointer across the text
intro:
VariableWeightText makes type put on weight under the cursor. The hand presses,
the letters take more ink, and the line stays exactly where it was.

That last clause is the whole item, and it is why most versions of this only
ever appear on a single centred word.

A variable font's weight axis changes the **advance width** of every glyph it
touches. Go from 400 to 700 and the letters get wider, so a line whose letters
are individually weighted reflows continuously as the cursor crosses it:
characters shuffle sideways, the line end breathes, and anything laid out after
it moves too.

So each character is measured once at the heaviest value the axis will ever
reach, which is the widest it can ever be, and held in a box that wide with the
letter centred in it. One measuring pass, and after it nothing moves again. It
is the difference between an effect you can put on a paragraph and one you can
put on a word.

Two smaller things. The falloff has a shoulder rather than being linear, because
pressure does not fall off in a straight line from a nib and a linear ramp reads
as a triangle of bold sliding along the line. And the axis is a setting rather
than a constant: weight is the obvious one, but a width or slant axis works the
same way and only the strings change.

name: VoronoiCells
description: The plane divided by which scattered point is nearest, with the sites drifting so every border moves with them

notes: Nine cells is the whole search. Each site is jittered inside its own lattice cell and capped so it can never leave, so the nearest site to a pixel is in that pixel cell or one of the eight around it: nine hashes and nine distances, no list, no sorting and no texture.

The borders come from the second nearest site. Halfway between two sites the two distances are equal, so their difference goes to zero at the boundary, which is a usable distance to the edge for nothing. It is slightly wrong where three cells meet, by an amount nobody has noticed.
The wobble radius is capped just under a half. A site that crosses into its neighbour cell breaks the assumption the three by three search rests on, and the field tears along the lattice.
Nine hashes, nine distances and a smoothstep per pixel, with no loop over anything but the fixed three by three. Measured with pnpm gputime, which asks the GPU rather than timing the draw call.

near.description: Cell colour at the near end of the ramp.

mid.description: Cell colour through the middle. Between two colours a ramp gives one hue and a tint of it; passing through a third is what makes a field of flat cells read as lit from somewhere.

far.description: Cell colour at the far end.

edge.description: The borders between cells. Near-black with a little of the cell hue still in it, because a true black line across a saturated cell reads as a gap rather than as an edge.

cells.description: Cells across the short edge. Few and large reads as stained glass; past about twenty the borders are closer together than the cells are wide and it becomes a texture.

wobble.description: How far each site drifts from the middle of its own cell, in cell widths. Capped just under a half on purpose: a site that crosses into its neighbour cell breaks the nine-cell search and the field tears along the lattice. At 0 nothing moves, which costs nothing to draw and is a legitimate way to use it.

thickness.description: Border width, in lattice units. At 0 there are no borders and the cells are held apart by colour alone, which is quieter and entirely usable.

softness.description: Softness of the border, on top of the one pixel of antialiasing that is always there. A little helps more here than on a straight line, because a Voronoi border meets its neighbours at angles that are never the same twice.

depth.description: How much a cell darkens away from its own site. Just enough that a large cell does not read as a flat sticker; past about 0.4 it is a gradient competing with the borders for attention.

seed.description: Where every site sits and which cell takes which colour. Every value is a different field and none is better than another.

period.description: Seconds for one circuit of the sites. The loop closes exactly on it, because each site completes a whole turn of its own small circle in that time.

instruction: the sites drift and every border moves with them

credit.what: The parameter set and the pair of colours. Their Voronoi names two cell colours, a border, a scale, a seed and an edge intensity and softness, which is the right set, and the blue and magenta are theirs: far enough apart in hue to separate every cell from its neighbours without either reading as a highlight. The tessellation is Georgy Voronoy from 1908. The code here is this repo own.
credit.author: Shader Effects Inc.

name: WaterCaustics
description: The net of focused light on the floor of a pool, worked out from a wavy surface rather than drawn

notes: Nothing here draws a caustic. There is a height field and one step of optics: a ray through a surface of height h lands at p + d * grad(h) on a floor at depth d, and the brightness is one over the determinant of that mapping's Jacobian, which is the factor the area changed by. The filaments are where that determinant passes through zero and the mapping folds

Built that way so the caustics behave rather than merely look right. Deepen the water and they spread and brighten, because a longer throw focuses harder. Flatten the waves and they fade rather than thin. They close into cells because the zero set of a determinant is a closed curve, which is the part a hand-drawn version never gets

Eighteen waves, not six, and that is the whole difference between this and a plaid. A sum of a few plane waves is quasi-periodic however the directions and weights are chosen, so the caustics lay themselves out on a lattice: six gave columns, and reweighting them only changed which way the columns ran. Twenty-odd modes across a decade of wavelength is the smallest thing that stops reading as a pattern

The curvature is summed in quadrature, not plainly. Waves at independent phases add as the root of their number, so dividing by the plain sum flattens the surface as modes are added. Going from six waves to eighteen that way took the curvature down by about half and the caustics disappeared into an almost black frame, which reads as a broken shader rather than as the normalisation it was

Wave speeds follow deep-water dispersion, as the root of the wavelength, rounded to whole turns per period. Without it every mode drifts at one speed and the result reads as a moving photograph of water rather than as water. The rounding bends the dispersion by an amount nobody can see and removes a join everybody would

The Hessian is analytic. A wave contributes -k^2 (u (x) u) sin(phase), so the second derivative is one sine per wave with no finite differencing, which at this scale would be dominated by the sampling rather than by the surface

Filament width is measured against how fast the determinant is changing, with fwidth, so a line is the same number of pixels wide anywhere in the frame and at any resolution. A constant threshold gives hairlines where the field is slow and slabs where it is fast

The brightness is not normalised to a peak. Light is conserved, so a patch squeezed to a tenth of its area is ten times as bright, and tone-mapping that with 1 - exp(-x) is what makes the tight folds blow out. An early version divided by the softening width instead, which capped every filament at the same brightness and produced a contour map: even outlines with nothing bright inside them

The three channels focus at three depths, because water disperses and the short wavelengths bend further. That is the colour at the edge of a filament. At 0.22 it was three separate rings of red, green and blue and the thing read as a topographic map; the useful range is a few hundredths
Built for a dark ground and declared as one. Light added to deep water is the whole idea, and added light on paper is invisible
One full-screen triangle and eighteen sines. The cost is linear in `waves` and nothing else in the shader loops
Measured with `pnpm budget` at 1280 by 720: 1.1ms for a draw and a forced flush, against MeshGradient at 1.10 and MarbledPaper at 2.40 on the same run

0.230 mean absolute change per frame on a 0 to 255 scale, worst 0.244, against MarbledPaper at 0.166 and WindField at 0.104. The liveliest backdrop in the set and deliberately so: a caustic that does not shimmer is a photograph of one. `period` is the dial if that is too much, and the change is very close to linear in it

water.description: The water, which is what the floor looks like where no light is focused on it. Deep and desaturated: it is what the filaments are bright against, and a pale one leaves them nowhere to go.

light.description: The light added where the surface focuses it. Added rather than mixed, so the brightest cores overexpose towards white the way more light does, instead of desaturating towards this colour.

scale.description: Waves across the short side of the frame, for the longest wave. Low is a lazy pool at dusk and high is a chop. The rest of the spectrum is built up from this, so it sets the size of the whole web.

depth.description: How hard the surface focuses, which is the throw from the surface to the floor. At 0 nothing is focused and the floor is flat water. Below about 0.8 the determinant never reaches zero, so there are no filaments at all, only a mottle. Past about 3 it folds everywhere and the web breaks into noise, which is also what a real pool does in a chop.

waves.description: Modes in the surface, spread geometrically over about a decade of wavelength. This is the one that decides whether it reads as water. Below about ten the sum is quasi-periodic and the caustics arrange themselves on a visible lattice however the rest is tuned. It is also the whole cost of the shader.

thickness.description: Filament width in pixels, measured against the rate the determinant is changing, so it means the same thing anywhere in the frame and at any resolution.

exposure.description: How much light there is. The optics hand back an unbounded brightness and this is where it meets a screen that stops at white, so it sets how much of the web blows out rather than how bright the dim parts are.

contrast.description: Pulls the dim half down without touching the blown-out cores. The difference between light through a metre of water and light through a centimetre. Raise it to put text over this.

dispersion.description: Difference in focal depth between red and blue, as a share of depth. At 0 the net is monochrome. Keep it small: by about 0.2 the three channels have separated into their own rings and the thing reads as a topographic map rather than as light.

period.description: Seconds for one cycle. Every mode completes a whole number of turns in it, so the surface is exactly where it started and the loop has no join. This is also the dial for how busy the item is, and the change per frame is very close to linear in it.

heading.description: Which way the waves run. The directions fan out from here by the golden angle, so turning this turns the whole surface rather than rearranging it.

seed.description: Seed for the wave directions and phases. Two of these side by side want two seeds, or they are the same pool twice.

instruction: the surface moves on its own
intro:
WaterCaustics is the bright net of light on the floor of a swimming pool,
worked out rather than drawn.

Nothing in the shader draws a caustic line, and nothing knows where one is.
There is a wavy water surface and a floor some distance below it. Where the
surface happens to be concave it acts as a lens, squeezes a patch of light into
a smaller patch of floor, and the brightness there is however much the patch
shrank by. The net is what is left when you plot that.

name: WindField
description: The wind on a weather map, combed into streaks that travel along the flow, with the speed read as colour

notes: Line integral convolution, not a particle system. Each pixel walks a short way up the flow and a short way down it, samples a fixed noise field at each step, and sums those samples under a travelling kernel: along a streamline they agree and the pixel is bright, across the flow they disagree and cancel

That is not a stylistic choice. A particle's position depends on the one before it, so an advected field cannot be seeked, cannot be recorded, drifts on a dropped frame, and is wrong on the first frame after a resize, because the trail is feedback on the canvas. The page this was taken from runs fourteen thousand particles with a 0.07 erase per frame and there is no value of t you can ask it for

The streaks move because the kernel's phase moves, not because anything in the field is advected. `turns` is a whole number of turns over the period and is rounded in core.ts rather than trusted, because it is the one value that can stop the loop closing and it arrives from a prompt
Each system orbits its own home once per period, so the weather changes without the loop failing to come home
Field space is y from 0 to 1 and x across the aspect ratio, rather than uv. A system placed in uv is an ellipse on a wide canvas

Colour is a legend rather than a palette. Speed picks the hue through two interpolations, because a straight line between two colours gives one hue and a tint of it, and a chart like this is read by hue

Built for a dark ground and declared as one. The streaks are drawn by addition onto the ground, which is what lets them overlap without going muddy, and on paper that makes them brighter than the paper rather than darker

Four systems by default rather than eight. Eight small vortices read as a decorative swirl; four large overlapping ones read as a chart, because a real synoptic map is mostly one system's skirt running into another's
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes

Seven field evaluations each way, each followed by four noise samples taken in a straight line along the direction that evaluation gave. The field is what costs, and a streamline is locally straight over a couple of pixels, so the samples that make the combing are nearly free

The step has to be about one noise cell. Longer and consecutive samples are independent, which is static; much shorter and they are identical, which is smear. The first version stepped 7px through 7px cells and produced neither: it read as wet paint

Measured with `pnpm budget` at 1280 by 720: 2.0ms for a draw and a forced flush, against DustMotes at 1.6 on the same run. The comparison is the part to trust rather than the absolute: DustMotes read 0.7 earlier in the same session on the same machine, so these numbers drift with whatever else is running and are only worth anything beside a reference taken at the same time

0.104 mean absolute change per frame on a 0 to 255 scale, worst 0.125, sampled at six phases. It was 0.044 at a 36 second period; halving the period to 24 to get the take inside its media budget doubled it, which is the trade and is still inside the band a backdrop wants
maxDpr is capped at 1.5 rather than the usual 2. What it draws is noise at a cell of about two pixels, so the fourth sub-pixel is paid for and not seen
No textures, no buffers and no feedback. There is nothing to allocate between frames

A field of fine hard-edged noise is the case a codec has nothing to work with: there is no redundancy in it, so the settings that are generous for a photograph are extravagant here. The take is 24s at crf 40 and webmCrf 54 for that reason, and the first attempt at 36s and crf 34 came out 3832 kB against a 3500 limit

ground.description: The ground, and what shows where there is no wind. Dark, because the streaks are added onto it: that is what lets them cross each other without going muddy, and it is also why this item does not work on paper without inverting the idea.

calm.description: The slowest air, at the bottom of the ramp. Cool and close to the ground, so the still parts of the field recede and the fast parts are what you look at.

mid.description: The middle of the ramp. It exists so the ramp is read by hue rather than by lightness: a straight line from calm to strong gives one hue and a tint of it, which is the look of a gradient rather than of a chart.

strong.description: The fastest air, which in practice means the air close in around a system. Warm, because that is the convention every wind map uses and conventions are worth keeping where they cost nothing.

systems.description: How many pressure systems are in the field. Few and large reads as weather; many and small reads as decoration, because a real chart is mostly one system's skirt running into another's. This is also the main cost: the field is evaluated eighteen times per pixel and each evaluation walks this many systems.

drift.description: The prevailing wind across the frame, before any system touches it. At 0 the systems sit in dead air and the field has no direction, which is the single clearest way to make this look like a screensaver.

wander.description: How far each system travels from its home over a period, as a share of the height. Small: weather moves, but a backdrop that moves its structure around is a backdrop you keep looking at. At 0 the field is fixed and only the streaks travel, which is a legitimate and very quiet way to use this.

scale.description: Cell size of the noise the streaks are made of. It sets how coarse the combing is, and nothing else in here does. Large values give a few wide ribbons; small ones give fine hair, and below about 3 it starts to alias into sparkle.

length.description: How long a streak is. This is the distance the walk covers, so it is also how far the shader can see along the flow: long streaks follow a curve further and make the field legible, and past about 120 they start to straighten the tight air near a system centre into chords.

turns.description: Whole turns the streaks travel along the flow in one period. Whole, because a fraction means the loop never comes home, and core.ts rounds it rather than trusting it. With the default period of 36 seconds, 3 is a streak pattern that takes twelve seconds to repeat.

contrast.description: How hard the result is stretched away from its mean. Line integral convolution of a uniform field sits in a narrow band around the middle, so at 0 this is a flat wash with a hint of structure. Past about 0.8 the streaks go to hard black and white and the field stops reading as air.

seed.description: Seed for the systems: where they sit, which way they turn, how big and how strong. The same seed gives the same weather, so a recording and a live page agree streak for streak.

period.description: Seconds for one cycle. Long, because a backdrop has to survive being ignored: this is both how long a system takes to go round its home and the time in which the streaks make `turns` complete passes.

instruction: the wind runs on its own

credit.what: the field of named pressure systems behind the Wind Field Routing page, and the speed-as-colour ramp that goes with it. The method here is line integral convolution rather than fourteen thousand advected particles, because an advected field cannot be seeked
credit.author: Ray Velez

intro:
WindField is the wind on a weather map: a few pressure systems, a prevailing
drift, and the air between them combed into streaks that travel along the flow
with their speed read as colour.

It is **line integral convolution**, not a particle system, and that is the most
important thing about it.

name: WovenThreads
description: Cloth: warp one way, weft the other, and one of them on top at every crossing

notes: The interlacing is the item, and it is one comparison per crossing. Two sets of lines crossing is a grid: the threads pass through each other and the surface has no structure at all. The comparison is what turns it into cloth

Changing that comparison from alternating to shifting is the difference between plain weave and twill, and the diagonal appears in the surface the moment it does. That is why denim has a diagonal in it

The threads are round, shaded by their own cylindrical profile: the height across a cylinder is the root of one minus the square of the across-coordinate, and the slope of that is the normal. Flat threads are stripes
The thread that goes under is darkened where it passes beneath, which is the shadow of the one above it. Without it the interlacing reads as a hard edge rather than as depth

The cloth moves by having its threads wander along their length rather than by being translated, so the weave breathes the way fabric does when there is air in the room. A translated weave reads as a backdrop sliding past

Because the wander moves a thread's centre, the nearest thread is found from the undisplaced grid and then corrected by that thread's own offset. Exact for any wander under half a pitch, which is far more than cloth does
Two GLSL traps in one file: half is a reserved word and step is a builtin, and a variable named either fails at compile time rather than at run time
One WebGL2 context, one full-screen triangle, no buffers and no attributes
Measured at 0.035 mean absolute change per frame on a 0 to 255 scale and 1.23ms at 640 by 360, which makes it one of the quietest items here: the threads wander rather than travel
Four evaluations of a two-term wave, for the two threads and their index corrections, plus two square roots for the profiles. No textures, no noise and no render targets
The index correction is a branch rather than a loop, and it runs at most once per axis because the wander is bounded below half a pitch
Recorded at 15fps with a raised crf. A fine weave is high-frequency detail across the whole frame, and at 30fps the take was 5.6MB against a 3.5MB budget

ground.description: What shows between the threads. On an open cloth this is most of what you see, so it is doing as much work as either thread colour. Set it dark and a loose weave reads as mesh over a void.

warp.description: The threads running one way. Warp is the set held under tension on the loom, which is why it is the one that runs the length of a bolt.

weft.description: The threads running the other way, passed through the warp by the shuttle. Two slightly different colours is what makes the weave legible: identical ones give a surface whose structure you can only read from the shading.

pitch.description: Distance from one thread to the next, in CSS pixels. This is the count of the cloth: fine pitches read as a shirt, coarse ones as sacking or canvas. Below about 5 the shading of a round thread has nowhere to happen and the weave flattens into a check.

width.description: Thread width, as a share of the pitch. At 1 the cloth is closed and no ground shows; below about 0.6 it is a gauze and you are mostly looking at the gaps. Real cloth sits near the top of the range because a loom beats the weft up tight.

float.description: How many crossings a thread floats over before going under, which is the weave itself. 1 is plain weave, the alternating one. 2 and 3 are twills and bring a diagonal with them, which is the single most recognisable thing about denim. Past 4 the floats are long enough that the cloth reads as satin, shiny and structureless.

relief.description: How strongly the round threads are lit by their own profile. At 0 the cloth is flat colour and the weave is only readable as a pattern; this is what makes it read as made of something.

light.description: Where the light comes from. It falls differently on the two thread directions, since each is only lit across itself, so turning it shifts which set of threads is the brighter one. That is a real property of cloth and the reason fabric changes as you turn it.

crimp.description: How dark the thread underneath goes where it passes beneath. This is the shadow of the thread on top. At 0 the interlacing is a hard edge instead of depth, which is the difference between cloth and a woven-looking pattern.

wander.description: How far the threads wander from their lines, as a share of the pitch. Small: real cloth is regular, and this is the slack in it rather than a wave. At 0 it is a perfect machine weave, which is a legitimate and very still way to use this.

period.description: Seconds for one cycle of the wander. Long, because this is a surface and not an animation.

instruction: the threads wander on their own
intro:
WovenThreads is cloth. Warp threads one way, weft the other, and at every
crossing one of them is on top.

That last clause is the whole thing. Every version of this effect draws two sets
of lines crossing, which is a grid: the threads pass through each other and the
surface has no structure at all. What makes cloth cloth is the interlacing, and
the interlacing is **one comparison per crossing**.

Change that comparison from alternating to shifting and the weave changes with
it. `float: 1` is plain weave, the checkerboard. `float: 2` is a twill, and a
diagonal appears in the surface, which is the single most recognisable thing
about denim. Past four the floats are long enough that it reads as satin:
shiny, and structureless.

Two things besides.

**The threads are round.** Each is shaded by its own cylindrical profile: the
height across a cylinder is the root of one minus the square of the
across-coordinate, and the slope of that is the normal. Flat threads are
stripes.

**The thread underneath is darkened where it passes beneath**, which is the
shadow of the one above it. Without it the interlacing reads as a hard edge
rather than as one thread going under another.
